1asked 4×Still's life & motivation

When and where was A.T. Still born?

Ans: Still's birth → August 6, 1828 → Lee County, Virginia

Why: A.T. Still was born on August 6, 1828 in Jonesville, Lee County, Virginia. He lived from 1828 to 1917.

Heads up: One 2025 TA version keyed 'Aug 6, 1826 – Lee County, Virginia'. The course lecture gives Still's dates as 1828–1917, born in Lee County, VA, so 1828 is correct.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The other choices are other famous births: A is Elvis Presley (Tupelo), B is Abraham Lincoln (Kentucky), C is Michael Jackson (Gary, Indiana). Other versions of this question pair Virginia/1828 against Missouri or Kansas dates; Still moved to Missouri and Kansas later but was born in Virginia. His father Abram Still was a Methodist circuit-rider preacher and physician.

Explanation

3asked 9×2026Still's life & motivation

A.T. Still had some significant experiences that were influential in the development of osteopathy. Which of the following represents one of these influential experiences?

Ans: What drove Still → 1864 spinal meningitis killed 3 of his children → sought better medicine

Why: In February 1864, three of his children died of spinal meningitis despite the best medicine of the day. This loss drove Still to look for an alternative to orthodox (heroic) medicine.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A: his father Abram, not Still, was the missionary to the Shawnee in Kansas (Still helped him doctor at the Wakarusa Mission). B: Still was exposed to bonesetting ideas as an adult, not treated by a bonesetter as a child. C: at age 10 he relieved his own migraine by 'suspending the action of the great occipital nerve', not with magnetic healing. E: Baker University refused to let him teach his methods.

4Still's life & motivation

Why did A.T. Still develop the osteopathic approach?

Ans: Still's motivation → three children died of spinal meningitis → searched for a better way

Why: Still developed osteopathy after the tragic loss of 3 children to spinal meningitis, then spent about 10 years studying anatomy before announcing his approach.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A is wrong because Still taught that the physician does not cure disease; the physician removes structural impediments so the body can heal itself. C reverses the history: people were fed up with toxic and addictive drugs. D is also reversed: Still saw the neuromusculoskeletal system as an access point to the underlying physiology.

6Still's life & motivation

Which event led A.T. Still to question and ultimately sever all his ties to contemporary medical practice in the late 19th century?

Ans: Turning point → 1864 meningitis outbreak killed his children → rejected orthodox medicine

Why: The outcome of the 1864 meningitis outbreak, in which 3 of his children died, led Still to break from orthodox medicine.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A: Still served as a Civil War surgeon, but he wrote that the war 'left my family unharmed'; meningitis was the turning point. C: his apprenticeship under his father Abram was simply how he trained. D: calomel (mercury) was part of the heroic medicine he later rejected, but it was not the triggering event.

7Still's life & motivation

All of the following were influential to A.T. Still in developing osteopathy EXCEPT:

Ans: EXCEPT → Still rejected heroic medicine → 'preference' for it is false

Why: Still rejected heroic medicine (Benjamin Rush's bloodletting, purging and mercury). He did not prefer it.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A: the meningitis deaths of his children were the main trigger. C: at age 10 he relieved his own migraine by resting his neck, an early structure-function lesson. D: he trained by apprenticeship with his physician father. E: he was likely exposed to European bonesetting during the Civil War, and bonesetting is listed as an influence.

Medicine in the 1800s

No questions in this section match the current Show filter.

8asked 6×2026Medicine in the 1800s

After the Civil War in 1864, Still concluded that the orthodox medical practices of his day were frequently ineffective and often harmful. Which of the following was the main form of medicine practiced by physicians at the time?

Ans: Orthodox 1800s medicine → bloodletting, mercury purging, blistering → heroic medicine

Why: Heroic medicine, championed by Benjamin Rush, was the main form of medicine practiced by MDs. It used bloodletting and leeches, purging with mercury (calomel), blistering, and high doses of opium, alcohol and arsenic.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Homeopathy (A) was Hahnemann's 'like cures like' system, an alternative sect. Eclecticism (E) grew out of Samuel Thomson's herbal medicine, which also inspired naturopathy (B). Magnetic healing (C) was a fringe practice that influenced Still. None of these was the mainstream.

9Medicine in the 1800s

Which pairing of a type of medicine with its description is correct?

Ans: Benjamin Rush → depletion (purging, bloodletting, blistering) → heroic medicine

Why: Heroic medicine was advocated by Benjamin Rush: purging with mercury, bloodletting and leeches, blistering, and a focus on eliminating symptoms.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A is wrong because Samuel Thomson, the self-taught herbalist, founded Thomsonian medicine (eclecticism), not homeopathy. C is wrong because Samuel Hahnemann and the Law of Similars belong to homeopathy, not heroic medicine.

16asked 12×2026Schools, licensure & the AOA

The first state to license DOs was:

Ans: First DO licensure → 1896 → Vermont

Why: Vermont was the first state to license osteopathic physicians, in 1896.

Explanation & sources

1.5 · 6 questions · Questions 19–24

1918 flu & road to parity

No questions in this section match the current Show filter.

19asked 6×20261918 flu & road to parity

The Spanish Flu Pandemic of 1918 is significant in osteopathic history. Which of the following is a true statement regarding this pandemic?

Ans: 1918 OMT protocol → thoracic pump → increase lymphatic drainage

Why: The 1918 OMT influenza protocol aimed to increase lymphatic drainage via the thoracic pump. It also decreased the work of breathing and improved thoracic compliance.

Heads up: The 2026 IA1 poll shortened option E to 'Medical care had a 5% mortality for influenza cases', which by itself is close to the slide's 5–6%. The fuller wording used here (influenza cases that also developed pneumonia) is clearly false, and C matches the slide 'Increasing lymphatic drainage via thoracic pump', so C is the answer.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A understates the benefit: influenza mortality was 0.25% with osteopathic care vs 5–6% with standard care, far more than 50% less. B: it was H1N1, not H3N2. D: about 50–100 million people died (about 500 million infected). E: standard care had 33% mortality when pneumonia developed (vs 10% with osteopathic care); 5–6% was the figure for influenza alone.

201918 flu & road to parity

The treatment of patients during the Spanish Flu Pandemic in 1918 was influential for the development of osteopathy because:

Ans: 1918 flu → OMT patients had far lower mortality → boost for the profession

Why: Patients treated with OMT had much better outcomes: influenza mortality 0.25% and pneumonia mortality 10%, vs 5–6% and 33% with standard care.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

B is wrong because lymphatic techniques decrease, not increase, the work of breathing. C contradicts the data. D is wrong because pharmacology was not added to the osteopathic curriculum until 1929.

211918 flu & road to parity

The findings of the AMA committee that investigated education at schools of osteopathy included:

Ans: 1950s AMA committee → found DO schools equivalent → same admission requirements

Why: The 1955 AMA committee found that admission requirements were the same as MD schools. It concluded that osteopathic instruction could not be called 'cult healing'.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The real findings: clinical study time was the same (not less, B); 'pure medicine' was 90–95% of instruction (not 60–65%, C); standard medical texts were used (D); and instruction time was 25% higher (not lower, E), mostly from extra teaching on MSK disease and manipulation.

22asked 6×20261918 flu & road to parity

Which of the following events in osteopathic history was followed by a significant strengthening of the AOA and the opening of several new COMs?

Ans: After 1961 California merger → AOA fought back → new COMs from 1969 (MSUCOM)

Why: After the 1961 California merger, the remaining DOs and the AOA fought back and won (licensure restored in 1971; the 1962 law was struck down in 1974). New COMs then opened, starting with MSUCOM in 1969, the first new COM in 53 years.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A: the 1910 Flexner Report closed schools; only 5 of 8 osteopathic schools survived. B: adding pharmacology (1929) brought the curricula closer to MD schools but was not followed by a wave of new COMs. C: WWII helped DOs gain patients at home, since DOs could not serve as military physicians. E: the 1918 flu boosted the profession's reputation.

231918 flu & road to parity

A is the opposite: no new DOs could be licensed in California after the 1962 referendum. B describes the AMA's 1967 offer to transfer osteopathic students to MD schools, a separate event. C overstates it: existing DOs could keep practicing, but new DO licensure stopped until 1974.

25asked 7×2026Tenets & philosophy

Which of the following is NOT one of the principles of osteopathic philosophy?

Ans: Four tenets: unit, self-regulation, structure-function, rational treatment → homeostasis/allostasis balance isn't one

Why: The four tenets are: the body is a dynamic unit of function; it has self-regulatory, self-healing mechanisms; structure and function are interrelated; and rational treatment is based on these. A 'balance between homeostasis and allostasis' is not a tenet.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A, B, D and E are the four tenets almost word for word. C borrows physiology vocabulary to sound plausible. The tenet uses 'self-regulatory (homeostatic)', but there is no allostasis principle.

C (treating or suppressing symptoms) is the disease-oriented approach of heroic medicine. Osteopathy focuses on finding health and supporting the body's own healing.

AnswerBiomechanical = D; Behavioral = C; Respiratory-circulatory = E; Metabolic = A; Neurological = B

64asked 2×Planes & axes

Fill in the blanks: Flexion and extension occur in the ____ plane around the ____ axis. Side bending occurs in the ____ plane around the sagittal axis. Rotation occurs in the ____ plane around the ____ axis.

AnswerFlexion/extension: sagittal plane, transverse (frontal/lateral) axis. Side bending: frontal (coronal) plane, sagittal (A-P) axis. Rotation: horizontal (transverse) plane, vertical (longitudinal) axis.

Ans: Motion happens IN a plane, AROUND the axis perpendicular to it

Why: Each motion happens in one plane around the axis perpendicular to that plane: flexion/extension = sagittal plane, transverse axis; side bending = frontal plane, A-P axis; rotation = horizontal plane, vertical axis.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The naming trap: the frontal (lateral/transverse) axis runs side to side and is the axis for flexion. The frontal plane is the plane for side bending. Synonyms: frontal = coronal; horizontal = transverse plane; vertical = longitudinal axis; sagittal axis = A-P axis.

Headings: A. flexion and extension; B. neutral; C. rotation; D. rotation and sidebending; E. sidebending. Description: Normal motion of the vertebral segments in a sagittal plane.

Ans: Sagittal plane → forward/backward bending → flexion and extension

Why: Motion in the sagittal plane (about a transverse axis) is flexion and extension.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Neutral (B) is a range of sagittal positioning where Fryette's first principle applies, not a motion. Rotation (C) is about a vertical axis. Sidebending (E) is in the coronal plane about an A-P axis.

68asked 2×2026Planes & axes

For each description, select the physiologic motion most closely associated with it (each heading may be used once, more than once, or not at all). Headings: A. flexion and extension; B. neutral; C. rotation; D. rotation and sidebending; E. sidebending. Description: Motion of vertebral segments around a vertical axis.

Ans: Vertical (longitudinal) axis → turning motion → rotation

Why: Motion around the vertical (longitudinal) axis is rotation.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Flexion/extension (A) is about a transverse axis. Sidebending (E) is about an A-P axis in the coronal plane. D combines two motions and does not describe a single axis.

69Planes & axes

A passenger's driver hits the brakes quickly, and the passenger is thrown forward and backward against the seat. In which plane of motion was the passenger moving forward and backward?

Ans: Forward/back = flexion/extension → asks for PLANE → sagittal

Why: Forward and backward motion is flexion/extension, which occurs in the sagittal plane. The question asks for the plane, not the axis.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

If the question asked for the axis, the answer would be frontal. Horizontal (B) is the rotation plane. Frontal (C) is the side bending plane. Longitudinal (D) is an axis, not a plane.

  • 2023 TA Review - Written Exam 1 · TA review · slides 35-36
Lecture slide (1)
70Planes & axes

A skier leans forward to stick her tongue to a ski-lift bar, then yanks her head backward. Along which axis of motion was she moving forward and back?

Ans: Forward/back = flexion/extension → asks for AXIS → frontal (lateral) axis

Why: Flexion/extension moves around the frontal (lateral/transverse) axis, while the motion itself occurs in the sagittal plane.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Sagittal (A) is the plane, or the axis for side bending. Transverse (C) here would refer to the rotation plane. 'Y-axis' (D) is the vertical axis used for rotation.

71Planes & axes

A man on a ski lift turned to his right to look at someone, then turned back to the left and felt back pain. In which plane of motion was he moving?

Ans: Turning = rotation → horizontal (transverse) plane

Why: Turning is rotation, which happens in the horizontal (transverse) plane around the vertical axis.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Sagittal (B) is the flexion/extension plane. Frontal (C) is the side bending plane. D is a joke option.

75asked 2×Lateral gravity line

Which of the following is a landmark the plumb line is drawn through?

Ans: Lateral line → EAM, humeral head, L3, femoral head, behind mid-knee, anterior to malleolus → B closest

Why: The lateral line passes just anterior to the lateral malleolus (the ankle). B is the only option near a true landmark.

Heads up: The keyed option says 'anterior to the MEDIAL malleolus'. The 2026 slides and the TA's own slide note say just anterior to the LATERAL malleolus. B is still the intended answer because the other three options are clearly wrong.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A: the line passes through the external auditory meatus, not behind the ear canal. C: it passes just behind the mid-knee, not in front of the kneecap. D: it passes through the femoral head, not the lesser trochanter. The center of gravity is about 5 cm anterior to S2.

77Lateral gravity line

A plumb line (gravity line) is dropped along the lateral side of a standing patient. Which physical landmark is a correct point of lateral symmetry?

Ans: Lateral line points → femoral head is on the list → D

Why: The femoral head is one of the points of lateral symmetry.

Each other option is a near miss: A should be the external (not internal) auditory meatus; B should be the humeral head (not the greater tuberosity); C should be the middle of L3 (not L5); E should be just anterior (not posterior) to the lateral malleolus.

A patient comes to your OMM clinic concerned about their posture. You use a plumb line to look at their landmarks. Which of the following findings are a sign of postural misalignment?

Ans: Normal: just BEHIND mid-knee, just ANTERIOR to lateral malleolus → C and E deviate

Why: Normally the line passes just behind the mid-knee and just anterior to the lateral malleolus. A line anterior to the knee (C) or posterior to the lateral malleolus (E) both mean misalignment.

Heads up: The TA key marks only C. E (just posterior to the lateral malleolus) also contradicts the slide's landmark list (just ANTERIOR to the lateral malleolus), and the stem asks which findings 'are' signs, so C and E are both correct.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A (middle of L3), B (external auditory meatus) and D (humeral head) are normal landmarks.

79asked 7×2026Lateral gravity line

In the assessment of this patient using the lateral gravity line, which landmark shows the most deviation?

Ans: Compare to ideal line: head/ear far forward of the line (and lumbar region off) → EAM most deviated

Why: The line should pass through the external auditory meatus, but this patient's head and ear sit well forward of it, which is the most obvious deviation. The 2026 answer slide also accepts the L3 vertebral body, where the lumbar curve falls off the line.

Heads up: The 2026 IA2 poll marks both B and D green. Earlier years (2021–2025 clickers) key B only. If an exam version allows only one answer, choose B (external auditory meatus).

The ankle (A) is in its normal place, just in front of the line. The femoral head (C) is close to the line. S2 (E) is not a lateral line landmark; the body's center of gravity sits about 5 cm anterior to S2.

If all plumb line points are anterior to the gravity line, this means the patient has…

Why: When the whole body leans forward of the line, this is anterior postural deviation, and weight is supported by the metatarsals.

82Static landmarks

The doctor then asks the patient to turn around and observes her posteriorly. What posterior landmarks are being used? (Select all that apply.)

Ans: Posterior line: inion, vertebral midline, sacral midline, coccyx midline, midway between both malleoli

Why: The posterior symmetry line runs through the inion, the midline of the vertebrae, the midline of the sacrum, the midline of the coccyx, and a point midway between both malleoli.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A is wrong: the apex of the coronal suture is a lateral line landmark; posteriorly you use the inion. C is wrong as written: the point is midway between the two ankles (left and right malleoli), not between the lateral and medial malleolus of one ankle.

During an osteopathic exam you review the anatomical landmarks of the spine. Which of the following landmarks is incorrect?

Ans: Angle of Louis = T4, not T5 → C is incorrect

Why: The angle of Louis is at T4, not T5.

86Static landmarks

Match each landmark with its vertebral level: spine of scapula; suprasternal notch; xiphoid process; inferior angle of the scapula; angle of Louis. Choices: A. Anterior to T9; B. Anterior to T4; C. Aortic arch lies superior; D. T7; E. T3; F. Vertebral body of T2. (One landmark has two correct answers.)

AnswerSpine of scapula = E (T3); suprasternal notch = F (T2 body); xiphoid = A (anterior to T9); inferior angle of scapula = D (T7); angle of Louis = B and C.

Ans: Scapula spine T3 → notch T2 → Louis T4 → inferior angle T7 → xiphoid T9

Why: Functional landmarks: spine of scapula = T3, suprasternal notch = T2 body, angle of Louis = anterior to T4 (aortic arch just superior), inferior angle of scapula = T7, xiphoid = anterior to T9.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Also know that the iliac crest marks the L4-L5 interspace and that the 12th rib can be followed to T12. Somatic dysfunction and group curves can shift these landmarks.

90Spinal curves & development

Fill in the blank (development of spinal curves): Birth: whole spine is kyphotic/lordotic/neutral. 13 months: lumbar spine is kyphotic/lordotic/neutral. 3 years: lumbar kyphosis/lordosis begins to appear. 8 years: lumbar kyphosis/lordosis is obvious. 10 years: clear adult stance (cervical, thoracic, lumbar = ?).

AnswerBirth: kyphotic. 13 months: lumbar neutral. 3 years: lumbar lordosis begins. 8 years: lumbar lordosis obvious. 10 years: adult stance (cervical lordosis, thoracic kyphosis, lumbar lordosis).

Ans: Kyphotic C-curve → lumbar neutral (13 mo) → lordosis appears (3 y) → obvious (8 y) → adult (10 y)

Why: The spine starts as one kyphotic C-curve, the lumbar spine becomes neutral by 13 months, lordosis appears by 3 years, is obvious by 8, and the adult stance is clear by about 10 years.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Adult curves alternate: cervical lordosis, thoracic kyphosis, lumbar lordosis, sacral kyphosis.

91Spinal curves & development

Match the development of the spinal curves with when they occur (Birth, 13 months, 3 years, 8 years, 10 years): A. Lordosis obvious; B. Lumbar spine neutral; C. Whole spine is a C-curve; D. Clear adult stance; E. Lordosis begins to appear.

AnswerBirth = C; 13 months = B; 3 years = E; 8 years = A; 10 years = D

Ans: C-curve at birth → neutral 13 mo → lordosis begins 3 y → obvious 8 y → adult 10 y

Why: Order: C-curve at birth, lumbar neutral at 13 months, lordosis begins at 3 years, lordosis obvious at 8 years, adult stance at 10 years.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

This matching set uses the same timeline as the fill-in-the-blank version, so learn it once as a sequence.

92asked 3×Spinal curves & development

What could produce these disorders? Name some causes of each of these postural deviations: kyphosis, lordosis and scoliosis.

AnswerKyphosis: osteoporosis, compression fracture, depression, ankylosing spondylitis. Lordosis: pregnancy, obesity, high heels. Scoliosis: unequal muscle use (e.g., carrying a bag), unequal growth, short leg, genetics.

Ans: Kyphosis → bone loss/fracture/mood; lordosis → anterior load (pregnancy, obesity, heels); scoliosis → asymmetry

Why: Kyphosis: osteoporosis, compression fracture, depression, rheumatologic disease such as ankylosing spondylitis. Lordosis: pregnancy, obesity, high heels. Scoliosis: unequal muscle use, unequal growth, short leg, genetics.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Lordosis causes share one idea: weight carried in front (or heels tipping the pelvis) pulls the lumbar curve deeper. Short leg as a cause of functional scoliosis returns in Week 5.

102Postural types

What are characteristics of the military-bearing posture? (Select all that apply.)

Ans: Military: head back, chest elevated, ↑ lordosis, anterior tilt, knees extended, ankles plantar flexed

Why: Military bearing: head tilted posteriorly, chest elevated with anterior cervical and posterior thoracic deviation, increased lumbar lordosis, anterior pelvic tilt, knees extended, ankles plantar flexed.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

C, D and F are each reversed: the lumbar lordosis is increased, the pelvis tilts anteriorly, and the ankles are plantar flexed (not dorsiflexed).

103Postural types

Match each description to the correct posture (flat back, military-bearing, anterior postural deviation, swayback, posterior postural deviation): (1) body deviates anteriorly, weight supported by the metatarsals; (2) increased cervical lordosis, slight upper thoracic kyphosis, flattening in the lower thoracic and lumbar spine; (3) anterior cervical and posterior thoracic deviation, increased lumbar lordosis, anterior pelvic tilt, ankles plantar flexed; (4) body deviates posteriorly, balance kept by anterior thrust of the pelvis, increased lordosis from the mid-thoracic spine down; (5) increased cervical and thoracic curves, decreased lumbar lordosis, posterior pelvic tilt, hyperextended hips and knees.

AnswerFlat back = 2; Military-bearing = 3; Anterior postural deviation = 1; Swayback = 5; Posterior postural deviation = 4

Ans: Metatarsals → anterior; flat lumbar → flat back; plantar flexion → military; pelvic thrust → posterior; hyperextension → sway

Why: Key features: anterior deviation = weight on the metatarsals; flat back = flattened lumbar curve; military = chest up, increased lordosis, ankles plantar flexed; posterior deviation = anterior pelvic thrust; swayback = decreased lordosis, hyperextended hips and knees.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Swayback and posterior deviation both push the pelvis forward. Swayback has a decreased lumbar curve, while posterior deviation has marked lordosis from the mid-thoracic spine down.

104asked 7×2026Muscles in posture

You are examining a patient with the posture pictured in this diagram. Which muscle(s) would you expect to be hypertonic?

111Muscles in posture

Hypertonic muscles can cause asymmetry. What muscles would be hypertonic in a flat back compared with a sway back postural alignment?

AnswerFlat back: rectus abdominis and glutei (psoas is long and weak). Sway back: rectus abdominis, hamstrings, TFL/ITB.

Ans: Flat back tight: RA + glutei; sway back tight: RA + hamstrings + TFL

Why: Flat back hypertonic: rectus abdominis and glutei; weak: back extensors, multifidus, iliacus and psoas. Sway back hypertonic: rectus abdominis, hamstrings, TFL/ITB; weak: obliques, iliopsoas, multifidus, thoracic extensors, glutei.

Heads up: The TA key lists the psoas as hypertonic in flat back, following the original slide. The 2026 Canvas correction says the flat-back psoas is long and weak, so it is left out here.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The rectus abdominis is tight in both. The glutei are the key difference: tight in flat back, weak in sway back.

112Muscles in posture

Bonus: Which posture would present with tight hamstrings? Which with weak abdominal muscles?

AnswerTight hamstrings: sway-back (posterior pelvic tilt; also rectus abdominis and TFL tight). Weak abdominals: lordotic (kyphosis-lordosis) posture with anterior pelvic tilt and tight hip flexors and lumbar extensors.

Ans: Hamstrings pull pelvis into posterior tilt → sway-back; weak abs let pelvis tip forward → lordotic

Why: Tight hamstrings pull the pelvis into posterior tilt, as in sway-back. Weak abdominals let tight hip flexors tip the pelvis into anterior tilt, the lordotic (kyphosis-lordosis) pattern.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

From the postural table: lordotic posture has shortened lumbar extensors and hip flexors with weakened abdominals; sway-back has weakened lower abdominals and shortened hip extensors.

Definition & TART

113asked 5×Definition & TART

Which of the following best defines somatic dysfunction?

Ans: Somatic dysfunction → impaired/altered function of somatic framework → D

Why: Somatic dysfunction is an impaired or altered function of related components of the somatic framework: skeletal, arthrodial and myofascial structures plus their related vascular, lymphatic and neural elements.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

B is the definition of the red reflex (erythema test), not of somatic dysfunction. A is wrong because the sympathetic response in SD causes vasoconstriction, not vasodilation. C describes the freedom of motion, which is how an SD is named, not what an SD is. The term 'somatic dysfunction' replaced 'osteopathic lesion' in 1968.

114asked 3×Definition & TART

What does TART stand for?

AnswerTissue texture change, Asymmetry, Restriction of motion, Tenderness.

Ans: TART → the four objective findings used to diagnose somatic dysfunction

Why: TART lists the objective findings that diagnose somatic dysfunction: Tissue texture change, Asymmetry, Restriction of motion, Tenderness.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The letter order varies between sources (some start with Tenderness), but the four findings are always the same. Common wrong substitutions are 'Atrophy' for Asymmetry and 'Redness' for Restriction. The red reflex is a special test, not a TART criterion.

What is the correct form of the TART acronym?

Explanation & sources

Any option with 'Atrophy' or 'Redness' is wrong. Redness belongs to the red reflex test, and atrophy is not one of the four criteria. B and D are identical distractors that both swap in Redness.

Which of these is not correctly categorized as a TART sign?

Why: The R in TART is Restriction of motion. The red reflex is a separate special test used to judge acute vs chronic SD.

Tenderness, asymmetry and tissue texture change are all TART criteria. Normal skin gets initial redness that fades quickly; lingering redness suggests acute SD and early blanching suggests chronic SD.

Full range of motion is the opposite of the R (restriction). Inflammation and arthritis are diagnoses, not palpatory TART criteria. Warmth, edema and bogginess are examples of tissue texture change.

120Definition & TART

True or false when referring to a somatic dysfunction? Patients can only have one SD per body part.

Ans: Type II can sit inside a Type I curve → multiple SDs possible → False

Why: A region can have more than one SD at once. A classic example is a Type II dysfunction at the apex or end of a Type I group curve.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Because Type II and Type I can coexist, you must decide which to treat first. The course rule is to treat the Type II dysfunction before the Type I curve.

121Definition & TART

True or false when referring to a somatic dysfunction? The body can compensate for them after a while.

Ans: Long-standing SD → body adapts → compensation elsewhere → True

Why: Over time the body compensates for an SD. Chronic SD typically shows asymmetry with noticeable compensation in other areas.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Acute SD tends to be segmental without much compensation yet. Type I group curves are often compensatory, forming gradually.

122Acute vs chronic

You palpate a patient's paraspinal muscles and notice bogginess, edema, tenderness, and warmth. Which best describes this dysfunction?

Ans: Boggy, edematous, tender, warm → acute tissue findings → A

Why: Boggy, edematous, warm and more tender tissue is the acute pattern.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Chronic SD feels cool, dry, ropy/fibrotic and less tender. Type I and Type II describe spinal mechanics, not tissue quality. A viscerosomatic reflex can produce acute-looking changes, but the question asks what describes the palpatory finding itself.

123asked 3×Acute vs chronic

What changes take place in an acute somatic dysfunction?

Ans: Acute → inflammation, fluid → boggy, edematous, congested → C

Why: Acute SD tissues are boggy, edematous and congested from the vascular and chemical changes of injury.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Cool dry skin (A), mushy/flaccid/ropy muscle (B) and common somatovisceral effects (D) are all chronic findings. In acute SD somatovisceral effects are minimal.

124asked 2×2026Acute vs chronic

A 50-year-old male with no history of low back pain presents with acute low back pain after gardening for several hours yesterday. Structural examination reveals tissue texture changes to the right lumbar paraspinal region. Which of the following would most likely be appreciated at this time?

Why: Acute SD musculature shows hypertonicity, along with warm moist skin, boggy edema and sharp pain.

125Acute vs chronic

Your gym friend is complaining about muscle pain and asks you for help. You begin with palpation and decide that it is an acute change. How would you describe an acute change in musculature?

Ans: Acute → warm (inflamed) + boggy (edema) → C

Why: Acute tissue is warm and boggy.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Cold, firm, mushy and dry are chronic descriptors. E mixes a chronic temperature (cold) with an acute texture (boggy). Remember: acute = warm, moist, boggy, red; chronic = cool, dry, ropy, fibrotic.

Why: Rubor (redness) reflects the inflammatory, vasodilated state of acute SD.

127asked 7×2026Acute vs chronic

What changes take place in chronic somatic dysfunctions?

Ans: Chronic → fibrosis replaces muscle → contracture with decreased tone → E

Why: In chronic SD, fibrotic tissue replaces contractile muscle, producing contracture (fixed shortening) with decreased tone that feels mushy, ropy and fibrotic.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Warmth, sharp pain and boggy edema are acute findings. Chronic muscle is not hypertrophied; tone is decreased. Chronic ROM is limited because of the contracture or fibrosis.

129asked 2×2026Acute vs chronic

130Acute vs chronic

A 22-year-old male presents with a 7-month history of right-sided back pain that worsens after prolonged standing. On exam, you find tissue texture changes including cool temperature, ropy and fibrotic consistency, and decreased tenderness over the right paraspinal muscles. Which of the following best describes the pain associated with this type of somatic dysfunction?

Ans: 7 months + cool, ropy, less tender → chronic → dull ache → A

Why: Chronic SD pain is a dull ache (sometimes burning), less intense than acute pain.

Explanation

Sharp, severe pain is acute. Throbbing and radiating pain are not the textbook SD descriptors. Burning appears in some chronic lists but 'radiating' suggests nerve root pain.

133Acute vs chronic

Which of the following are correctly matched between acute/chronic somatic dysfunctions and their findings? (There may be more than one correct.)

Ans: Sharp pain + hypertonia = acute; mushy, ropy, low tone = chronic → A and F

Why: Acute SD has sharp, severe pain with hypertonic muscle. Chronic SD has decreased tone that feels mushy, fibrotic and ropy.

134Acute vs chronic

Compare and contrast acute vs chronic somatic dysfunction findings: tenderness, tissue texture changes, moist or dry, temperature, red reflex/erythema test.

AnswerAcute: more tender; hypertonic, boggy, edematous; moist; warm; redness lingers. Chronic: less tender; atrophic, fibrotic, ropy; dry; cool; early blanching.

Ans: Acute = inflamed (warm, wet, boggy, red) vs chronic = fibrosed (cool, dry, ropy, blanching)

Why: Acute findings come from inflammation (vasoactive mediators, edema). Chronic findings come from long-standing sympathetic vasoconstriction and fibrosis.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Learn the table as two pictures rather than isolated facts. Acute pain is sharp and severe; chronic pain is a dull ache. Somatovisceral effects are minimal in acute SD and common in chronic SD.

135Acute vs chronic

Match each finding to acute or chronic somatic dysfunction: A. Boggy on palpation; B. Doughy on palpation; C. Dull ache, burning pain; D. Sharp, severe pain; E. Skin is scaly and dry; F. Skin has an acute red reflex; G. Fibrotic; H. Congested soft tissue.

AnswerAcute: A, D, F, H. Chronic: B, C, E, G.

Ans: Boggy/sharp/red/congested → acute; doughy/dull/scaly/fibrotic → chronic

Why: Acute: boggy, sharp severe pain, acute red reflex, congested (edematous) soft tissue. Chronic: doughy, dull ache, scaly dry skin, fibrosis.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The tricky pair is boggy vs doughy: boggy is acute edema, doughy is chronic congestion from a poor lymphatic pump. 'Congested soft tissue' is listed with boggy and edematous on the acute side of the course table.

136Acute vs chronic

Match each finding with acute or chronic somatic dysfunction: edematous/erythematous/boggy tissues; increased tissue moisture, warmth; hypertonic muscles; painful restriction with movement; severe and sharp tenderness; cool, dry skin with slight tension; decreased or no edema; decreased muscle tone, flaccid, fibrotic, ropy; restriction with decreased or no pain; dull, achy, or burning tenderness.

AnswerAcute: edematous/erythematous/boggy; moist, warm; hypertonic; painful restriction; sharp severe tenderness. Chronic: cool dry skin; little or no edema; decreased tone, flaccid, fibrotic, ropy; painless restriction; dull, achy, burning tenderness.

Ans: First five findings → acute; last five findings → chronic

Why: The list splits cleanly: the first five are acute (inflamed, painful) and the last five are chronic (cool, fibrotic, less painful).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Restriction occurs in both, but acute restriction is painful while chronic restriction has little or no pain. Muscle tone is increased (hypertonic) in acute and decreased in chronic SD.

137Acute vs chronic

Label the following somatic dysfunction findings as acute or chronic: sharp severe pain with hypertonic musculature; dull ache, burning pain; tissue congestion, doughy tissues, poor lymphatic pump; skin warm, moist, acute red reflex; boggy, edematous, congested soft tissue; common to have somatovisceral effects; sluggish mobility; limited ROM due to contracture or fibrosis; skin cool, dry, scaly, pale, itchy, pigmentation change; decreased muscle tone, mushy/flaccid, ropy, fibrotic.

AnswerAcute: sharp pain with hypertonia; warm moist skin with red reflex; boggy edematous tissue; sluggish mobility. Chronic: dull/burning ache; doughy congestion; common somatovisceral effects; contracture-limited ROM; cool dry scaly skin; decreased tone, ropy.

Ans: Inflamed, sluggish → acute; doughy, fibrotic, visceral effects → chronic

Why: Sluggish mobility (range not always restricted) is acute, while ROM limited by contracture or fibrosis is chronic. Somatovisceral effects are common in chronic and minimal in acute SD.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Acute red reflex: local bradykinin and histamine override sympathetic vasoconstriction, so redness lingers. Chronic red reflex: initial redness then blanching before the surrounding skin.

Red reflex

138asked 3×Red reflex

A new 22-year-old patient presents for a comprehensive history and physical. If the patient has a history of scoliosis, diagnosed at age 10, what would their red reflex look like?

Ans: 12-year history → chronic → early blanching → D

Why: A 12-year-old problem is chronic, and the chronic red reflex is initial redness followed by blanching before the surrounding skin.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Lingering redness indicates acute SD, so B pairs the wrong response with chronic. A and C pair the responses with acute. Chronic blanching comes from long-standing hypersympathetic vasoconstriction and fibrosis.

139Red reflex

A patient presents with shortness of breath due to COPD. He has been smoking 1 pack a day for the last 30 years. You perform a red reflex test on his back as part of your osteopathic examination. What do you expect to find?

Ans: 30-year COPD → chronic viscerosomatic changes → only chronic option = fibrotic, ropy → C

Why: Long-standing COPD produces chronic segmental changes, and flaccid, fibrotic, ropy musculature is the only chronic finding offered.

Heads up: None of the options describes the chronic red reflex itself (redness, then early blanching). The key picks C because it is the only chronic finding listed.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Prolonged redness (B) is the acute red reflex. Sharp pain, boggy tissue and minimal somatovisceral effects are all acute findings. The true chronic red reflex result would be early blanching.

1402026Red reflex

A 34-year-old patient presents with acute thoracic back pain after lifting a heavy box. During physical examination, the physician runs a firm stroke with two finger pads along the paravertebral area (Red Reflex / Erythema Test). The test results in sustained, exaggerated redness in the T4–T6 region that lasts significantly longer than surrounding tissues. Which underlying mechanism best accounts for this palpatory finding?

Ans: Acute SD + lingering redness → local bradykinin/histamine override vasoconstriction → C

Why: In acute SD, bradykinin, histamine and other vasoactive mediators cause local hyperemia. The region is facilitated, so it overreacts to slight irritation and redness lasts longer.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A, B, D and E describe chronic mechanisms: long-standing sympathetic vasoconstriction, fibrosis, poor lymphatic pump and blanching. Sympathetic outflow is increased in acute SD too, but the local mediators override it.

Barriers

No questions in this section match the current Show filter.

141asked 2×2026Barriers

A 20-year-old female presents for a general maintenance examination without complaints. Structural examination is negative for somatic dysfunction. The patient without a cervical somatic dysfunction actively sidebends her cervical spine to an endpoint of 45 degrees. This limit is most appropriately described as the

Ans: Active motion limit, no SD → physiologic barrier → C

Why: The physiologic barrier is the limit of active (patient-generated) motion.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The anatomic barrier is the limit of passive motion set by bone and ligament. The elastic barrier is the zone of passive stretch between the physiologic and anatomic barriers. A restrictive barrier requires somatic dysfunction, which this patient lacks. 'Rotational barrier' is not a term.

Asked in

  • 2026 Textbook - The Basics (Ch. 1 Review Questions) · Textbook chapter questions · TB_Basics.pdf p.13 Q7 (answer key p.17)
  • 2026 Textbook Q&A Compilation - The Basics · Textbook chapter questions · slide 13 (answer slide 14); textbook TB_Basics.pdf p.13 Q7
Lecture slide (1)
1422026Barriers

A physician performs passive motion testing on a patient's lumbar spine. Movement toward left sidebending meets a firm end-feel prior to reaching the expected limit of active movement, significantly shortening the patient's available range of motion. Passive movement beyond this newly encountered barrier is impossible without causing tissue damage. How should this new limit to motion be classified?

Ans: Early abnormal stop inside the active range → restrictive barrier → C

Why: A restrictive barrier is an early, abnormal stop caused by somatic dysfunction that lies before the physiologic barrier. It is what OMT treats.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The anatomic barrier lies beyond the physiologic barrier, not before it, even though the stem's tissue-damage wording sounds anatomic. The physiologic barrier is the normal end of active motion. Neutral point shifting and hypermobility are not barrier types. A pathologic barrier (permanent stop from tissue disease, spurs or joint damage) is not offered.

Asked in

  • 2026 Textbook Q&A Compilation - Somatic Dysfunction Practice Questions · Practice questions · slide 147 (answer slide 148)
Lecture slide (1)
1432026Barriers

A 22-year-old female presents to the office with the complaint of sharp, non-radiating pain at the base of her neck. She reports that she was a seatbelt-restrained driver in a motor vehicle accident 2 weeks ago and that she hit her head against the steering wheel. She denies any numbness, weakness, or paresthesias. Physical examination reveals that the patient can actively rotate her head 65° to the left and 75° to the right, limited by pain. The type of barrier that is most likely disrupted in this patient is

Ans: Active ROM reduced → normal physiologic barrier disrupted → restrictive barrier created → D

Why: Active motion ends at the physiologic barrier. When somatic dysfunction occurs, that normal barrier is disrupted and a restrictive (or pathologic) barrier is created in its place.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Restrictive and pathologic barriers are what is created, not what is disrupted. An anatomic barrier disruption would mean torn ligament or fracture, and she has no neurologic signs. The elastic barrier is a passive zone that is not tested by active rotation.

Asked in

Lecture slide (1)
144Barriers

Match each to A. Anatomical barrier, B. Physiological barrier, C. Restrictive barrier: (1) How far you can forward bend (or bend your knee) without an SD; (2) Limited by ligaments and bones; (3) How far you can sidebend your neck to the right after tweaking it.

Answer1-B (physiologic, springy end-feel); 2-A (anatomic, hard end-feel, e.g. olecranon in elbow extension); 3-C (restrictive).

Ans: Normal active limit = physiologic; bone/ligament limit = anatomic; SD limit = restrictive

Why: Physiologic = normal limit of active motion. Anatomic = absolute passive limit set by bones and ligaments. Restrictive = early stop caused by somatic dysfunction.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Order from neutral outward in a healthy joint: physiologic barrier, then the elastic zone, then the anatomic barrier. An SD adds a restrictive barrier inside the physiologic range.

145asked 3×Fryette's principles

Fryette's principles define Type 1 Mechanics as:

Ans: Type 1 → neutral, sidebending first, rotation opposite → A

Why: Type I: from neutral, sidebending precedes rotation and rotation goes to the opposite side, involving two or more segments.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

B and C describe Type II dysfunction (traumatic, non-neutral). D is Fryette's third principle. In Type I, disc compression on the sidebent side pushes disc material to the other side, which rotates the bodies opposite.

146asked 2×Fryette's principles

Which of the following statements concerning Fryette's law I is true?

Ans: Law I = neutral → sidebending and rotation opposite → C

Why: Fryette's first law: in neutral, sidebending and rotation occur to opposite sides.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A is Law II (non-neutral, same side), not Law I. B wrongly pairs opposite-side coupling with flexion. D pairs neutral with same-side coupling, which mixes up the two laws.

147Fryette's principles

A 25-year-old man presents with low back stiffness after sitting at his desk for long hours. On exam, when his lumbar spine is in a neutral position, you notice that as you side bend him to the right, the spinous processes rotate toward the left. Which of Fryette's principles does this describe?

Ans: Neutral + sidebending with opposite rotation (intended) → Law I → A

Why: The question intends neutral coupling with rotation opposite the sidebending, which is Fryette's Law I.

Heads up: Wording flaw: if the spinous processes go left, the bodies rotate right, the same side as the sidebending. The TA key still marks Law I because the stem says neutral and means opposite-side coupling.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Law II requires a flexed or extended (non-neutral) spine, as in an acute lifting injury. Law III says motion in one plane reduces motion in the other planes. Rotation is named for the anterior vertebral body, so spinous processes move opposite to the named rotation.

148Fryette's principles

A 40-year-old woman presents with acute back pain after lifting a heavy box. Exam shows that when her lumbar spine is flexed, sidebending her to the right is accompanied by rotation to the right as well. Which Fryette's law best explains this coupled motion?

Ans: Flexed (non-neutral) + same-side coupling → Law II → B

Why: Fryette's Law II: in a non-neutral (flexed or extended) spine, rotation and sidebending occur to the same side.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Law I is neutral with opposite-side coupling. Law III states that motion in one plane reduces motion in the other planes. Acute lifting injuries typically produce Type II dysfunctions.

149asked 2×2026Fryette's principles

A 20-year-old female presents for a general maintenance examination without complaints. Structural examination is negative for somatic dysfunction. The examiner evaluates the physiologic motion of T3 on T4. Which of the following most accurately describes this segment's Fryette Type 2 mechanics?

Ans: Type 2 → sufficiently flexed/extended → same-direction coupling → E

Why: Type II mechanics: with sufficient flexion or extension, a single segment sidebends and rotates to the same side (rotation into the concavity).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A is Fryette's third principle. B correctly describes Type I, not Type II. C and D mismatch the position and the coupling direction.

Which of these Fryette's Principles are correctly matched?

Explanation & sources

A gives the third principle's text with the label 'first'. C gives the first principle's text with the label 'third'. Order: 1 = neutral/opposite, 2 = non-neutral/same, 3 = motion in one plane affects the others.

151Fryette's principles

What does Fryette's third principle of spinal mechanics state?

Ans: Third principle → motion in one plane limits the other planes → A

Why: Fryette's third principle: moving a segment in one plane reduces its motion in the other two planes. Example: a flexed segment has less sidebending and rotation.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

C is the second principle (Type II) and D is the first (Type I). B is a vague statement, not a Fryette principle. The third principle applies to the entire spine.

152Fryette's principles

Fill in the blanks for Fryette's Principles: (1) Principle 1/Type 1 SD: sidebending/rotation precedes sidebending/rotation, and they are in the same/opposite directions. (2) Principle 2/Type 2 SD: found at the ____ and/or ____ of type 1 curves. (3) Principle 3: if a vertebral unit was flexed, its range of sidebending and rotation would/would not be reduced.

Answer(1) Sidebending precedes rotation; opposite directions. (2) Apex and/or extremes (ends) of Type 1 curves. (3) Would be reduced.

Ans: Type 1 = S before R, opposite; Type 2 at apex/ends; Law 3 = reduced

Why: Type I: sidebending first, opposite rotation. Type II: found at the apex or extremes of Type I curves. Third principle: flexion reduces sidebending and rotation.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

This is why Type I is written N SxRy and Type II is written F/E RxSx. Type II can also occur by itself or at transitional areas.

Type I vs Type II

153Type I vs Type II

Which is true of a Type 1 somatic dysfunction?

Ans: Type 1 → neutral group, SB and R opposite → C

Why: In Type I mechanics sidebending and rotation occur in opposite directions (e.g. T6-T8 N Sr Rl).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Type I involves two or more segments, not one. It is neutral, so flexion and extension do not change it. Sidebending precedes rotation in Type I; rotation first is Type II.

154Type I vs Type II

True or false when referring to a somatic dysfunction? A type 1 SD of the spine is acute.

Ans: Type 1 → gradual, compensatory group curve → usually chronic → False

Why: Type I group curves form gradually, usually as compensation, so they are typically chronic. Type II is the one linked to acute trauma or abrupt twisting.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Type I is maintained by the long erector spinae muscles. Type II is maintained by short deep muscles such as the rotatores and intertransversarii.

Why: Type II dysfunctions are found at the apex or extremes of Type I curves, and the apex is the mid-point of the curve.

Explanation & sources

Type II is usually acute and traumatic (B wrong). Opposite-side coupling (C) and sidebending first (D) are Type I features. Type II should be treated before Type I, so it is not 'less severe' (E).

1572026Type I vs Type II

During a structural examination, a physician identifies a multi-segment group curve spanning T4–T8 that is neutral, sidebent right, and rotated left (T4–T8 N SR RL). At the apex of this curve (T6), palpation reveals an acute single-segment dysfunction that worsens in flexion and improves in extension (T6 E RR SR). Which dysfunction should be treated first, and why?

Ans: Type II at apex of Type I curve → treat Type II first → B

Why: The course rule: Type II dysfunctions should be treated before Type I. Fixing the apex Type II often lets the group curve improve.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

C is wrong because Type I couples sidebending and rotation to opposite sides. D is wrong because Type I is maintained by the long erector spinae, Type II by short deep muscles. Waiting for skin changes (E) has no basis.

158Type I vs Type II

Which muscles are commonly involved in Type 2 SD?

Ans: Type 2 → single segment → short deep restrictors (rotatores) → C

Why: Type II SD is maintained by short deep restrictors: rotatores (brevis), intertransversarii and multifidus.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Erector spinae, including longissimus, maintain Type I group curves. Trapezius is a superficial muscle not used to explain Fryette mechanics. Deep intrinsic muscles and the facets determine Type II behavior.

159asked 2×Type I vs Type II

A patient presents with "I went to pick up a box and now my back hurts." According to Fryette's principles, which muscles are affected in this type of somatic dysfunction?

Ans: Lifting injury → acute Type II → short restrictors → rotatores brevis → C

Why: A sudden lifting/twisting injury gives an acute Type II SD, maintained by short restrictors such as the rotatores brevis and intertransversarii.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Iliocostalis and spinalis are parts of the erector spinae, which maintain Type I curves. Serratus posterior inferior is an intermediate-layer extrinsic back muscle and not a Fryette restrictor.

160Type I vs Type II

The muscular TA Gregory is attempting to break the deadlifting world record. While bending over, he seems to have twisted his back and injured himself. In regards to this type of somatic dysfunction, which of Gregory's muscles is least likely to be directly involved in his injury?

Ans: Bent + twisted → Type II → short deep muscles; erector spinae = Type I → C

Why: A twisting injury while bent gives a Type II SD maintained by short deep muscles. The erector spinae maintain Type I group curves, so they are least likely involved.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Rotatores (brevis and longus), intertransversarii and interspinalis are short segmental muscles that span one or two levels. The rotatores are dense in muscle spindles, which is why twisting motions provoke Type II dysfunction.

Lecture slides (2)
161Type I vs Type II

Which muscles maintain a type I and a type II somatic dysfunction, respectively?

AnswerType I: erector spinae (long restrictors). Type II: short restrictors, i.e. rotatores, multifidus and intertransversarii.

Ans: Group curve → long muscles (erector spinae); single segment → short deep muscles

Why: Long multi-segment muscles (erector spinae) hold multi-segment Type I curves. Short one-segment muscles (rotatores, intertransversarii, multifidus) hold single-segment Type II dysfunctions.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The erector spinae are iliocostalis, longissimus and spinalis. Because Type II lives in small deep muscles, muscle energy is usually preferred over a broad myofascial technique.

169asked 2×Naming for freedom

When naming a somatic dysfunction, name the:

Ans: SD named for preference/position of ease → freedom → A

Why: An SD is named for its freedom, which is the same as its preference or position of ease.

Explanation & sources

The restriction is the opposite of the name in every plane. A restriction is a barrier with a firm end-feel. In muscle energy the patient is placed into the restrictive barrier and pushes toward the freedom.

170Naming for freedom

True or false when referring to a somatic dysfunction? It is named for the patient's restriction.

Ans: SD named for freedom (ease), not restriction → False

Why: SDs are named for the freedom (position of ease), not the restriction.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

To get the restriction, flip every component of the name: F↔E, Rr↔Rl, Sr↔Sl. Example: T6 ERlSl is restricted in flexion, right rotation and right sidebending.

171asked 11×2026Naming for freedom

In evaluation of a patient with thoracic pain, your diagnosis on palpation is T6 ERlSl. This means that T6 is restricted in?

Ans: Name = freedom; flip every letter (E→F, Rl→Rr, Sl→Sr); motion is T6 on T7 → B

Why: T6 ERlSl is free in extension, left rotation and left sidebending, so it is restricted in flexion, right rotation and right sidebending. Segmental motion is always described relative to the vertebra below (T6 on T7).

Heads up: On the 2026 IA3 poll everyone received credit for this question (announced at IA5). B is still the correct answer on the answer slide in every year and in the textbook version.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A flips flexion but keeps the left side, so it is half right. C has the right motions but the wrong reference vertebra (T5). D and E keep extension, which is the freedom, and also use T5.

172Naming for freedom

Mr. Smith bent over forward and to the right to pick up a heavy box, and you diagnose T10 F RrSr. In what motions may Mr. Smith have restriction?

Ans: Freedom F Rr Sr → flip every letter → restricted E, Rl, Sl → D

Why: The restriction is the exact opposite of the freedom: extension, left rotation and left sidebending.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A is the freedom. B flips the rotation but keeps flexion, and C flips flexion but keeps right rotation. Both are half-flips.

173asked 7×2026Palpation to diagnosis

On palpation of your patient you notice posterior transverse processes of three vertebrae on the left. Flexion and extension yield no change in the transverse process asymmetry. Which of the following is correct regarding this patient's somatic dysfunction?

Ans: Posterior TP left → rotated left; group + no F/E change → neutral Type I → sidebent right → D

Why: Posterior TP on the left means rotated left. A group that does not change with flexion or extension is neutral (Type I), so sidebending is opposite: N Sr Rl.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A, B and C are non-neutral Type II patterns, which change with flexion or extension. E has the right type but the wrong sides (rotation would then be right, with posterior TPs on the right).

1742026Palpation to diagnosis

A 27-year-old female presents to the office for evaluation of acute-on-chronic back pain. Osteopathic examination reveals reproducible lumbar paraspinal muscle tenderness. When palpating this region, the physician's left thumb is more anterior than the right thumb. This finding does not improve or worsen when the patient bends forward or backward. The most likely somatic dysfunction is

Ans: Left thumb anterior → right TP posterior → rotated right; no F/E change → neutral → sidebent left → E

Why: If the left thumb is anterior, the right TP is posterior, so the segment is rotated right. No change with flexion or extension means neutral (Type I), so it is sidebent left.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

F is the trap: it reads the anterior left thumb as left rotation. A to D are non-neutral and would change with forward or backward bending.

1752026Palpation to diagnosis

A 55-year-old man presents to the office with chronic low back pain. The pain began shortly after he started work as an accountant several years ago. His job requires prolonged sitting at a desk. Osteopathic examination reveals: ropy tissue texture changes in the L2–L4 region; L3 left transverse process is posteriorly displaced; L3 left transverse process does not change with lumbar flexion or extension. The most likely diagnosis is

Ans: Chronic group L2-L4 + no F/E change → neutral; posterior left TP → rotated left → sidebent right → B

Why: Chronic, ropy, multi-segment and unchanged by flexion or extension means a neutral Type I group (L2–L4). Left posterior TP means rotated left, so sidebending is right.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A is a group but flexed. C has neutral mechanics but the wrong sides. D and E name a single segment, but the findings span L2–L4; E is also a Type II pattern. In course notation this is L2-L4 N Sr Rl.

176asked 8×2026Palpation to diagnosis

A patient presents to your office with chronic low back pain. While lying prone, the patient's entire lumbar spine appears to have a lateral convexity to the right. State a possible diagnosis.

Ans: Group curve → Type I; convex right = concave left → sidebent left → rotated right (toward convexity) → D

Why: A whole-region curve is Type I. Sidebending is named toward the concavity (left), and Type I rotation goes to the opposite side, toward the convexity (right).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

C is the classic trap: it names sidebending toward the convexity. A and B are Type II, which is a single segment, and A also has opposite sides. The information given is enough, so E is wrong.

177asked 7×2026Palpation to diagnosis

While evaluating a patient's upper back, you notice that T3's transverse process is posterior on the left. Flexing T3 worsens the prominence of the posterior transverse process on the left. Extension allows the left transverse process to move anteriorly with ease. What can be said regarding this somatic dysfunction at T3?

Ans: Posterior left, worse in flexion → T3 ERlSl → restricted F, Rr, Sr → flexion limits right rotation → E

Why: The findings give T3 E Rl Sl. Its restrictions are flexion, right rotation and right sidebending, so flexing T3 engages the barrier and limits right rotation.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A names Type II correctly but gives opposite-side coupling, which is Type I. B is wrong because head extension extends T2 on T3. C is backward: left rotation is the freedom. D is wrong because extension makes the Type II asymmetry disappear; it does not convert it to Type I.

1782026Palpation to diagnosis

While evaluating a patient seated on the examination table, you place your thumbs over the transverse processes of T3. In the neutral position, your left thumb is noticeably more posterior than your right thumb. You instruct the patient to bend forward (flexion), and the left transverse process becomes significantly more prominent. When the patient slumps backward into extension, your thumbs become level. What is the correct diagnosis for T3?

Ans: Posterior left → RL; level in extension → E; Type II same side → SL → B

Why: Posterior left TP = rotated left. Asymmetry disappears in extension = extended. Type II couples to the same side: T3 E RL SL.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A gets the rotation right but picks flexion, the position that worsens it. C and E put the rotation on the wrong side. D is a neutral Type I pattern, but this finding changes with flexion and extension.

Ans: Single segment, worse in flexion → T2 E Rl Sl (Type II) → improves with extension → B

Why: This is a Type II T2 E Rl Sl. An extended dysfunction improves (the asymmetry disappears) in extension.

181asked 3×2026Palpation to diagnosis

A 25-year-old male complains of upper back pain. Structural examination reveals T2 is restricted with left rotation. Flexing the body down to T2 causes the segment to further rotate to the right, while extending the area causes T2 to return to the neutral position. The most appropriate nomenclature for this dysfunction is?

Ans: Restricted left rotation → rotated right; worse in flexion, neutral in extension → E; Type II → SR → B

Why: Restricted in left rotation means the freedom is right rotation. It worsens in flexion and normalizes in extension, so it is extended. A single non-neutral segment follows Type II, so it sidebends right: ERRSR.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A and C have the rotation on the wrong side. D picks flexion, the position that worsens it. E is a neutral pattern, but this segment changes with flexion and extension.

182asked 3×Palpation to diagnosis

While evaluating a patient's upper back, you notice that T4's transverse process is more posterior on the right. Ans: Posterior right → RR; better in flexion → F; Type II → SR, rotation written first → E

Why: Rotated right, better in flexion and worse in extension gives T4 F RR SR. Name for the freedom.

184Palpation to diagnosis

A patient has a group dysfunction T3-T6 N Sr Rl. Upon further evaluation, at the level of T6 the asymmetry in the TPs gets worse in flexion and becomes more symmetrical in extension. What is the patient's diagnosis at T6?

Ans: Group rotated left → T6 rotated left; symmetrical in extension → E; Type II same side → D

Why: T6 shares the left rotation, and its asymmetry clears in extension, so it is a Type II T6 E Rl Sl at the end of the group curve.

Explanation & sources

185Palpation to diagnosis

A patient comes in with lower back pain. After performing an osteopathic structural exam, the physician states the patient is restricted in forward flexion and the vertebra is shallow (posterior) on the left compared to the right. What is the motion of the facet joint causing this dysfunction?

Ans: Restricted flexion → ERS; posterior left → RL SL; left facet can't open → stuck closed → A

Why: Restricted flexion with left posterior = E RL SL. In flexion both facets should open; the left facet stays closed, so the segment pivots and rotates/sidebends left.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

B and D are flexion dysfunctions, but this patient is restricted in flexion. C names an ERS left but blames the wrong facet; the closed facet is on the side of rotation. Flexed dysfunctions (FRS) come from a facet stuck open, on the side opposite the rotation.

186Mechanism of injury

True or false when referring to a somatic dysfunction? SDs usually match the positions of their mechanisms of injury (e.g., if you tweak your back bending forward to pick something, or someone, up, it will be a flexion SD).

Ans: Injured position becomes the freedom → SD matches mechanism → True

Why: The review deck states that SD usually matches the position of the mechanism of injury. The position the patient was in when hurt becomes the freedom.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Bending forward and to the right when injured gives F Rr Sr. The restriction is the opposite (E, Rl, Sl), which is why these patients cannot straighten up.

187asked 9×2026Mechanism of injury

A man presents to your office with acute pain on the lower lumbar spine, unable to straighten his back. He was trying to pick up a box while bent forward and leaning over to the right. What is the most likely somatic dysfunction that you will palpate in this traumatic presentation?

Ans: Acute trauma → Type II; can't extend → F; leaning right → RR SR, rotation first → E

Why: Acute trauma gives a Type II single segment. He cannot straighten (extend), so the freedom is flexion. Injured while leaning right gives rotated and sidebent right, written rotation first: FRRSR.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A and B are neutral group (Type I) curves, which are chronic and compensatory. C is extended and leans left. D is flexed but lists sidebending first with opposite sides, which is not Type II.

Direct vs indirect

1922026Direct vs indirect

An osteopathic physician evaluates a patient with mid-back pain and diagnoses a T6 E RL SL somatic dysfunction. The physician chooses to perform a Direct technique (such as Muscle Energy Technique) to treat the dysfunction. Into which positioning combination must T6 be placed to properly engage the restrictive barrier?

Ans: Name = freedom; direct → into barrier → flip every letter → F RR SR → B

Why: T6 E RL SL is free in extension, left rotation and left sidebending. A direct technique goes into the barrier: flexion, right rotation, right sidebending.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A is the freedom, which is where an indirect technique (e.g. counterstrain) would position the segment. C and D flip only some components. E is a neutral Type I setup.

1932026Related topics

A 14-year-old female is brought to the office for a sports physical examination. Vital signs and cardiopulmonary examination are normal. Musculoskeletal examination reveals a somatic dysfunction of the atlantoaxial joint. This somatic dysfunction is assessed in the

Ans: Atlantoaxial = rotation joint → rotation occurs in transverse (horizontal) plane → E

Why: The atlantoaxial joint is mainly a rotation joint, and rotation occurs in the transverse (horizontal) plane about a vertical axis.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The A-P axis and coronal plane go with sidebending. The sagittal plane and transverse axis go with flexion and extension. Note the trap between 'transverse axis' (flexion/extension) and 'transverse plane' (rotation).

194asked 3×Related topics

If you have somatic dysfunction of the sacrum, what are the effects on your health?

Ans: Sacrum → S2-S4 pelvic splanchnics (parasympathetic) → more gut motility → diarrhea → C

Why: The sacral region carries parasympathetic outflow (S2-S4, pelvic splanchnics). Sacral SD can increase parasympathetic drive to the gut, which increases motility and causes diarrhea.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Parasympathetic tone speeds the gut, so A pairs it with the wrong effect. Hypersympathetic drive slows the bowel and causes constipation (D), which is the effect of a thoracolumbar SD. B pairs sympathetic drive with the wrong effect.

4.1 · 5 questions · Questions 195–199

Fascia

No questions in this section match the current Show filter.

195Fascia

Which of the following houses muscle and guides its contraction and motions?

Ans: Envelops muscle + guides its motion → fascia

Why: Muscles grow within and are enveloped by fascia, and fascia guides their contraction and motion. That is why the lecture calls it myofascia.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Ligaments connect bone to bone and do not house muscle. Cartilage covers joint surfaces. 'Fibrous connective tissue' is too general; fascia is the specific structure. Tendons insert into bone through Sharpey's fibers.

Asked in

  • 2022 TA Review (Middletown) - Exam 1 · TA review · slides 82-83
196asked 2×Fascia

According to FOM3, fascia is what type of connective tissue?

Ans: FOM3: fascia = irregular connective tissue arranged as concentric tubes → dense irregular, tubes

Why: FOM3 defines fascia as loose or dense irregular connective tissue, organized as concentric tubes (pannicular, axial/appendicular, meningeal, visceral).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Dense regular tissue is tendon and ligament, not fascia. 'Loose regular' is not a fascia type. 'Loose irregular, sheets' gets the tissue partly right but the layers are described as tubes, not sheets.

  • 2023 TA Review (Harlem) - Exam 1 · TA review · slides 135-136

197Fascia

You remove the platysma from your cadaver. What layer of fascia did you remove?

Ans: Platysma lies in superficial fascia → pannicular layer

Why: The platysma is a muscle embedded in the superficial (subcutaneous) fascia, which FOM3 calls the pannicular layer.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Axial and appendicular fascia is the deep investing layer under the pannicular layer. Meningeal fascia surrounds the CNS. Visceral fascia surrounds the body-cavity organs.

Asked in

  • 2020 TA Review (Middletown) Exam 1 · TA review · slides 77-80
198Fascia

You remove the platysma from your cadaver. What layer of fascia is being revealed?

Ans: Remove pannicular (platysma) layer → next deeper = axial/appendicular

Why: Removing the platysma takes away the pannicular layer and exposes the next deeper tube, the axial and appendicular (deep investing) fascia.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Pannicular is the layer you removed, not the one revealed. Meningeal and visceral layers lie much deeper, around the CNS and the organs. Order from outside in: pannicular, axial/appendicular, then meningeal and visceral.

199Fascia

Which cells are NOT a component of fascia?

Ans: Fascia cells = fibroblasts, myofibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells → reticulocytes are not

Why: The cells of fascia are fibroblasts, myofibroblasts, macrophages and mast cells. Reticulocytes are immature red blood cells found in blood.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The other four are all resident cells of fascia. Its extracellular matrix holds collagen, elastic fibers, laminin and fibronectin.

Muscle receptors

200Muscle receptors

What are the two receptors specific to muscle?

Ans: Receptors specific to muscle → muscle spindle + Golgi tendon organ

Why: The two receptors specific to muscle are the muscle spindle (in the belly) and the Golgi tendon organ (at the myotendinous junction). Together they give continuous feedback and adjust muscle tone.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Nociceptors, Ruffini endings, Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles are found in skin, joints and other tissues, not only in muscle. Each wrong option pairs one muscle receptor with a general receptor.

What is the function of each muscle receptor?

Ans: GTO senses tension; spindle senses stretch (length) → B

Why: The Golgi tendon organ detects tension and the muscle spindle detects stretch (length and rate of change of length).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A swaps the two. Neither receptor is a pain receptor, which rules out C, D and E. Memory hook: GTO = Tension, both have a T.

202Muscle receptors

What is the role of the muscle spindle and golgi tendon?

Ans: Lecture: spindle + GTO 'provide continuous feedback and adjustment of muscular tone' → C and D

Why: The lecture states these two receptors provide continuous feedback and adjustment of muscular tone, so the answer combines C and D.

224Muscle spindle

What is the stretch reflex?

AnswerMuscle spindle reflex: a quick stretch fires spindle afferents (Ia, II), which excite alpha motor neurons so the stretched muscle contracts powerfully. It is protective (e.g., knee-jerk). The spindle senses length and rate of change of length.

Ans: Fast stretch → spindle Ia burst → alpha motor neuron → same muscle contracts

Why: The stretch reflex is contraction of a muscle in response to passive stretch. It protects against injury and regulates muscle length automatically, as in the knee-jerk reflex.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A goal of myofascial treatment is a stimulatory effect on the stretch reflex in hypotonic muscles. The reflex also relaxes the antagonist through reciprocal inhibition.

242asked 3×2026Golgi tendon organ

A 46-year-old female presents to Urgent Care with complaints of leg pain and tight hamstrings. The pain began after going to an 'advanced' yoga class, for which she was not prepared. After passively and slowly stretching her hamstring muscles you reassess to find minimal change in the hypertonicity. You then recall that adding an active component to the stretch by having her contract the hypertonic muscles against resistance can enhance the effectiveness. Which physiologic principle is being employed?

Ans: Tight muscle contracts isometrically against resistance → then stretch → post-isometric relaxation

Why: Post-isometric relaxation: right after an isometric contraction of the tight muscle, it is in a refractory state, so you can take up the slack without stretch-reflex opposition. GTO tension provides the inhibition.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

GTO physiology is the receptor mechanism, but the named principle (technique) is post-isometric relaxation. A different question asks for the receptor and the answer there is the GTO. Crossed extensor uses the opposite limb, and contracting the antagonist would be reciprocal inhibition.

243asked 4×2026Reciprocal inhibition & crossed extensor

A patient comes in after going to an 'advanced' yoga class, for which she was not prepared. She complains of very sore and tight hamstring muscles. You decide to have her contract the antagonist muscles as a way to ease into the treatment. Which physiologic principle are you employing?

Ans: Contract antagonist (quads) → reflex relaxation of hamstrings → reciprocal inhibition

Why: Contracting the antagonist (quadriceps) reflexively relaxes the tight hamstrings. This is reciprocal inhibition, and it occurs with any contraction.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

GTO physiology would mean contracting the tight hamstring itself. The crossed extensor reflex uses the opposite limb. Reciprocal inhibition uses a very gentle force (think ounces, not pounds), which suits sore, acutely tight muscles.

A 30-year-old male comes into the clinic with a right hypertonic biceps. You tell the patient to engage the right triceps, eliciting which reflex?

Ans: Same-side antagonist (triceps) contracts → agonist (biceps) relaxes → reciprocal inhibition

Why: Contracting the ipsilateral antagonist (right triceps) reflexively relaxes the right biceps. That is reciprocal inhibition.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The Golgi tendon reflex would mean contracting the biceps itself. The cross-extensor reflex would use the left arm. The spindle reflex contracts a stretched muscle.

245Reciprocal inhibition & crossed extensor

Which of the following reflexes occurs during any contraction?

Ans: Every agonist contraction → antagonist must relax → reciprocal inhibition

Why: Reciprocal inhibition occurs in the stretch reflex and in any contraction: when an agonist contracts, its antagonist must relax.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The Golgi tendon reflex needs significant tension. The spindle reflex needs a stretch. The crossed extensor reflex involves the opposite limb.

246asked 2×Reciprocal inhibition & crossed extensor

You visit your PCP and have your reflexes tested. The doctor taps your patellar tendon with the reflex hammer. What actions will your muscles elicit?

Ans: Tap stretches quads spindle → quads contract + hamstrings relax (reciprocal inhibition), same leg

Why: The tap stretches the quadriceps spindle, so the quadriceps (extensor) contracts through the stretch reflex. Through reciprocal inhibition the hamstrings (flexor) relax in the same leg.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The knee jerk is a single-leg reflex, so the contralateral options are wrong. Both muscles cannot relax, because the extensor must contract to kick.

248asked 2×Reciprocal inhibition & crossed extensor

After hitting the gym a little too hard and doing too many bicep curls, you feel extreme pain and can't move your biceps on the right. Your friend asks you to tuck your left elbow to your side and have your palm face up, then push upwards while they provide isometric resistance. What technique did your friend use and what is the goal?

Ans: Injured R biceps + contract L biceps → same muscle, other limb → crossed extensor

Why: Contracting the left biceps to relax the injured right biceps uses the crossed extensor reflex: contracting a muscle group in one limb relaxes the same group in the opposite limb.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Reciprocal inhibition would contract the right triceps. Isolytic lengthening uses an operator force greater than the patient's to stretch fibrotic tissue; D pairs that name with the crossed extensor definition. 249Reciprocal inhibition & crossed extensor

A 14-year-old boy presents with right hamstring tightness following a soccer game. The physician decides to use a form of muscle energy that takes advantage of the crossed extensor reflex. The patient is instructed to contract his left hamstring while the physician monitors the restricted right hamstring. Which of the following best explains the physiologic basis of this technique?

Ans: Contract L hamstring → crossed spinal pathway → R hamstring relaxes

Why: Through crossed extensor pathways, voluntary contraction of the left hamstring reflexively relaxes the right hamstring.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The GTO acts only on its own muscle, so it cannot explain relaxation on the other side. The reflex relaxes, not contracts, the opposite flexor. E is a true mechanism (reciprocal inhibition) but not the technique described.

250asked 2×2026Types of muscle contraction

Why: Lifting a weight is a concentric contraction: the muscle shortens and its origin and insertion approximate.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

It is not isotonic in the textbook's view because tension changes as the weight swings through its arc. Eccentric is lowering. Isometric is holding still. Isolytic is a lengthening contraction overpowered by an outside force.
