Ans: Holding steady = no length change → isometric

Why: Holding a weight still is isometric: muscle force equals the load, so length does not change and origin and insertion stay put.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Concentric shortens and eccentric lengthens. Isolytic needs an outside force that lengthens the muscle. Isometric is the most common contraction used in muscle energy.

Why: Lowering a weight is eccentric: the biceps contracts while it lengthens under an external force.

253asked 2×2026Types of muscle contraction

Why: Isolytic contraction: the counterforce is greater than the patient's force, so the muscle lengthens while contracting. It is used to break adhesions in fibrotic, shortened tissue.

Explanation

Eccentric also lengthens, but 'breaking adhesions' with an operator force is the defining feature of isolytic. Concentric shortens and isometric does not move.

255Types of muscle contraction

Isometric would hold still (Dr = Pt). Concentric and isotonic shorten the muscle (Dr < Pt). Eccentric is the general term for lengthening contractions, but it is not an option here.

Concentric also shortens, but the stem's 'no change in tension' points to isotonic. When tension varies through the arc, the textbook calls a curl concentric. Isometric holds still and isolytic lengthens.

258Types of muscle contraction

Match each contraction type (isotonic, isometric, isolytic) to its description: A. Lengthening the muscle as the patient actively contracts it; B. Contracting a muscle while fixing only one end of the muscular attachment; C. Origin and insertion points are maintained in a stationary position while the muscle is contracted against resistance.

AnswerIsotonic: B; Isometric: C; Isolytic: A.

Ans: Stationary attachments = isometric; one end fixed = isotonic; lengthened while contracting = isolytic

Why: Per the course: isometric keeps origin and insertion stationary against resistance, isotonic fixes only one end of the attachment, and isolytic lengthens the muscle while the patient contracts it.

Heads up: The 2023 TA answer slide matched Isotonic to C and Isometric to B. The 2026 Lect 6 slide 31 defines isometric as origin and insertion kept stationary (C) and isotonic as fixing only one end (B), so those two are swapped on that slide. Isolytic to A is correct.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Isometric is the most common contraction in muscle energy. Isotonic is often used for hypotonic, reflexively inhibited muscles. Isolytic treats fibrotic, chronically shortened tissue.

Stretching a hypertonic muscle engages the barrier, which is direct. Perpendicular and parallel stretches are both direct stretching techniques, and shortening is not stretching. Counterstrain is the classic indirect technique that shortens a muscle.

What is the physiological principle at play for the bilateral linear cervical stretch?

Ans: Slow linear stretch → avoids rate-sensitive spindle firing → no reflex contraction

Why: The stretch is done slowly so the spindle, which senses rate of change of length, does not trigger a stretch reflex. That is preventing muscle spindle activation.

263Technique physiology

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A slow stretch gives a static response but does not 'inhibit' afferents. B describes reciprocal inhibition. A quick stretch causes the dynamic response and a strong contraction.

279asked 4×2026Myofascial release

When performing indirect myofascial release, which barrier is engaged?

Ans: Indirect = move away from restrictive barrier → toward the anatomic barrier side

Why: Indirect MFR moves tissue away from the restrictive barrier, toward ease. The textbook says this direction moves toward the anatomic barrier (the limit of passive motion), which is more comfortable for the patient.

Heads up: All keys mark anatomic (the 2026 course MFR text, and 'C. Anatomic' on the 2023 TA slide, which used a different letter order). A note on the TA copy questioned this, but the course textbook explanation supports anatomic, so A stands.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The restrictive (pathologic) barrier is what direct MFR engages. The physiologic barrier is the limit of active, patient-made motion. The elastic barrier is the range between physiologic and anatomic where passive ligament stretch occurs.

You are consulted to see a severely debilitated 87-year-old male with complaints of mid thoracic pain. He was in the intensive care unit for 3 weeks and was transferred to a medical/surgical bed yesterday. His back pain is localized to the mid thoracic region and seems to be musculoskeletal in nature. Which osteopathic manipulative techniques would be best suited to relieve this patient's symptoms?

Why: Fragile, hospitalized patients do best with gentle techniques. Direct myofascial release can treat musculoskeletal pain without stressing him.

Heads up: Textbook key E. Note: the 2026 review deck (slide 39) lists unstable/infirm patients and metastases in the area of treatment as contraindications for ME, HVLA and dMFR. Choose E here as the gentlest of these options, but do not use dMFR directly over a metastasis.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Muscle energy needs patient effort and is contraindicated in ICU or low-vitality patients. HVLA is contraindicated with bone metastases (risk of pathologic fracture). Diaphragm release and pedal pump are lymphatic techniques, relatively contraindicated in advanced cancer and unlikely to help musculoskeletal pain.

283asked 3×2026Myofascial release

A patient complains of neck pain that is worse at the end of the work day. Structural examination reveals somatic dysfunction in the upper cervical segments. The physician slowly turns the patient's neck in the direction of limited movement, loads the soft tissues with a gentle constant force, then waits a few seconds until the tissues release and more motion is possible. This technique is an example of

Ans: Toward restriction (barrier) + constant load until release → direct MFR

Why: Moving into the restrictive barrier and loading the tissue with a constant force until release is direct myofascial release.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Indirect MFR moves away from the barrier. Articulatory technique moves a joint repeatedly through its range. Counterstrain and FPR both use positions of ease (shortening), which are indirect.

284asked 3×2026Myofascial release

A young male presents for a routine physical. Structural examination reveals he has the most common fascial pattern noted in the population. The most likely compensatory pattern is

Ans: Zink common compensatory pattern (80%) → OA L, CT R, TL L, LS R

Why: Zink's common compensatory pattern (about 80% of healthy people) alternates at the four junctions: OA left, cervicothoracic right, thoracolumbar left, lumbosacral right (L/R/L/R).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

R/L/R/L is the uncommon compensatory pattern (about 20%). Patterns that do not alternate (A, B, E) are uncompensated, seen in unhealthy, stressed or recently traumatized patients.

285asked 2×Thoracic anatomy & motion

The main motion of the thoracic vertebrae is:

Ans: Ribs limit sidebending, SPs limit extension → rotation is the largest thoracic motion

Why: Rotation is the greatest motion allowed in the thoracic spine. It is limited mainly by ligament tension.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Flexion and extension are limited: extension by the shingled spinous processes (and the ALL), flexion by the interspinous ligaments, ligamentum flavum and PLL. Sidebending is limited by the ribs. "Sidebending and rotation" describes coupled motion, not the main single motion.

286asked 3×Thoracic anatomy & motion

What is the true thoracic kyphosis of the T-spine?

Ans: Thoracic functional divisions → T4-T9 = true kyphosis (apex T5-T6)

Why: The lecture divides the thoracic spine into functional regions. T4-T9 is the true thoracic kyphosis, with its apex at T5-T6.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

C7-T1 is the cervicothoracic junction. T1-T3 is a transitional (lordotic) region, and T12-L1 is the lordotic thoracolumbar junction. T5-T6 is only the apex, not the whole kyphotic region. The kyphosis comes mainly from vertebral bodies that are a bit taller posteriorly than anteriorly.

287asked 7×2026Thoracic anatomy & motion

Extension of the thoracic spine is most affected by which of the following?

Ans: Long overlapping thoracic SPs → shingle effect → blocks extension

Why: Thoracic spinous processes are long and overlap like shingles, so they block extension. The ALL also limits extension, but less.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The PLL (with the interspinous ligaments and ligamentum flavum) limits flexion, the opposite motion. The ribs limit sidebending. The transverse processes are not the main block to extension. The Canvas version of this question words it "most limit extension" with the same answer.

288asked 2×Thoracic anatomy & motion

Which of the following restricts the motion of flexion in the thoracic spine?

Ans: Flexion stretches posterior ligaments → PLL (with interspinous ligaments, ligamentum flavum)

Why: Thoracic flexion is limited by tension in the posterior longitudinal ligament, the interspinous ligaments and the ligamentum flavum.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Spinous processes and the ALL limit extension. The ribs limit sidebending. Keep the pair straight: flexion is stopped by the PLL group, extension by the shingled SPs.

289asked 3×Thoracic anatomy & motion

Lateral flexion and unilateral joint motion is restricted by which of the following?

Ans: Rib attachments at costovertebral/costotransverse joints → restrict lateral flexion

Why: The ribs articulate with the thoracic vertebrae and restrict lateral flexion (sidebending) and unilateral joint motion.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Spinous processes and the ALL limit extension. The PLL limits flexion. Transverse processes are attachment points, not the main restrictor. The rib cage is the main reason the thoracic spine is stiffer than the cervical or lumbar spine.

290asked 8×2026Thoracic anatomy & motion

The superior articular facets of the thoracic vertebrae face which directions?

Ans: Thoracic superior facets → BUL → posteriorly, superiorly, laterally

Why: Thoracic superior facets face back, up and lateral (BUL). Cervical and lumbar superior facets face back, up and medial (BUM).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The options with anteriorly, inferiorly and medially describe the inferior facets, which face the opposite way to mate with the superior facets below. Mnemonic: BUM-BUL-BUM for cervical, thoracic, lumbar.

291Thoracic anatomy & motion

Fill in the blank: The superior articular facets of the thoracic vertebrae face back, up and ____. The superior articular facets of the cervical vertebrae face back, up and ____.

AnswerThoracic: lateral (back, up, lateral = BUL). Cervical: medial (back, up, medial = BUM).

Ans: BUM-BUL-BUM → cervical medial, thoracic lateral, lumbar medial

Why: Superior facets face back and up at every level. Only the third direction changes: thoracic = lateral (BUL), cervical = medial (BUM).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Lumbar superior facets are also back, up and medial (BUM), so the full mnemonic is BUM-BUL-BUM from top to bottom. A common trap is giving the thoracic answer (lateral) for a lumbar or cervical question.

292Thoracic anatomy & motion

In the lumbar spinal segments, what position will you normally find the facet joints facing?

Ans: Lumbar → BUM (back, up, medial) → backwards and medial

Why: Lumbar superior facets face backward and medial (BUM). Back, up and lateral is the thoracic pattern.

Heads up: The 2023 TA answer slide highlights C (back, up, lateral), which is the thoracic orientation. The same slide's mnemonic and the 2026 lecture (BUM-BUL-BUM: lumbar = back, up, medial) make D correct.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

C (back, up, lateral) is the thoracic orientation, the classic trap. A and B combine directions that do not go together. Mnemonic BUM-BUL-BUM: cervical, thoracic, lumbar.

293asked 2×2026Thoracic anatomy & motion

A 20-year-old female presents for a general maintenance examination without complaints. Structural examination reveals T10 is flexed, rotated and sidebent right. The associated dermatome at the level of T10 is at the

Ans: T10 dermatome → umbilicus

Why: The T10 dermatome is at the level of the umbilicus.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

T11 is just below the umbilicus and T12 is just above the inguinal ligament (suprapubic). L1 covers the anterior thigh just below the inguinal ligament and L2 the middle and anterior thigh. The epigastrium sits above T10.

294asked 3×Rule of 3s & landmarks

According to the rule of threes, which group of vertebrae have spinous processes that project one half segment below?

Ans: Rule of 3s: T1-3 same, T4-6 half below, T7-9 one below → T4-T6

Why: Rule of 3s: T1-T3 SPs are level with their own TPs, T4-T6 SPs sit one half segment below, and T7-T9 SPs sit one full segment below.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

T1-T3: same level. T7-T9: one full level below. T10-T12 reverse the pattern (T10 full, T11 half, T12 same), so the group as a whole is not "half below," although T11 alone is.

295Rule of 3s & landmarks

According to the "Rule of 3's" of the thoracic spine, the spinous processes of T1-T3 would be located on what plane level in relation to its own transverse process?

Ans: T1-T3 → SP level with its own TP → same level

Why: For T1-T3 the spinous process is at the same level as its own transverse processes.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Halfway below describes T4-T6 (and T11). A full level below describes T7-T9 (and T10). No thoracic SP sits above its own TPs.

296Rule of 3s & landmarks

Which of the following statements is true regarding the Rule of Three's for thoracic spinal diagnosis?

Ans: T4-6 SP half below → between own TP and TP below

Why: For T4-T6 the SP lies halfway between its own TPs and the TPs of the vertebra below.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A: T1-T3 SPs are level with their own TPs. C: T7-T9 SPs lie at the TPs of the vertebra below, not above. D: T10-T12 run the pattern in reverse (T10 full, T11 half, T12 same), not the T1-T3 rule in reverse.

2972026Rule of 3s & landmarks

Based on the Rule of 3's for the thoracic spinous processes, which of the following statements is correct?

Ans: T2 in T1-T3 group → SP level with own TPs

Why: T2 is in the T1-T3 group, where the SP and TPs are at the same level.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

B: the T7 SP is one full level below, at the T8 TPs, not up at T6. C: the T5 SP is half a level below, between T5 and T6, not T4 and T5. D: the T11 TPs are above the T11 SP (half a level), while the T12 SP is level with the T12 TPs, so the T11 TPs are not in line with the T12 SP.

298Rule of 3s & landmarks

During a thoracic spine OMM lab, a medical student palpates the spinous process of T5 on her OMM partner. Which group of thoracic vertebrae has the same anatomical relationship between their spinous and transverse processes as T5?

Ans: T5 in T4-T6 → SP half segment below → between own TP and TP below

Why: T5 belongs to the T4-T6 group: each SP sits halfway between its own TPs and the TPs of the vertebra below.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A describes T1-T3 (and T12). C describes T7-T9 (and T10). D is false; the rule of 3s exists precisely because the pattern is predictable.

299asked 2×Rule of 3s & landmarks

Using the "rule of threes," the transverse process of T5 can be located:

Why: T4-T6 SPs project half a segment below their own TPs. So the T5 TPs sit halfway between the T4 and T5 spinous processes.

300Rule of 3s & landmarks

You are completing the palpation part of your thoracic rubric during your mock practical. Placing your fingers on your partner's back, you locate T7, which is associated with the inferior angle of the scapula. According to the rule of threes, where is the spinous process of the T7 vertebra located?

Ans: T7 in T7-T9 → SP one full segment below → at T8 level

Why: T7-T9 spinous processes project one full segment below, so the T7 SP lies at the level of the T8 TPs.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A is wrong twice: the T7 SP is not at its own level, and the spine of the scapula is T3, not T7. C is wrong because thoracic SPs never project above their own level. Landmarks: spine of scapula = T3, inferior angle = T7.

301Rule of 3s & landmarks

If you are at the spinous process of T8, what level TPs are just lateral to it?

Ans: SP of T8 (T7-T9 group) projects one level down → T9 TPs beside it

Why: The T8 SP projects one full segment down, so the TPs just lateral to it belong to T9.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

C (T8) is the trap: it assumes SP and TP are level, which is true only for T1-T3 and T12. T7 and T6 go the wrong direction. Read carefully whether a question gives the level of the SP or the TP.

302Rule of 3s & landmarks

During a structural exam, a medical student palpates the transverse processes of T8. These transverse processes are located:

Ans: T8 SP projects down to T9 → T8 TPs stay at T8 level (T7 SP level)

Why: TPs belong to their own vertebra, so the T8 TPs are at the level of T8. Because T7-T9 SPs project one level down, the SP found beside them is the T7 SP.

Heads up: The 2025 TA key marks C ("At the level of T9"). By the rule of 3s, the T8 SP lies at the T9 TPs, but the T8 TPs themselves lie at the T8 level, beside the T7 SP. The key appears to confuse SP with TP, so A is given here.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

C reverses the rule: it is the T8 spinous process that sits at the T9 level. B and D use the half-segment (T4-T6) pattern, which does not apply to T8.

303Rule of 3s & landmarks

The spinous process of T10 can be found over which spinal vertebra?

Why: T10 follows the T7-T9 rule: its SP lies one full segment below, over T11.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

B assumes SP and body are level (true for T1-T3 and T12). C and D go upward, which never happens. E skips two levels.

304asked 2×2026Rule of 3s & landmarks

A 20-year-old female presents for a general maintenance examination without complaints. Structural examination reveals T10 is flexed, rotated and sidebent right. The transverse process of this segment can be found

Ans: T10 SP = one level down (T7-9 rule) → T9 SP lies at T10 TPs

Why: Work the rule in reverse: which SP sits at T10? T9 is in the T7-T9 group, so the T9 SP lies at the T10 TPs.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

B: the T10 SP is one level lower, at the T11 TPs. C: the T11 SP is about half a level below T11. D and E use the half-segment rule, which does not apply to T9-T10. The FRS detail in the stem is a distractor.

305Rule of 3s & landmarks

You palpate the spinous process of T8 and put a thumb on either side of it, finding an anterior TP on the right. Which is correct?

Ans: TPs beside T8 SP belong to T9 → anterior right = posterior left → T9 rotated left

Why: The TPs beside the T8 SP belong to T9 (T7-T9 SPs project one level down). An anterior TP on the right means the left TP is posterior, so T9 is rotated left.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

C and D name the wrong level (the SP is T8, the TPs are T9). F gets the level right but reads the anterior TP as posterior. A and B go up a level instead of down. Two traps in one: SP vs TP level, and anterior vs posterior.

Which landmarks are helpful in determining thoracic levels during a physical exam?

Why: Surface landmarks: spine of the scapula = T3, inferior angle of the scapula = T7, 12th rib followed to T12, iliac crests = L4-L5 interspace.

Explanation

A: the inferior angle is T7, not T9. D: the 12th rib leads to T12, not T9. B is not a landmark. Anterior landmarks from lecture: suprasternal notch = T2, angle of Louis = T4, xiphoid = T9.

Type I group curves

307asked 10×2026Type I group curves

You find 3 posterior transverse processes on the right side at T3-5. Which of the following is a true statement?

Ans: 3 adjacent segments posterior right → group curve = Type I → rotated right, sidebent left

Why: Several adjacent segments rotated the same way is a group curve, which follows Type I (neutral) mechanics: rotation toward the posterior TPs (right) and sidebending the opposite way (left).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A says Type I but flips the directions; posterior TPs on the right mean rotation right. B couples rotation and sidebending to the same side, which is Type II. D is false because Type I curves do not change with flexion or extension; a change would point to Type II. Older versions used "the facets are controlling vertebral mechanics," which also describes Type II.

308asked 3×2026Type I group curves

An elderly patient presents for a general wellness visit without complaints. Structural examination reveals a group curve in the thoracic region. Which of the following is most associated with this segment's spinal mechanics?

Ans: Group curve → Type I → sidebend into concavity, rotate into convexity

Why: A group curve follows Type I mechanics: it sidebends into the concavity and the bodies rotate toward the convexity.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A: rotation is greatest at the apex, not the base. B and C describe Type II (same-side coupling, rotation into the concavity). E: the posterior TP is on the convex side, where the bodies rotate.

309asked 4×2026Type I group curves

A scoliotic patient presents with right upper back pain. Structural examination reveals a type I dysfunction from T3-T8 and a prominent kyphosis. The right scapula is posterior. Upon forward flexion there is paraspinal muscle prominence on the right upper thoracic area. What spinal motion pattern would you suspect in this scenario?

Ans: Type I T3-T8 + right paraspinal prominence → rotated right → sidebent left

Why: A Type I curve with paraspinal prominence on the right is rotated right and sidebent left (dextroscoliosis, T3-8 NRRSL). Motion is free in those directions.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

D flips both directions. A, B and E use same-side coupling or flexion/extension terms that belong to Type II, and Type I rotation is not limited to the apex segment. The posterior right scapula rides on the posteriorly displaced right ribs.

310asked 3×2026Type I group curves

A patient has a type I curvature from T6-T12, convex left. The apex of the segment is T9. You would expect the thoracic spine to

Ans: Type I convex left → sidebent right, rotated left → free left rotation

Why: Convex left = sidebent right, rotated left (T6-T12 NSrRl). The region moves freely into its dysfunction, so it freely rotates left.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

B: translating right equals sidebending left, which is restricted. C: the apex rotates maximally to the left, not right. D: the curve is sidebent right. E is Type II coupling.

311asked 2×2026Type I group curves

A 40-year-old male presents with a thoracic curve. History reveals it has had a dull, achy quality. Structural examination reveals a large paraspinal hump on the left side. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Ans: Curve + dull achy (chronic) → Type I; left hump → rotated left, sidebent right

Why: A curve with a dull, achy (chronic) quality is a Type I group curve. A left paraspinal hump means rotation left, so sidebending is right: T7-9 NRLSR.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A and E are single-segment Type II diagnoses, and E rotates right. B couples rotation and sidebending to the same side, which Type I never does. C is a single segment with the same error. NRLSR is textbook notation for neutral, rotated left, sidebent right (NSrRl).

312asked 2×Type I group curves

A patient with chronic low back pain lies prone and you notice that her entire lumbar spine appears to have a lateral convexity to the left. What is a possible diagnosis?

Ans: Whole region curved = Type I; convex left → sidebent right, rotated left

Why: A whole region in a curve is Type I. Convex left means the spine is sidebent right, and Type I rotates opposite: rotated left.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A uses Type II for a group curve. C is the pattern for a curve convex right. D couples the same side, which is not Type I.

313Type I group curves

You perform the standing flexion test and see a thoracic rib hump on the left from T1-T10. What is your diagnosis?

Ans: Rib hump left over many segments → Type I rotated left → sidebent right

Why: A rib hump marks the side of rotation (the convexity) of a Type I group curve. Hump on the left → rotated left, sidebent right: T1-T10NSrRl.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

C flips the directions. B and D add E or F, but group curves are neutral and do not change with flexion or extension. Type I always couples rotation and sidebending to opposite sides.

314Type I group curves

A patient with scoliosis has restriction from T2–T5. When bending forward, a rib hump is noticed on the left. Which of the following is the correct diagnosis?

Ans: Multiple segments = Type I; hump left → rotated left → sidebent right

Why: A group dysfunction (T2-T5) follows Type I. Rib hump on the left = rotated left, so sidebent right: T2-T5 NSrRl.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

B flips the directions. C, D and E are Type II (F/E with same-side coupling), which describe single segments.

315Type I group curves

A patient comes in with upper-mid back pain. You find posterior TPs on the left starting from the level of the spine of the scapula down for 4 segments. What is the patient's diagnosis?

Ans: Spine of scapula = T3, 4 segments → T3-T6; posterior left → NSrRl

Why: The spine of the scapula = T3, so four segments down is T3-T6. Posterior TPs on the left = rotated left; Type I sidebends opposite: T3-T6 NSrRl.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A and B start at T4, one level too low. D flips the directions. Rule of 3s is not needed here because T1-T3 SPs and TPs are level.

316Type I group curves

An elderly man, Mike, presents to your office complaining of dull back pain that has been persistent for the past 10 years. On palpation, the patient's skin is cool, dry, and the tissues feel doughy. While performing a forward flexion test, you take note of posterior TPs on the right side starting from the spine of the scapula down for 4 segments. What is the most likely somatic dysfunction that you will palpate?

Ans: Chronic + spine of scapula (T3) ×4 segments, posterior right → T3-T6 NSlRr

Why: Chronic pain with cool, doughy tissue fits a chronic Type I curve. Spine of scapula = T3, four segments = T3-T6; posterior TPs right = rotated right, sidebent left.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

B flips the directions. C and D start one level too low at T4, and C also flips the directions. Acute findings (warm, moist, boggy) would fit a more recent dysfunction.

317Type I group curves

A patient comes in with upper back pain. On forward flexion test you see a rib hump on the right from the level of the spine of the scapula to the inferior border of the scapula. On palpation, the TPs do not get better in flexion or extension. On gross examination, the patient's right shoulder is higher. What is your somatic dysfunction diagnosis?

Ans: Spine of scapula T3 → inferior angle T7; no F/E change; hump right → T3-T7 NSlRr

Why: Landmarks give T3 (spine of scapula) to T7 (inferior angle). TPs that don't change in flexion or extension = neutral Type I. Hump right = rotated right, so sidebent left.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A and C use F or E, but the TPs do not change with flexion or extension. D has the wrong levels and flips the directions. The higher right shoulder is a postural clue, not part of the naming.

318Type I group curves

A 1st year medical student presents with upper back pain. On observation there is hypertonicity starting at the level of the spine of the scapula to the inferior angle. When you palpate the transverse processes, your left thumb goes deeper. When you ask the patient to bend forward and back, neither makes the transverse processes even. The vertebrae are easier to translate to the right. What is the diagnosis of their somatic dysfunction?

Ans: T3-T7 landmarks; left thumb deeper = right TP posterior; translate right = sidebent left

Why: Spine of scapula to inferior angle = T3-T7. The left thumb goes deeper, so the right TP is posterior (rotated right). No change with flexion or extension = neutral. Easier to translate right = sidebent left. Answer: T3-T7 NSlRr.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A and B are single Type II segments. C uses E for a curve that does not change with extension. D has the right pattern at the wrong levels. Translation trap: translating right = sidebending left.

319Type I group curves

A 40 year old male presents after 'throwing' out his back while lifting a heavy box. The transverse processes from T4 to T9 are all rotated right, with no change in flexion or extension. How would you write this dysfunction?

Ans: T4-T9 all rotated right, no F/E change → Type I → sidebent left

Why: Six segments rotated right with no change in flexion or extension = Type I group curve: sidebent left, rotated right (NSlRr).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A and B are Type II notations. C lists rotation before sidebending; Type I notation writes sidebending first (NSxRy) because sidebending precedes rotation. D couples the same side. "Threw out his back" hints at trauma, but the palpatory findings define the diagnosis.

320asked 8×2026Type I group curves

Patient presents with back pain. On forward bending you find a rib hump on the right that begins at the spinous process of T8 and ends at spinous process of T12. The TPs in that area are all rotated to the right and do not change in flexion or extension. What is your diagnosis written in "shorthand"?

Ans: SP T8 sits at T9 TPs; SP T12 at T12 → T9-T12; right, no F/E change → NSlRr

Why: Convert the SP landmarks with the rule of 3s: the T8 SP lies at the T9 TPs (T7-T9 project one full level down) and the T12 SP is level with T12. TPs right with no change in flexion/extension = Type I, rotated right, sidebent left: T9-T12NSlRr.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A and C are Type II diagnoses, which change with flexion or extension. B couples sidebending and rotation to the same side. D shifts the top down a level but also stops at T11; the T12 SP is level with its own TPs (T12 follows T1-T3). Lecture version: SP T7 to SP T10 = T8-T11NSlRr. Other versions of this question use different distractors, same answer.

321Type I group curves

You perform the standing flexion test and see a thoracic rib hump on the left from T1-T10. Where would you find a type 2 somatic dysfunction?

Ans: Type II hides at apex or ends of Type I; T1-T10 apex ≈ T5

Why: Type II dysfunctions are found at the apex or the ends of a Type I curve. The apex of a T1-T10 curve is about T5.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

T2 and T3 are neither the apex nor an end (the ends are T1 and T10). T7 is past the apex. Type II should be treated before the Type I curve.

322Type I group curves

After assessing Mike by observation, AROM, PROM, forward flexion test, red reflex and TART, your Type I diagnosis is consistent with the rib hump (T3-T6 N Sl Rr). You assess each segment within that group curve to find a Type II SD. Where will the Type II SD likely be located?

Ans: Type II found at apex or extremes of Type I curve → first, apex, last

Why: Type II dysfunctions sit at the transition points of a Type I curve: the first, apex and last segments.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A is too broad. C misses the apex. D misses the ends. The course wording is "found at apex or extremes of Type I curves."

323asked 8×2026Type II diagnosis

In a type II somatic dysfunction of the thoracic or lumbar spine coupled motion is most influenced by which of the following?

Ans: Type II → short restrictors (rotatores) + facets control coupling

Why: Type II dysfunctions are maintained by the short restrictors (rotatores, intertransversarii), and the facets control which way the segment couples.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Discs and long superficial muscles (erector spinae) maintain Type I group curves. Costovertebral joints mainly limit sidebending. The longitudinal and interspinous ligaments limit flexion and extension rather than steering coupled motion. Type II is a single segment, often traumatic, and is treated before Type I.

324asked 7×2026Type II diagnosis

You are reviewing a patient's last visit. The diagnosis documented in the chart includes somatic dysfunctions of the thoracic spine including a notation of T3FRrSr. If this diagnosis is still present on this follow-up visit, which of the following findings would you expect on palpatory exam.

Ans: T3 = spine of scapula; FRrSr → right TP posterior (shows in extension)

Why: T3 is at the spine of the scapula. FRrSr means the segment is rotated right, so the right TP is posterior.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A and C describe a Type I group curve, not a single Type II segment; C also puts the rotation on the wrong side. B is backward: a flexed dysfunction becomes symmetric in flexion and worsens in extension. E: the inferior angle of the scapula marks T7, not T3.

3252026Type II diagnosis

You diagnose your lab partner with a somatic dysfunction of thoracic spine as T7ERrSr. Which of the following findings would you also expect on exam?

Why: T7 is at the inferior angle of the scapula. ERrSr means the segment is rotated right, so the right TP is posterior.

Explanation

B is backward: an extended dysfunction becomes symmetric in extension and worsens in flexion. A and E describe a Type I group curve. D: the spine of the scapula marks T3, not T7.

326Type II diagnosis

On examination of your patient, you find a posterior transverse process on the right at the level of the spine of the scapula. The right transverse process becomes less posterior with flexion and becomes more prominent in extension. How would you name this somatic dysfunction?

Ans: Spine of scapula = T3; posterior right, better in flexion → FRrSr

Why: Spine of scapula = T3. The right TP is posterior (rotated right), and it improves with flexion and worsens in extension, so the SD is flexed: T3FRrSr.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

B describes rotation left with extension as the freedom. C and D use T7, which is the inferior angle. A Type II SD is named for the position where its asymmetry disappears.

327Type II diagnosis

Your patient has a posterior TP on the right at the spine of the scapula. When he bends forward the TP disappears under your finger on the right. What is his freedom and what is his restriction?

AnswerDiagnosis T3 FRrSr. Freedom: flexion, rotation right, sidebending right. Restriction: extension, rotation left, sidebending left.

Ans: Spine of scapula = T3 → posterior right TP disappears in flexion → FRrSr; barrier is the opposite

Why: The SD is named for its freedom (position of ease): flexed, rotated right, sidebent right. The restriction is the opposite: extension, rotation left, sidebending left.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Do not confuse the diagnosis with the barrier. Direct techniques such as muscle energy and HVLA take the segment toward the restriction (ERlSl); indirect techniques such as counterstrain go toward the freedom.

328asked 3×2026Type II diagnosis

You palpate a posterior transverse process at T2 on the left. It significantly worsens with the patient sticking out their chest and looking up at the ceiling, and becomes symmetrical with the patient dropping their head to their chest. Which of the following is the correct somatic dysfunction diagnosis?

Ans: Posterior left; worse in extension, symmetric in flexion → flexed → T2FRlSl

Why: A posterior left TP means rotation (and Type II sidebending) left. It becomes symmetric with flexion (head to chest) and worse with extension, so the SD is flexed: T2FRlSl.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A and B rotate right, but the posterior TP is on the left. C is an extended SD, which would become symmetric in extension and worsen in flexion, the opposite of this exam.

329Type II diagnosis

You palpate a posterior T6 vertebral transverse process on the left side. When the patient flexes forward the posterior transverse process becomes less prominent and becomes more prominent in extension. What is your thoracic diagnosis?

Ans: Posterior left TP; better in flexion, worse in extension → T6FRlSl

Why: Posterior left TP = rotated left. It improves in flexion and worsens in extension, so the SD is flexed: T6FRlSl.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

3302026Type II diagnosis

You examine your lab partner and find the following: a posterior transverse process at T4 on the right; no transverse process asymmetry at T3 or T5; symmetry of the T4 transverse processes with your partner sticking out their chest. Which of the following is the correct diagnosis for this dysfunction?

Ans: Single segment → Type II; symmetric with chest out (extension); posterior right → T4ERrSr

Why: Only T4 is asymmetric, so it is a single-segment Type II. The TPs become symmetric with extension (sticking out the chest), so it is extended; posterior right = rotated right: T4ERrSr.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A names flexion, but the asymmetry disappears in extension. B and E name the wrong level and rotation. C is a group curve, yet T3 and T5 are normal.

331Type II diagnosis

A dad tweaks his back bending over and to the right to pick up his toddler. He develops a somatic dysfunction at T10. Which would you expect to be correct?

Ans: Sudden tweak bent forward + right → Type II FRrSr → freedom = flexion

Why: A sudden "tweak" while bent forward and to the right creates a Type II dysfunction that holds that position: T10 FRrSr. An SD is named for its freedom, so flexion is free.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A is a Type I pattern (opposite sides). B: flexion is the freedom; extension is the restriction. D and E: the segment prefers rotation and sidebending right, so left is the barrier. Read the verbs: "prefers/likes/freedom" vs "restricted/barrier."

332Type II diagnosis

On diagnosis, you find that the transverse processes of T3 to T7 are rotated to the left and do not change with flexion or extension. You also find that the transverse processes of the apex of the curve improve with flexion. What would be your shorthand diagnosis of the Type II dysfunction?

Ans: T3-T7 curve apex = T5; apex better in flexion; rotated left → T5FRlSl

Why: The group curve is T3-T7 NSrRl. Type II sits at the apex or ends, and the apex is T5. Its TPs improve with flexion, so it is flexed, rotated and sidebent left: T5FRlSl.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A is the Type I curve, not the Type II. B: an extended SD improves with extension, not flexion. C is an end segment, but the stem points to the apex. D is not a valid Type II (F with opposite-side coupling).

333asked 10×2026Facets open/closed

You examine your partner and note the following diagnosis: T5 F Rr Sr. Which of the following is correct?

Ans: Flexed SD → facet stuck open, opposite side to rotation → FRrSr → left open

Why: In a flexed dysfunction a facet is stuck open, on the side opposite the rotation and sidebending. FRrSr → left facet locked open.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A (right closed) is ERrSr. B (right open) is FRlSl. C (left closed) is ERlSl. Lecture summary: ERrSr = closed right, ERlSl = closed left, FRrSr = open left, FRlSl = open right. "Flexion is the weird one."

336Facets open/closed

A new patient is examined in the OMM clinic. The physician diagnoses a flexion somatic dysfunction with sidebending and rotation to the right. What is the orientation of the facet joint causing the rotation and sidebending to the right?

Why: In a flexion SD the culprit facet is stuck open on the side opposite the rotation and sidebending. Rotated and sidebent right → left facet locked open.

337asked 2×Facets open/closed

You diagnose a somatic dysfunction of T3 ERlSl on your patient. Describe the positions of the posterior facets:

Ans: Extended SD → left facet stuck closed → in flexion it stays closed → turns left

Why: An extended SD has a facet stuck closed. In extreme flexion both facets should open, but the left stays closed, so the vertebra pivots and rotates and sidebends toward the closed side (left).

339asked 2×Facets open/closed

A thoracic segment has a flexion somatic dysfunction: the right facet is locked open and the segment is rotated left. You test it in flexion. What happens?

AnswerNo asymmetry: both facets can open easily, so there is no rotation or sidebending asymmetry. Flexion is the most comfortable position for the patient.

Ans: Flexed SD (facet stuck open) + flexion → both facets open → asymmetry disappears

Why: A flexed SD has a facet stuck open. Flexion asks both facets to open, which they can, so the TPs become symmetric. FRS "disappears" in flexion.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The asymmetry shows in the opposite motion: in extension the right facet cannot close, so the segment turns left. The same logic runs in reverse for an extended SD: it disappears in extension and worsens in flexion.

340asked 2×Facets open/closed

A thoracic segment has a flexion somatic dysfunction with the right facet locked open. You test it in extension. What happens?

AnswerThe asymmetry is exaggerated: the left facet closes normally, but the right facet is locked open and cannot close, so the segment sidebends and rotates left. Diagnosis (position of ease) = flexed, rotated left, sidebent left (FRlSl).

Ans: Right facet stuck open + extension → right cannot close → segment turns left → FRlSl

Why: Extension asks both facets to close. The right facet is stuck open, so the segment pivots and turns to the opposite side (left). The asymmetry is worse in extension.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Contrast with flexion, where both facets open and the asymmetry disappears. A flexed SD always has its open facet on the side opposite the rotation (FRlSl = right open).

341asked 2×Facets open/closed

A thoracic segment has an extension somatic dysfunction with the right facet locked closed. You test it in extension. What happens?

AnswerNo asymmetry: both facets can close easily, so there is no rotation or sidebending asymmetry. Extension is the most comfortable position for the patient.

Why: An extended SD has a facet stuck closed. Extension asks both facets to close, which they can, so the TPs become symmetric. ERS "disappears" in extension.

342asked 2×Facets open/closed

A thoracic segment has an extension somatic dysfunction with the right facet locked closed. You test it in flexion. What happens?

AnswerAsymmetry worsens: the left facet opens, but the right facet is locked closed, so the segment pivots on it and rotates and sidebends right. Diagnosis = ERrSr (extended, rotated right, sidebent right).

Ans: Right facet stuck closed + flexion → right cannot open → pivots → turns right → ERrSr

Why: Flexion asks both facets to open. The right facet is stuck closed, so the segment pivots around it and rotates and sidebends toward it (right). The asymmetry is worse in flexion.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

In an extended SD the closed facet is on the same side as the rotation (ERrSr = right closed). In extension both facets close and the asymmetry disappears.

Viscerosomatic levels

343asked 7×2026Viscerosomatic levels

Patient presents with back pain that improves with manipulation only briefly then returns the next day. On forward bending you find a rib hump on the right that begins at the spinous process of T10 and ends at spinous process of T12. The TPs in that area are all rotated to the right and do not change in flexion or extension. You suspect a visceral origin of this somatic dysfunction. What is highest on your differential?

Ans: SP T10-T12 → segments T11-T12 → T10-T11 level → kidney/upper ureter

Why: Rule of 3s: the T10 SP lies at the T11 TPs and the T12 SP at T12, so the segments are T11-T12. A curve that keeps coming back after OMT suggests a viscerosomatic reflex, and T10-T11 (T9-T12) supplies the kidney and upper ureter.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Hepatitis, gastritis and gallbladder disease map to T5-T9 (upper GI). Pneumonia maps to T1-T6. An older version offered "kidney infection (pyelonephritis)," same level and same answer.

3442026Viscerosomatic levels

Examination of a hospitalized patient reveals the following somatic dysfunction: T6-7 F RrSr. There are associated acute changes of bogginess and marked tenderness consistent with an acute reflex at these levels. Which of the following diagnoses could cause this somatic dysfunction based on visceral segmental innervation?

Ans: Acute T6-7 → T5-T9 upper GI; right rotation → liver → hepatitis

Why: T6-7 falls in T5-T9 (upper abdominal viscera). Right-sided T5-T9 findings fit the liver, gallbladder and duodenum.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Pneumonia maps to T1-T6, which only touches T6. Kidney maps to T10-T11. Appendicitis maps to T10-T11 on the right. Acute viscerosomatic changes are boggy, warm and tender.

3452026Viscerosomatic levels

A patient is evaluated in the emergency department and found to have an acute somatic dysfunction of T7-8 with a marked red reflex on the left side with edema. You suspect a visceral cause for the somatic dysfunction. Which of the following clinical diagnoses is consistent with these TART findings based on shared segmental innervation patterns?

Ans: T7-8 = T5-T9 upper GI; left-sided → stomach → gastritis

Why: T7-8 is in T5-T9 (upper GI). Left-sided findings fit the stomach (left: stomach, spleen, tail of pancreas).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Hepatitis is also T5-T9 but right-sided. Colitis maps lower (T10-T11 for the right colon, T12-L2 for descending and sigmoid). UTI maps to T10-T11 (kidney, upper ureter) or T12-L2 (bladder). Sinusitis maps to T1-T4 (head and neck).

346asked 8×2026Scoliosis types & naming

A mother brings her 11-year-old daughter in for a scoliosis evaluation. She does not complain of back pain, and her past medical history is unremarkable. There is a family history of scoliosis; her mother was diagnosed with scoliosis as a child. Your physical exam shows no leg length discrepancy but does reveal asymmetry of the posterior chest wall on bending forward of the trunk. Which of the following statements is correct regarding this patient's diagnosis?

Ans: Congenital scoliosis → ~75% progressive → "often progress" is true

Why: Congenital curves are about 75% progressive, so "congenital curves often progress" is true.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A: idiopathic causes 70-90% of curves, not short leg. B: a functional hump levels out when the patient sidebends toward the convexity (the hump), not the concavity. C: scoliosis is named for the convexity, and the short, tight erector spinae are on the concave side, so short muscles on the left means convex right (dextroscoliosis). D: functional curves can become structural, not the reverse.

347asked 4×2026Scoliosis types & naming

An elderly patient presents for a general wellness visit without complaints. Structural examination reveals a group curve in the thoracic region. The most likely cause in this patient is

Ans: Most common cause of scoliosis → idiopathic (70-90%)

Why: Idiopathic scoliosis accounts for 70-90% of scoliotic curves, so it is the most likely cause. Osteopathic thinking holds that some are compensation for an unlevel sacral or cranial base.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Cerebral palsy is neuromuscular. Congenital malformation is congenital (about 75% progressive). Psoas syndrome and inflammation are acquired causes. Short leg syndrome, listed in another version, is also acquired or functional.

348asked 2×Scoliosis types & naming

A 16-year-old male's school screening indicated scoliosis. He has no back pain; his father had scoliosis as a child, untreated. There is no leg length discrepancy, but there is asymmetry of the back on forward bending. You suspect:

Ans: Adolescent + family history + no short leg + forward-bend asymmetry → idiopathic

Why: An adolescent with a family history, no leg length discrepancy and asymmetry on forward bending most likely has idiopathic (structural) scoliosis, the most common type.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Functional scoliosis needs a cause such as a short leg, muscle hypertonicity or compensation, and none is given. Neuromuscular scoliosis comes with conditions such as CP or muscular dystrophy. A heel lift is for a short leg, which he does not have.

349Scoliosis types & naming

Structural scoliosis:

Ans: Structural = idiopathic, genetic predisposition, fixed → can be called genetic

Why: Structural scoliosis is also called idiopathic, and it often has a genetic predisposition.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A: OMT can ease symptoms and may slow progression, but it does not reverse a structural curve. B: structural curves do not reduce with forward bending, sidebending or rotation. C: they can be C- or S-shaped; neither is "usually" the rule.

350Scoliosis types & naming

In the wonderful land of Wakanda, you were peacefully walking in the palace until you see Bridget, Jasmine, and Janet fighting Killmonger as he tries to attack. As they defeat Killmonger, Bridget's love, you notice an unequal leg length and very curved spine as they tie him up. What vertebral disorder does Killmonger have?

Ans: Unequal leg length + curved spine → scoliosis

Why: A lateral spinal curve with an unequal leg length describes scoliosis. Short leg syndrome is a recognized cause.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Sway back, military posture and flat back are sagittal-plane postural types, not a lateral curve. A short leg tilts the sacral base, and the spine curves to keep the eyes level.

A 12-year-old adolescent undergoes a scoliosis screening at school. On forward bend test, the examiner notes a thoracic curvature that is convex to the left. Which of the following best describes this spinal curvature?

Ans: Convex left → levoscoliosis → spine sidebent right (toward concavity)

Why: Named for the convexity: convex left = levoscoliosis. The spine is sidebent right, toward the concavity.

Explanation & sources

354Scoliosis types & naming

A patient is side bent to the right. Which side of the curve is convex and which is concave?

AnswerConvex on the left, concave on the right.

Ans: Sidebending side = concave side → SB right → concave right, convex left

Why: The spine bends toward the concavity, so sidebent right = concave right, convex left (a levoscoliosis pattern).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Always name the curve for the convexity: convex left = levoscoliosis. In a Type I curve the bodies rotate toward the convexity, so rotation would be left.

355Scoliosis types & naming

Concept check: is the side of lumbar sidebending the concave or the convex side?

AnswerConcave side.

Ans: Bending toward a side shortens it → sidebending side = concavity

Why: The side the spine sidebends toward is shortened and becomes the concavity. The opposite side is the convexity.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Example: dextroscoliosis is convex right, so the spine is sidebent left and the left side is concave. The concave side has the shortened, tight muscles; ribs crowd together there.

359Scoliosis types & naming

When the ribs are pushed posteriorly on the Left with a Scoliotic curve:

Ans: Ribs posterior on left = convex left → SP swings to concave right

Why: Ribs are pushed posteriorly on the convex side, so the convexity is left. The vertebral body turns toward the convexity and the spinous process swings to the concave (right) side.

360Scoliosis types & naming

When vertebrae rotate in a scoliotic curve (rib hump), which direction does the vertebral body point and which direction does the spinous process point?

AnswerThe vertebral body rotates toward the convexity; the spinous process points toward the concavity.

Ans: Rotation toward convexity → body to convex side → SP (behind) swings to concave side

Why: In scoliosis the vertebral body turns toward the convexity and pushes the ribs back there (the rib hump). The spinous process, behind the body, points toward the concavity.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Example: right thoracic (dextro) curve = sidebent left, rotated right; the bodies face right and the SPs swing left. Ribs on the concave side crowd together.

361asked 3×2026Scoliosis types & naming

A 15-year-old female presents for routine follow-up for idiopathic scoliosis. History is significant for exertional dyspnea with an associated decreased respiratory excursion. Ans: Paravertebral hump → vertebral rotation pushes convex-side ribs back → spinal rotation

Why: The hump is caused by spinal rotation: the vertebrae rotate toward the convexity and push the ribs on the convex side posteriorly.

B and D put the change on the concave side; the hump is on the convex side. A and C blame muscle size, but the hump is bony (ribs), not muscular.

362asked 3×2026Scoliosis types & naming

A 15-year-old female presents for routine follow-up for idiopathic scoliosis. History is significant for exertional dyspnea with an associated decreased respiratory excursion. Structural examination is significant for obvious paravertebral humping on the right. A comprehensive evaluation for cardiovascular disease is unremarkable; however pulmonary function testing is abnormal. The most likely diagnosis is

Ans: Right hump → rotated right → Type I sidebent left → convex right → dextro

Why: A right paravertebral hump = rotated right. Type I sidebends the opposite way (left), so the convexity is right: dextroscoliosis, rotated right, sidebent left.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A is dextro but flips the rotation. C, D and E are levoscoliosis (convex left). E also couples the same side, which group curves do not do.

363Scoliosis types & naming

A 13 year old boy presents to your office after the school nurse noticed a rib hump from T3 to T12. After obtaining x-rays you calculate a cobb angle of 24 degrees and diagnose a moderate, dextroscoliosis. Which somatic dysfunction are you most likely to find?

Ans: Dextroscoliosis = convex right → sidebent left, rotated right → T3-12 NSlRr

Why: Dextroscoliosis = convex right = sidebent left, rotated right. A scoliotic curve is a neutral Type I curve: T3-12NSlRr.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A and D use F or E, which belong to single Type II segments. B and C describe a levoscoliosis (sidebent right, rotated left). Cobb 24 degrees is moderate (20-45).

The apex of a scoliotic curve is:

Ans: Apex = vertebra at the peak of the hump → most rotated

Why: The apex is the vertebra at the highest point of the curve. It is the most rotated vertebra, and it defines the curve's location.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

365asked 2×Scoliosis types & naming

Which is characteristic of scoliosis?

Ans: Scoliosis = lateral curve (sidebending) + coupled vertebral rotation

Why: Scoliosis is a lateral curvature (sidebending) of a group of vertebrae with coupled rotation toward the convexity, which makes the rib hump.

Heads up: The 2020 TA key (speaker notes) marks B, sidebending and flexion. The original options C and E were duplicates (sidebending and rotation). The 2026 lecture defines scoliosis as a lateral (coronal-plane) deviation with rotation toward the convexity, so C is given and the duplicate E is dropped.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Flexion and extension describe sagittal-plane curves (kyphosis, lordosis). These can accompany scoliosis but do not define it. A describes anteroposterior curves.

366asked 8×2026Scoliosis screening & reversibility

The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends scoliosis screening at routine health visits at ages 10, 12, 14, and 16. Which of the following are used in screening for scoliosis?

Ans: Screening → look for rib hump → Adam's forward bend test

Why: Screening uses the Adam's forward bend test: the patient bends forward and you look for a rib hump.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

X-rays confirm the curve and measure the Cobb angle after a positive screen. Bracing is treatment. Passive sidebending tests reversibility once a curve is found. Scoliosis is a coronal-plane curve, so sagittal-plane asymmetry is the wrong plane. Universal school screening is no longer routine in the US.

367asked 2×Scoliosis screening & reversibility

Which test will best screen for scoliosis?

Ans: Screen → Adam's test + level of horizontal planes

Why: Screen with Adam's forward bend test plus checking the horizontal planes (occiput, shoulders, scapulae, iliac crests, PSIS, greater trochanters) for levelness.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Thomas test checks hip flexor tightness. Straight leg raise checks lumbar radicular pain or hamstrings. Spurling's checks cervical radiculopathy, and x-rays confirm rather than screen.

You notice a rib hump on the right with Adam's forward flexion test; it gets better with sidebending right and left. What classification of scoliosis is this testing?

Explanation

Severity is the Cobb angle. Location is the apex vertebra (thoracic, lumbar, double major). Etiology is the cause (idiopathic, congenital, acquired, neuromuscular). Mnemonic RSLE ("wrestle").

369Scoliosis screening & reversibility

You are performing a musculoskeletal exam on your partner's thoracic spine and find a mid-thoracic left sided rib hump on Adam's forward bend test which minimizes with sidebending to the left. What is the significance of this finding?

Ans: Hump left lessens with sidebending left (toward hump) → reversible → functional

Why: The hump lessens when the patient sidebends toward it, so the curve is reversible, which means a functional curve.

A: a structural curve would not change. B: the hump is on the convex side, not the concave side. D: rib humps come from Type I group curves.

371Scoliosis screening & reversibility

While performing the Adam's Forward Bend Test, you notice a rib hump on your patient's thoracic region. When the patient sidebends, the rib hump does not improve. Which of the following describes the patient's diagnosis, and what is the first sign of this condition?

373Scoliosis screening & reversibility

A 16-year-old boy presents for evaluation of uneven shoulders noticed by his parents. During the Adam's forward bending test, his spinal curve corrects with sidebending and he is diagnosed with functional scoliosis. All of the following are characteristics of functional scoliosis except:

Ans: Functional scoliosis hypertonicity = Type I (bowstring), not Type II → C false

Why: The muscle hypertonicity behind functional scoliosis comes from Type I group dysfunction (a bowstring effect of long muscles), not Type II.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A, B and D are true: functional curves are postural or biomechanical, must be treated while flexible or they can become structural, and come from causes such as short leg syndrome or some neurological conditions.

374asked 2×Scoliosis screening & reversibility

Your patient has thoracic back pain; the leg length test shows one leg shorter. You also see a Type 1 SD with hypertonic muscle on one side creating a bowstring effect on the spine. What do you suspect?

Ans: Short leg + Type I hypertonic bowstring → secondary curve → functional

Why: A short leg and hypertonic muscle pulling like a bowstring are causes of a functional curve.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Structural and idiopathic curves have no such correctable cause. Neuromuscular scoliosis comes with conditions such as CP or muscular dystrophy. Functional causes: hypertonicity, weakness, compensation, short leg.

375Scoliosis screening & reversibility

You have a patient with a rib hump in the lower right thorax. When you stabilize their hips as you look at the hump and they side-bend to the left, the rib hump gets worse/more pronounced. Name that test and type of curve in their spine.

Ans: Hump changes with sidebending → flexible curve → functional; test is Adam's

Why: The test is Adam's forward bend with sidebending to check reversibility. The hump changes with sidebending, so the curve is still flexible, which the key reads as functional.

Heads up: Keyed A by the 2025 TA review. The stem only describes sidebending away from the hump (which exaggerates any curve), so it does not truly prove reversibility. The key treats any change with sidebending as a flexible (functional) curve.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

"Aaron's" test does not exist. A structural curve is fixed and should not change with sidebending. The cleaner check is sidebending toward the hump: a functional hump levels out.

376asked 8×2026Scoliosis screening & reversibility

A 35-year-old woman seen in clinic with a symptom of mid-thoracic pain, low back and right hip pain for the last 8 months. It started shortly after an MVA (motor vehicle accident), where she was rear ended. She was stopped at a red light, when a Yukon traveling 40 mph hit her car. She was wearing her seatbelt and the airbags did not deploy. PMHx: GERD PSHx: none Meds: Zantac 75 mg qd prn. Denies etoh, tobacco, ivdu. PE: BP 128/60, Neurological examination was within normal limits, ROM testing of the extremities was full both actively and passively; abdominal exam was normal; Osteopathic structural exam: T1FRrSr, T4FSrSr, Hypertonicity at left side T1-7, PSIS higher on left. Adams' test + rib hump on the right - improves with sidebending right and rotating left. Left medial malleolus superior but levels out after OMT. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?

Ans: Post-MVA onset + hump improves with sidebending + short leg levels after OMT → functional

Why: The curve started after trauma, the hump improves with sidebending and rotation (reversible = functional), and the apparent short leg levels out after OMT (not anatomic).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

An anatomic short leg would not level out after OMT. Congenital scoliosis is present from birth and is structural. A compression fracture would leave a fixed deformity that does not reverse with sidebending.

377asked 2×Cobb angle & treatment

To test the severity of scoliosis on postural X-ray, you measure the angles of the most tilted vertebra above the apex and the most tilted vertebra below the apex. What is this called?

Ans: Angle between most-tilted vertebrae above and below apex → Cobb angle

Why: The Cobb angle measures severity on a postural x-ray using the most tilted end vertebrae above and below the apex.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The other options are not standard measures. The apex vertebra defines location, not severity.

378asked 4×2026Cobb angle & treatment

A 12-year-old female presents for routine follow-up for her chronic thoracic scoliosis. She has minimal symptoms but is cosmetically not pleased with her appearance. Structural examination reveals a small paravertebral hump on the right that improves with right sidebending. A plain film radiograph is obtained and the Cobb angle of 12 degrees is measured which is stable from prior imaging. This angle represents the intersection of

Ans: Cobb = lines along end plates of end vertebrae in coronal plane

Why: The Cobb angle is formed by tangent lines along the end plates of the top and bottom vertebrae of the curve, measured in the coronal plane (an AP film).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A and B use lines parallel to flexed or extended positions, which is not the method. D and E use the sagittal plane, but scoliosis is a coronal-plane curve.

379Cobb angle & treatment

While reviewing your patient's x-ray you calculate a cobb angle of 13 degrees and classify the severity of the scoliosis as…

Ans: 13 degrees → 5-15 = mild

Why: Mild scoliosis is 5-15 degrees, so 13 degrees is mild.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Moderate is 20-45 degrees; severe is more than 50 degrees. "Extreme" is not a category.

380asked 2×Cobb angle & treatment

A 14-year-old adolescent undergoes a school scoliosis screening. The physician orders a standing postural x-ray which shows a Cobb angle of 35°, the severity of this scoliosis is classified as

Ans: 35 degrees → 20-45 = moderate

Why: Moderate scoliosis is 20-45 degrees, so 35 degrees is moderate. Curves over 30 degrees should be treated.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Mild is 5-15 degrees. Severe is more than 50 degrees, which compromises respiration. Another version used 30 degrees, also moderate.

You measure a Cobb angle of 40 degrees. What classification of severity of scoliosis is this?

Ans: 40 degrees → 20-45 = moderate

Why: 40 degrees falls in the moderate range (20-45 degrees).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Mild is 5-15 degrees. Severe is more than 50 degrees. Do not call it severe just because it is large; the cutoff is 50.

382Cobb angle & treatment

You have a young patient that you have found to have a Cobb angle of 30º. The C curve is concave right. Classify this case of scoliosis.

Ans: 30 degrees = moderate; concave right → convex left → levoscoliosis

Why: 30 degrees is moderate (20-45). Concave right means convex left, and scoliosis is named for the convexity: levoscoliosis.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A misgrades the curve and names it for the concavity. C names it for the concavity. D and E misgrade it as severe (more than 50).

383asked 5×2026Cobb angle & treatment

A 15-year-old female presents for routine follow-up for idiopathic scoliosis. History is significant for exertional dyspnea with an associated decreased respiratory excursion. Structural examination is significant for obvious paravertebral humping on the right. A comprehensive evaluation for cardiovascular disease is unremarkable; however pulmonary function testing is abnormal. Which of the following is most associated with this patient's condition?

Ans: Respiratory but not cardiac compromise → >50 but <70-75 → 52 degrees

Why: Curves over 50 degrees compromise respiratory function. Cardiovascular compromise starts around 70 degrees (75 in some sources), so 52 degrees fits lungs only.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

B (77 degrees) would also compromise cardiovascular function, but her cardiac workup is normal. C, D and E are causes (neuromuscular, acquired, congenital), not markers of respiratory-only compromise.

384asked 8×2026Cobb angle & treatment

A 17 year old girl came to the urgent care clinic complaining of upper back pain for the past month. She has a continuous pain in her upper back, especially while studying. Stress worsens the pain. PMHX (Past Medical History): none, PSHX (Past Surgical History): none, Meds: None Denies alcohol use, tobacco, IV Drug use. With forward bending, rib hump was seen on the right. Palpation of spine revealed dextroscoliosis from T4-T10. There was hypertonicity of the erector spinae muscles on the left side. Thoracic spine x rays revealed a Cobb angle of 20 degrees. The Beighton non-dominant limb hypermobility screening test score was positive for 2 out of 5 parameters. Which of the following is a true statement regarding this patient?

Ans: IA5: safe to perform OMT before orthopedic evaluation

Why: The IA5 slide says it is safe to perform OMT before orthopedic evaluation. OMT aims to improve function, posture and mobility and may slow progression.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A: a Beighton score of 2/5 does not indicate hypermobility, so HVLA is not contraindicated on that basis. B: muscle energy is direct; dextroscoliosis is sidebent left, rotated right, so ME positions toward the barrier (sidebend right, rotate left). C: OMT does not need to wait for an x-ray.

385Cobb angle & treatment

Which of the following is false regarding the treatment of scoliosis?

Ans: OMT is safe before orthopedic evaluation → "cannot" is false

Why: OMT can be performed before orthopedic evaluation, so C is the false statement.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A, B and D are true: surgery is considered for severe curves (especially over 45 degrees); orthotics, bracing, exercise and PT are options; and patient and family education is part of care.

386asked 2×Cobb angle & treatment

What is NOT an advantage of using OMT to treat scoliosis?

Why: OMT for scoliosis increases mobility. "Decreases mobility" is the one that is not an advantage.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The listed benefits are from lecture: mobilizing and slowing progression, relaxing and stretching contracted muscles, correcting SD, increasing mobility and normalizing tissues.

387asked 4×2026Cobb angle & treatment

A 12-year-old female presents for routine follow-up for her chronic thoracic scoliosis. She has minimal symptoms but is cosmetically not pleased with her appearance. Structural examination reveals a small paravertebral hump on the right that improves with right sidebending. Prognosis and management options are discussed. Surgery for scoliosis is most likely to have favorable results in which of the following cases?

Ans: Surgery → severe progressive curves with organ compromise → progressed despite bracing + respiratory compromise

Why: Surgery is for severe, progressive curves, especially those compromising respiration. A curve that progressed despite bracing and affects breathing fits best.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A: progression alone is first managed with closer monitoring and bracing. C and D: 30-35 degrees is moderate and usually braced. E: 40 degrees in a skeletally mature patient is below the usual surgical range (over 45-50 degrees). Course COMLEX rule: under 25 monitor, 25-45 brace, over 45 surgery.

388asked 3×2026Cobb angle & treatment

A 12-year-old female presents for routine follow-up for her chronic thoracic scoliosis. She has minimal symptoms but is cosmetically not pleased with her appearance. Structural examination reveals a small paravertebral hump on the right that improves with right sidebending. Which of the following is the most appropriate management in this patient?

Ans: Small hump that improves with sidebending (mild, functional) → OMT, PT, education

Why: A small hump that improves with sidebending is mild and flexible. The right care is OMT, physical therapy and patient/family education.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A: a heel lift is for a short leg, which is not described. C: monthly x-rays add radiation without changing care; mild curves are rechecked about every 6-12 months. D: surgery is for severe, progressive curves. E: orthotics or bracing are for moderate curves (about 25-45 degrees).

389asked 2×Short leg

How do you measure leg length discrepancy?

Ans: Clinical leg length → tape from ASIS to medial malleolus

Why: At the bedside, measure leg length from the ASIS to the medial malleolus of each leg.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

PSIS, lateral malleolus and greater trochanter are not the standard points. A standing postural x-ray is the most accurate test.

390asked 8×2026Short leg

What is the most accurate way to determine a leg length discrepancy?

Ans: Most accurate → standing postural x-ray (iliac crests, sacral base, femoral heads)

Why: The standing postural x-ray of the iliac crests, sacral base and femoral heads is the most accurate way to determine a leg length discrepancy.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

ASIS to medial malleolus is the bedside measurement but less accurate. Pant-leg complaints, knee flexion deformity and IT band tightness are clues, not measurements. The film is taken barefoot with L5 centered and both acetabula visible (about 2 mm error).

391Short leg

A 30-year-old man presents with functional scoliosis. On physical exam, you note a pelvic tilt and a possible leg length discrepancy. Which of the following is the most accurate method to confirm a diagnosis of short leg syndrome?

Ans: Most accurate confirmation → standing postural x-ray

Why: The standing postural x-ray of the iliac crests, sacral base and femoral heads is the most accurate confirmation.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Tape measurement (ASIS to medial malleolus) and palpating iliac crest heights are less accurate screening tools. The standing flexion test checks iliosacral motion, not leg length.

392asked 3×2026Short leg

A young adult presents with low back pain and measurements reveal an anatomic short leg on the right side. This is most associated with

Ans: Right short leg → sacral base low right → lumbar sidebends left, convex right

Why: With a right short leg the sacral base drops on the right, and the lumbar spine sidebends away (left) and rotates toward the short leg, giving a curve convex right.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A: landmarks are low on the short (right) side. D: the pelvis shifts toward the long leg (left). E: the tender iliolumbar ligament is on the short-leg side, which is the side of lumbar convexity (right). C: the textbook pairs a right short leg with a left-on-left forward torsion, not right-on-right.

393Short leg

While performing an osteopathic structural exam on your patient, you notice a lateral curve in the lumbar region. You examine further and discover the left medial malleolus is slightly higher than the right. What else would you expect to find on your physical examination?

Ans: Left malleolus higher → left leg short → lumbar sidebends right, rotates left

Why: The left medial malleolus is higher, so the left leg is short. The lumbar spine sidebends away from the short leg (right) and rotates toward it (left): L2-4NSrRl.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A: the curve is convex left (levoscoliosis), not dextro. B is the pattern for a right short leg. C: the left leg is the short one.

394asked 4×2026Short leg

A 75-year-old male complains of persistent buttock pain despite right total hip arthroplasty. Standing palpatory examination reveals the iliac crest and greater trochanter to be inferior on the left. Postural radiographic studies reveal an unlevel sacral base that is inferior on the left. The most likely cause of this patient's leg length discrepancy is

Ans: Hip arthroplasty + new leg length difference → most common cause = hip replacement

Why: Hip replacement is the most common cause of a short leg, and this patient just had a total hip arthroplasty.

Heads up: The textbook calls hip replacement the most common cause of an anatomic short leg. The 2026 review slide lists it as the "most common cause of functional short leg." Either way the answer is E.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A: dislocation would present acutely. B and C would make the left leg short only through a left hip process, and protrusio acetabuli (femoral head displaced medially) is uncommon. D: scoliosis is the result, not the cause. Treatment: balance the sacrum with OMT and heel lift, then re-evaluate.

395asked 3×2026Short leg

A 75-year-old male complains of persistent buttock pain despite right total hip arthroplasty. Standing palpatory examination reveals the iliac crest and greater trochanter to be inferior on the left. Postural radiographic studies reveal an unlevel sacral base that is inferior on the left. The structural exam finding most associated with this presentation is

Ans: Left short leg → pelvis shifts toward long leg → side shift right

Why: The left leg is short, so the pelvis side shifts toward the long leg (right).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A: the lumbar curve is convex toward the short leg (left). D: the innominate on the short side rotates anterior, not posterior. E: the anterior (deep) sacral base is on the short (left) side. B: pelvic rotation is not the defining finding.

396asked 3×2026Short leg

A 65-year-old female presents with acute low back pain. Observation reveals she has a frail body habitus with a wide-based, antalgic gait. Physical examination reveals a leg length discrepancy of 5/8th inches. A postural radiographic series is obtained and reveals the right femoral head is 1/2 inch cephalad when compared to the left. The most valid objective for heel lift therapy is to

Ans: Heel lift goal → level the sacral base (functional balance)

Why: The goal of lift therapy is to level the sacral base. A level base lets the spine above it rebalance.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Iliac crest and leg length numbers can differ from the sacral base and are not the target. Lumbar and thoracic curves improve secondarily once the base is level.

397asked 3×2026Short leg

A 65-year-old female presents with acute low back pain. Observation reveals she has a frail body habitus with a wide-based, antalgic gait. Physical examination reveals a leg length discrepancy of 5/8th inches. A postural radiographic series is obtained and reveals the right femoral head is 1/2 inch cephalad when compared to the left. The most appropriate initial management is

Ans: Frail, elderly, acute pain → start small → 1/16 inch heel lift, recheck 2 weeks

Why: In a frail, elderly patient with acute pain, start with a small 1/16-inch heel lift and recheck in 2 weeks.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The full measured difference is rarely given at once unless the leg suddenly lost length (for example, after a fracture). A 1/8-inch start suits a patient who is not fragile. Increasing without rechecking (D) or waiting 8 weeks (B) is too aggressive or too slow.

398Direct vs indirect

A direct technique is best described as:

Ans: Direct → engage the restrictive barrier → patient placed toward the barrier

Why: A direct technique starts by positioning the patient toward the restrictive barrier, which is opposite the somatic dysfunction.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A describes a passive technique and D an active one; active/passive is a separate axis from direct/indirect. C is the definition of an indirect technique. Muscle energy and HVLA are the course's direct techniques.

399asked 7×2026Direct vs indirect

When considering osteopathic manipulative treatment, which of the following statements accurately describes an indirect technique?

Ans: Indirect → position of ease → ease = the diagnosis → position equals the SD

Why: An indirect technique places the patient in the position of ease, which equals the diagnosis (the somatic dysfunction), at the start of the modality.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A, B and C all describe a direct technique: into the barrier, opposite the diagnosis, stretching the hypertonic muscle. D describes an active technique, which is a separate axis. Counterstrain is the course's example of an indirect, passive technique.

400asked 2×Direct vs indirect

What is the difference between a direct technique and an indirect technique?

Ans: Indirect → away from barrier → into ease → hypertonic muscle shortened

Why: An indirect technique moves away from the barrier into the position of ease, which shortens the hypertonic muscle. A direct technique goes toward the barrier and stretches it.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A and D swap the direction for each technique. C pairs the right direction for direct with the wrong muscle effect: moving into the barrier lengthens (stretches) a hypertonic muscle. Counterstrain is the classic shortening (indirect) technique.
