401Direct vs indirect

A first-year medical student presents with upper back pain after long hours of slouching. Exam reveals T4 FRrSr. For the first treatment, you position the patient into extension, left rotation, left sidebending. For the second treatment, you position the patient into flexion, right rotation, right sidebending. Which of the following best describes the techniques used?

Ans: FRrSr = freedom → ERlSl is the barrier (direct) → FRrSr is the ease (indirect)

Why: The diagnosis names the freedom. Positioning into the opposite (ERlSl) engages the barrier, so the first is direct. Positioning into FRrSr matches the diagnosis, so the second is indirect.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A and B ignore that the two positions are mirror images. C reverses them. Quick rule: a position that reads the same as the diagnosis is indirect; the exact opposite is direct.

402Direct vs indirect

What are direct vs indirect techniques?

AnswerIndirect: patient placed in the position of ease (equal to the diagnosis) at the start, e.g., counterstrain. Direct: patient positioned toward the restrictive barrier (opposite the diagnosis) at the start, e.g., muscle energy and HVLA.

Ans: Ease = diagnosis → indirect; barrier = opposite of diagnosis → direct

Why: Indirect means starting in the position of ease, which equals the somatic dysfunction. Direct means starting at the restrictive barrier, opposite the diagnosis.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Counterstrain is indirect; muscle energy and HVLA are direct. Myofascial release can be done either way. Direct/indirect describes where you position; active/passive describes whether the patient contracts.

403asked 3×Technique types

Match each item to one description: Indirect technique; Counterstrain; Muscle energy; HVLA; Direct technique. Descriptions: A. Active and direct. B. Passive and direct. C. Passive and indirect. D. Positioned toward the barrier. E. Patient is placed in a position of ease (which equals the diagnosis, the somatic dysfunction).

AnswerIndirect technique–E; Counterstrain–C; Muscle energy–A; HVLA–B; Direct technique–D.

Ans: ME = active + direct; HVLA = passive + direct; CS = passive + indirect

Why: Muscle energy is active and direct, HVLA is passive and direct, counterstrain is passive and indirect. Direct means toward the barrier; indirect means the position of ease, equal to the diagnosis.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The 2023 version used only three items (HVLA, muscle energy, counterstrain) matched to direct-active, direct-passive and indirect. The only active technique of the three is muscle energy, because the patient contracts against the physician.

Active, direct is muscle energy. Passive, direct is HVLA. No technique in this lecture is active and indirect. The patient must stay passive, even while being returned to neutral, or the reflex can restart.

408Technique types

What are active vs passive techniques?

AnswerActive: the patient contracts or moves on request (muscle energy, active myofascial release). Passive: the patient stays relaxed while the physician does the work (counterstrain, indirect; HVLA, direct).

Ans: Patient effort → active (ME); no patient effort → passive (CS, HVLA)

Why: Active techniques use the patient's own muscle effort, as in muscle energy. Passive techniques keep the patient relaxed, as in counterstrain and HVLA.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Active/passive is independent of direct/indirect: HVLA is passive but direct, counterstrain is passive and indirect. Myofascial release can be done actively or passively.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Lawrence Jones developed counterstrain, which is indirect, passive and acts on the muscle spindle (option C describes counterstrain). E has the right person but the counterstrain mechanism. Mitchell first published ME in 1958; his son published the ME manual in 1979.

410ME basics

Fill in the blanks: "____ is a direct and active osteopathic treatment modality developed by ____ which requires the physician to engage a restrictive barrier, while having the patient move into their freedom. It uses gentle isometric contractions to cause muscle relaxation through autogenic or reciprocal inhibition and lengthening of a hypertonic muscle (or group of muscles)."

Ans: Direct + active + isometric contraction into freedom → muscle energy → Fred Mitchell

Why: Only muscle energy is direct and active with isometric contractions, and it was developed by Fred Mitchell, DO.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Counterstrain (Jones) is indirect and passive. Still's technique and cranial osteopathy (Sutherland) do not use patient isometric contraction against a barrier. Autogenic inhibition is the Golgi tendon organ effect behind post-isometric relaxation.

Explanation

C is wrong because after each effort you take up the slack to the new barrier, not the freedom. D is wrong: ME has absolute contraindications (e.g., no consent, patient unable to follow commands) and relative ones.

412ME basics

Muscle energy is an example of a(n) ____ technique; it engages the ____ barrier.

Ans: ME → direct → engages the SD's restrictive barrier (never the anatomic)

Why: Muscle energy is direct and engages the restrictive barrier, the early abnormal stop caused by the somatic dysfunction.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The anatomic barrier is the limit of passive motion; forcing past it tears tissue, so no technique targets it. Indirect techniques move away from the restrictive barrier. ME starts at the "feather edge," the first point where tension is palpable.

413ME basics

Ans: ME is direct → 'indirect' is the exception

Why: Muscle energy is a direct technique, so "indirect" is the false statement.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Isokinetic strengthening, reciprocal inhibition and post-isometric relaxation are all among the 9 physiologic principles of ME. The others: joint mobilization using muscle force, respiratory assistance, oculocephalic reflex, crossed extensor reflex, isolytic lengthening, and using muscle force to move another region.

Each option on its own is a valid use, so "all of the above" is best. Muscle contraction also pumps lymph and venous blood, which is why ME helps edema and congestion. ME can also prepare a joint for HVLA.

417ME physiology

You are performing muscle energy and wonder about the physiology behind the technique. You conclude that you are:

Ans: Patient pushes toward freedom → tendon tension rises → GTO reflex → relaxation

Why: In muscle energy the patient pushes toward their freedom against your counterforce. That raises tendon tension, which fires the Golgi tendon organ and relaxes the muscle.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

C has the right reflex but the wrong push direction: the patient is placed into the barrier but pushes toward the freedom. A and D describe the spindle, which is the counterstrain story. E is a joke option.

418ME physiology

After positioning the patient into the restrictive barrier, you instruct them to gently push against your resistance for 3-5 seconds, then relax. You then reposition them further into the barrier. What is the relaxation called and what is the physiologic basis for why the muscles lengthen after contraction?

Ans: Isometric push → tendon tension → GTO inhibits same muscle → post-isometric relaxation

Why: This is post-isometric relaxation. The contraction raises tendon tension, and the Golgi tendon organs inhibit the alpha motor neurons of the same muscle (negative feedback), so you can take up the slack.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

B names reciprocal inhibition, which relaxes a muscle by contracting its antagonist, and pairs it with a wrong mechanism. C is used for injured limbs. D, the stretch reflex, causes contraction and is what ME avoids. E has the right name but the wrong mechanism; raising gamma gain increases tone.

Lecture slide (1)
419asked 2×ME physiology

Which of the following uses the Golgi tendon proprioceptors?

Ans: GTO inhibits the contracting muscle → basis of post-isometric relaxation

Why: In post-isometric relaxation, the Golgi tendon proprioceptors inhibit the active contraction after an isometric effort, leaving a refractory window for passive stretch.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The crossed extensor reflex uses learned crossed locomotion patterns. Isokinetic strengthening uses a slow concentric contraction to strengthen a weak muscle. Isolytic lengthening stretches a fibrotic muscle while it contracts (physician force > patient force). PIR uses gentle 10-20 lb pressure; the lecture example is hamstring spasm.

420ME physiology

Samantha has an acute left quadriceps spasm after a weight training session. To relax the left quadriceps, Dr. Mitchell tells her to apply a gentle contraction with her left hamstrings. Which muscle energy principle is used here?

Ans: Contract hamstrings (agonist) → reflex relaxation of quadriceps (antagonist) → reciprocal inhibition

Why: Reciprocal inhibition: a gentle contraction of the agonist (hamstrings) reflexly relaxes its antagonist (quadriceps). It is used to lengthen a muscle in cramp or acute spasm.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Post-isometric relaxation would have the spasming quadriceps itself contract. The oculocephalic reflex uses eye movements. Isolytic lengthening uses a strong contraction overpowered by the physician for chronic fibrosis, not acute spasm. Reciprocal inhibition force is very gentle (ounces, not pounds).

421asked 2×ME physiology

A 30-year-old male has a hypertonic sternocleidomastoid. You set him up at his barrier and tell him to look toward his freedom. Which physiologic principle of muscle energy is involved?

Ans: Eye motion drives neck muscle contraction → oculocephalic (oculocephalogyric) reflex

Why: The oculocephalic reflex uses voluntary eye motion: the cervical and trunk muscles contract reflexly to follow the eyes. The force is exceptionally gentle.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Reciprocal inhibition would mean contracting the opposing muscle directly; the lecture example is torticollis from acute SCM spasm, which is why D tempts. Here the cue is the eyes. This technique is contraindicated after recent eye surgery or eye trauma.

422asked 5×ME physiology

Which of the following mechanisms can be utilized when treating a patient with rib somatic dysfunctions?

Ans: Ribs move with breathing → use the patient's breath → respiratory assistance

Why: Respiratory assistance uses the patient's voluntary, exaggerated breathing as the corrective force, with the physician holding a fulcrum. It is the ME principle for rib dysfunctions such as an inhalation rib.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Eye motion (oculocephalic reflex) targets cervical and trunk muscles. Patients cannot selectively contract single intercostals. The crossed extensor reflex is for injured extremities. Isolytic contraction is for fibrotic, shortened muscle. The 2020 version asked about a rib 4 inhalation dysfunction, with the same answer.

423ME physiology

A patient with a broken right femur is being treated with muscle energy using the crossed extensor reflex. Which of the following correctly describes the crossed extensor reflex?

Ans: Injured limb can't be treated → work the opposite limb → crossed locomotion reflex

Why: The crossed extensor reflex uses learned locomotion patterns: voluntary flexor contraction on one side relaxes the contralateral flexor and contracts the contralateral extensor. It lets you treat a limb that is too injured or inaccessible (fracture, burn).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A is reciprocal inhibition. B is isokinetic strengthening. D is the oculocephalic reflex. Crossed extensor force is very gentle (ounces, not pounds); the lecture example is a severe acute hamstring strain.

424ME setup

When performing muscle energy, you place the patient in what direction in relation to their somatic dysfunction?

Ans: ME is direct → position into barrier → patient pushes back toward freedom

Why: Muscle energy is direct, so you position at the barrier, then the patient pushes toward the freedom against your equal counterforce (isometric).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Pushing toward the barrier would move the patient through it actively, which is not ME. Starting in the freedom is indirect positioning. After 3-5 s the patient relaxes, you take up the slack to the new barrier, and repeat 3-5 times.

425asked 2×ME setup

Which is true regarding the localization of forces used in muscle energy technique?

Ans: Contract 3-5 s → both relax → pause → take up slack to the new barrier

Why: After each contraction both relax, the physician pauses for neuromuscular adaptation, then takes up the slack and re-engages the new restrictive barrier.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A is wrong: the barrier is engaged at the feather edge in all three planes. B describes isolytic lengthening and C an isotonic (concentric) contraction; standard ME uses an equal and opposite counterforce (isometric). A common error is not letting the patient rest between contractions.

Explanation

B is wrong: ME engages barriers in three planes, not freedoms. C is wrong because the contraction is isometric, not isokinetic. D is wrong: always recheck the original somatic dysfunction; forgetting to re-evaluate is a listed common error.

Why: In ME the patient is placed into the barrier but pushes toward the freedom, which is the diagnosis: rotate right, sidebend left.

Why: For a Type I group curve, monitor at the apex (T7) and position into the barrier, which reverses the diagnosis: neutral, sidebent right, rotated left.

Explanation & sources

A and E monitor at the ends of the curve and add extension. B and C use Type II-style flexion or extension with same-side coupling. Type I (neutral) dysfunctions are maintained by long restrictor (polyarticular) muscles.

Explanation

A is a Kirksville Crunch, which is HVLA. B positions into the freedom (indirect). D mixes the planes and leaves out extension, so it does not lock the Type II segment.

436Counterstrain basics

A 23-year-old medical student presents with acute right-sided upper back pain after a back day at the gym. A tender point on the right transverse process of T5 is treated with counterstrain: the patient is passively positioned into comfort for 90 seconds, then slowly returned to neutral. Which of the following best explains the physiologic mechanism behind this treatment?

Ans: Shorten muscle → spindle firing drops → gamma gain resets → tender point softens

Why: Counterstrain shortens the hypertonic muscle, so the spindle stops firing inappropriately and gamma motor neuron activity (gamma gain) is reduced. The tender point softens.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A is the muscle energy (post-isometric relaxation) mechanism. C and D are other ME principles that require patient contraction. E is a distractor. High-yield: counterstrain resets gamma gain.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Each of A, B and C restates part of the lecture definition. The pressure used to find one is the amount that blanches your fingernail bed; it does not hurt healthy tissue and does not radiate.

439asked 3×Counterstrain treatment

When fine-tuning position for counterstrain, what is the minimum acceptable reduction of pain?

Ans: Tender point starts at 10 → must drop to ≤3 → at least 70% reduction

Why: The tender point is called a 10; the position of ease must bring it to 3 or less, a reduction of at least 70% (goal 100%).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

30% and 60% leave the point too tender. 95% is a good result, not the minimum. After positioning, hold 90 s, return slowly and passively to neutral, then recheck for 3 or less.

440Counterstrain treatment

In performing counterstrain, approximately how long would one hold the patient in a position of comfort to achieve a decrease in proprioceptive firing and to reduce stimulation of muscle contraction?

Ans: Counterstrain hold → 90 seconds

Why: Hold the position of comfort for 90 seconds. That lets proprioceptive firing fall in frequency and amplitude so the mechanoreceptors stop driving contraction.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

30, 45 and 120 seconds are distractors. During the hold you may feel a therapeutic pulse at the tender point, which signals good relaxation. Then return the patient slowly and passively to neutral.

441Counterstrain treatment

What is the primary treatment position for a posterior counterstrain tender point?

Ans: Posterior point → extension; anterior point → flexion

Why: Posterior tender points are usually treated in extension; anterior points in flexion.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Flexion is for anterior points. Sidebending and rotation are fine-tuning motions added in small arcs once the primary motion is set.

442asked 6×2026Counterstrain treatment

A 45-year-old male presents with upper back pain. Physical exam identifies tender points at the spinous processes of T2-4 with associated tender points along the sternum. The T2-4 sternum points are much more tender. In applying a counterstrain treatment, which of the following best describes the best initial tender point to treat and its treatment positioning?

Ans: Most tender = anterior → middle of a row = T3 → anterior point → flexion

Why: Treat the most significant points first (the sternal, anterior ones), and in a row treat the middle one first (T3). Anterior points are treated in flexion.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

C and E pick the less tender posterior points. D has the right point but the posterior-point motion. A pairs a posterior point with flexion. AT3 sits on the sternum at the level of the 3rd costosternal joint.

443Counterstrain treatment

On physical examination, you locate an anterior thoracic counterstrain tender point on the right lateral iliac crest. What is the most likely thoracic vertebral level associated with this tender point?

Ans: Anterior thoracic point on the iliac crest (midaxillary line) → AT12

Why: The anterior T12 tender point lies on the inner surface of the iliac crest at the midaxillary line.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

AT7-AT11 lie higher, on the anterior abdominal wall between the xiphoid and the lower abdomen, so T8, T9 and T10 are too high. AT1-AT6 are on the sternum at the matching costal levels.

444HVLA

Which of the following is FALSE regarding HVLA?

Ans: HVLA thrusts through the barrier → direct, not indirect

Why: HVLA is direct: the segment is locked into the barrier and the thrust goes through it. Calling it indirect is false.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A, C, D and E are true: HVLA is passive, uses a short quick thrust, is often delivered on exhalation, and may produce a pop (cavitation), though a pop is not proof of success.

445asked 9×2026HVLA

Which of the following is an indication for HVLA?

Ans: HVLA needs distinct SD with TART + firm restrictive end-feel → all listed

Why: HVLA is indicated for a distinct somatic dysfunction confirmed by TART (tissue texture change, asymmetry, restriction, tenderness) with a firm restrictive articular end-feel at the barrier.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Each option is one required piece, so "all of the above" is right. Pain alone is NOT an indication for HVLA. A rubbery, indistinct or hypermobile barrier means choose another technique.

447HVLA

You are evaluating a 22-year-old female for back pain and find a somatic dysfunction of T5 that improves with flexion. You decide to treat it with HVLA. Which of the following is considered an indication for HVLA?

Ans: HVLA needs a firm articular end-feel at the barrier → D

Why: A firm restrictive articular end-feel at the barrier (with TART findings) is the indication for HVLA.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Hypermobility is a relative contraindication. Pain alone is not an indication. A rubbery end-feel means the thrust will fail and another technique should be used.

448asked 3×HVLA

What end-feel is required for treatment with HVLA?

Ans: HVLA barrier must feel solid; rubbery/indistinct → choose another technique

Why: The barrier must have a firm, solid end-feel for HVLA to work.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

If the barrier feels rubbery, indistinct or hypermobile, the thrust will be ineffective and another modality should be chosen. Boggy describes acute tissue texture, not a joint end-feel.

449HVLA

A patient presents with back pain after a prolonged period of studying, and you decide to treat using HVLA after myofascial release. Which of the following describes the physiologic mechanism underlying HVLA?

Ans: Quick thrust suddenly stretches tight muscle → GTO fires → reflex relaxation

Why: The thrust suddenly stretches the tight muscle and tendon, strongly stimulating the Golgi tendon organs, which reflexly relax the hypertonic muscle. The lecture also credits a barrage of spindle afferents that turns down gamma activity.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

B describes counterstrain, which works by passive positioning, not a thrust. C is a muscle energy principle. D and E are distractors; increasing agonist contraction would defeat the treatment. ME loads the GTO slowly by isometric contraction; HVLA does it with a sudden thrust.

450asked 3×HVLA

After a Kirksville Crunch HVLA for a T5 somatic dysfunction, which of the following indicates the treatment was successful?

Ans: Reassess → barrier gone, motion improved = success; a pop proves nothing

Why: Success is judged by reassessment: the restrictive barrier is resolved and motion is improved.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A pop is a nitrogen bubble from joint distraction and may come from an unrelated joint; A.T. Still said "popping is no criterion to go by." Soreness and dizziness are side effects, not success. A felt release still has to be confirmed by rechecking.

451HVLA

Which factor is the most important when performing HVLA?

Ans: Consent + explanation + soft tissue prep + reassessment → all required

Why: Every option is part of safe, effective HVLA: consent, explanation, soft tissue preparation and reassessment.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Patient refusal is an absolute contraindication, so consent is mandatory. A.T. Still warned that restoring the joint before the muscles and ligaments is "putting the cart before the horse." Reassessment confirms whether the barrier resolved.

452HVLA

A 22-year-old has a somatic dysfunction of T5 that improves with flexion. With the patient supine and arms crossed, you place your left thenar eminence on the right transverse process of T5. You then sidebend the neck and torso to the left. After the patient exhales deeply, you apply a quick, short thrust through the patient's crossed arms toward the table. What technique is being used?

Ans: Supine + crossed arms + thenar fulcrum + thrust on exhale → Kirksville Crunch

Why: A supine thoracic thrust over a thenar-eminence fulcrum through the crossed arms is the Kirksville Crunch, an HVLA technique.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The Texas Twist is the prone thoracic HVLA. Muscle energy uses patient contraction, not a thrust. Counterstrain is a passive hold in the position of ease with no thrust.

453HVLA

A 22-year-old has a somatic dysfunction of T5 that improves with flexion. With the patient supine and arms crossed, you place your left thenar eminence on the right transverse process of T5, sidebend the neck and torso to the left, and after deep exhalation thrust through the crossed arms toward the table. What is the somatic dysfunction being treated?

Ans: Improves in flexion → F; fulcrum under right TP → Rr; sidebend left = barrier → Sr → FRrSr

Why: Improving with flexion makes it flexed (F). The fulcrum sits under the posterior right TP, so it is rotated right. Sidebending left is the barrier, so the freedom is sidebent right: T5 FRrSr.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Both E options contradict "improves with flexion." FRlSl puts the rotation on the wrong side. Type II dysfunctions rotate and sidebend to the same side.

454HVLA

During your practical, you diagnose your partner with an upper thoracic somatic dysfunction, T3 FRrSr. Your proctor instructs you to treat it with a Kirksville Crunch HVLA. How would you set the patient up?

Ans: Rotated right → fulcrum under right TP; upper thoracic (T1-T4) → hands behind neck

Why: Place the thenar fulcrum under the right (posterior) TP of T3, the side of the rotation. For upper thoracic segments (T1-T4) the patient clasps the hands behind the neck.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A and B put the fulcrum on the wrong side. D uses the crossed-arm hold, which the TA notes reserve for mid-thoracic segments (T5-T8), with the arm on the side of the dysfunction on top.

456asked 3×Contraindications

You are evaluating a 22-year-old for back pain and find a somatic dysfunction of T5 that improves with flexion. You plan HVLA. Which of the following is an absolute contraindication?

Ans: No consent → no treatment → patient refusal is absolute

Why: Patient refusal is an absolute contraindication to HVLA and to all OMT.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Acute radiculopathy, acute sprain/strain and hypermobility are relative HVLA contraindications in Lecture 6. Pain is not a contraindication, but pain alone is not an indication either. The 2025 Harlem version offered osteoporosis and acute whiplash as distractors; Lecture 6 lists both as relative.

457Contraindications

Which of the following is an example of a relative contraindication for HVLA?

Ans: Spasm → treat with caution (relative); fracture and bony malignancy → never (absolute)

Why: Severe muscle spasm (with acute whiplash and strain/sprain) is a relative HVLA contraindication in Lecture 6.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Fracture and bony malignancy are absolute contraindications. D is the indication for HVLA. Other relative ones: acute herniated disc, acute radiculopathy, osteopenia/osteoporosis, spondylolisthesis, hypermobility syndromes.

458Contraindications

What is the difference between a relative contraindication and an absolute contraindication to HVLA? Give examples.

AnswerAbsolute: never thrust (patient refusal, fracture/dislocation, Down syndrome, RA, Chiari malformation, achondroplasia, ankylosis/fusion, bony malignancy). Relative: use caution or another technique (hypermobility, acute herniated disc, acute radiculopathy, acute whiplash, osteoporosis, spondylolisthesis).

Ans: Absolute → do not perform; relative → caution, weigh risk, often choose another technique

Why: An absolute contraindication means HVLA must not be done. A relative contraindication means it may be done with caution, or another technique is safer.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Lecture 6 lists the upper cervical group (Down syndrome, RA, achondroplastic dwarfism, Chiari malformation) as absolute; cervical thrusts in RA and Down syndrome risk disrupting the transverse ligament of the dens. Hypermobility is relative because you cannot get a solid lock-out.

459asked 2×Contraindications

Which of the following is a contraindication to muscle energy?

Ans: Down syndrome → rheumatologic joint instability → listed for ME, HVLA and direct MFR

Why: The 2026 review slide lists rheumatologic joint instability (RA, scleroderma, Down syndrome) as a contraindication for ME, HVLA and direct MFR. Lecture 6 lists rheumatologic cervical instability as a relative ME contraindication.

Heads up: The 2020 TA key marks A (excessive patient muscular contraction). Lecture 6 lists that under ME safety, not contraindications, while the 2026 review slide puts Down syndrome (rheumatologic joint instability) in the ME/HVLA/dMFR contraindication column, so B is the better answer. If this exact TA question appears, know that the TA intended A.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Chiari malformation and achondroplasia are on the Lecture 6 HVLA (upper cervical) absolute list, not the ME list. Ehlers-Danlos is a hypermobility syndrome, a relative HVLA contraindication. Excessive patient contraction is a technique error (it can cause tendon avulsion or rib fracture), not a patient condition that rules out ME.

Which is a contraindication for counterstrain?

461Contraindications

A patient has a Type II thoracic dysfunction and a history of diabetes, hypertension and Chiari malformation. He requests a passive and direct treatment. What would you do?

Ans: Passive + direct = HVLA → Chiari = absolute HVLA contraindication → none

Why: The only passive, direct option is HVLA (Texas Twist), and Chiari malformation is an absolute contraindication to HVLA, so none of the choices fits.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Muscle energy is direct but active. Counterstrain is passive but indirect. Lecture 6 lists Chiari under the upper cervical HVLA contraindications, and the course indications handout lists it as an absolute HVLA contraindication.

Choosing a technique

462asked 3×2026Choosing a technique

A 14-year-old male presents with his mother with right ankle pain after twisting it playing basketball earlier today. Exam finds a preference for ankle inversion, tenderness of the anterior talofibular ligament, and bogginess over the lateral ankle. Negative ankle drawer sign; inversion and eversion still have hard end-feels. Ankle x-ray is negative. Which type of OMT would most likely be used to treat the patient's ankle?

Ans: Acute sprain → no direct techniques (ME, HVLA, dMFR) → indirect counterstrain

Why: An acute injury where damaged tissue could be further damaged is a contraindication to the direct techniques (ME, HVLA, direct MFR). Counterstrain is indirect and gentle, so it fits.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A and C are direct myofascial release. D and E are direct techniques. The negative drawer and x-ray rule out a torn ligament or fracture, which would contraindicate counterstrain too. CS is well tolerated in acute and chronic patients.

463Choosing a technique

A patient comes in with an acute injury with spondylolisthesis. You decide the best initial treatment is to shorten their hypertonic muscle. Which technique would you use?

Ans: Shorten hypertonic muscle → indirect → counterstrain

Why: Shortening the hypertonic muscle is the definition of an indirect approach, and counterstrain is the indirect technique listed.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Perpendicular stretch and muscle energy lengthen the muscle (direct). HVLA is direct, and both acute injury and spondylolisthesis are relative HVLA contraindications.

464asked 2×2026Choosing a technique

A 75-year-old male has chronic low back pain due to known metastatic prostate cancer to the lumbar vertebrae. The most appropriate osteopathic manipulative therapy is:

Ans: Bony mets → avoid direct force (HVLA, ME) and lymphatic pumping → gentle indirect FPR

Why: With bony metastases, direct techniques could cause a pathologic fracture, so a gentle indirect technique to the painful region, facilitated positional release, is most appropriate.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

HVLA and muscle energy are direct; metastases in the area of OMT are a contraindication. Counterstrain is indirect but the cervical spine is not where his pain is. Pelvic diaphragm release augments lymphatic flow, which may theoretically hasten metastatic spread.

7.1 · 13 questions · Questions 465–477

Rib classification

465asked 3×Rib classification

Sort ribs 1-12 into each category: true, false, floating, typical, and atypical. Give the defining feature of each.

AnswerTrue 1-7 (attach directly to sternum); false 8-12 (8-10 join costal cartilage above); floating 11-12 (vertebral bodies only); typical 3-9; atypical 1, 2, 11, 12 (sometimes 10).

Ans: Sternum direct → true 1-7 · no direct sternum → false 8-12 · no front attachment → floating 11-12

Why: True ribs (1-7) attach directly to the sternum. False ribs (8-12) do not; 8-10 join the costal cartilage of the rib above. Floating ribs (11-12) articulate only with the bodies of T11 and T12.

Heads up: The 2022-2025 TA keys and the Lect 8 slide list typical 2-9 and atypical 1, 11, 12. The 2026 review deck and IA7 slides call rib 2 atypical (tuberosity for serratus anterior), so use typical 3-9 and atypical 1, 2, 11, 12 for this exam.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The 2026 review deck memory tool: atypical ribs are the ones with a "1" or "2" (1, 2, 11, 12, sometimes 10). Rib 1 has one facet and no angle, rib 2 has a tuberosity for serratus anterior, rib 10 has a single unifacet, and ribs 11-12 have one facet, no neck, and no costotransverse joint.

466asked 4×2026Rib classification

A female with a history of asthma is receiving osteopathic manipulative treatment to improve her costal cage motion. The operator lastly palpates the false ribs. The most appropriate list of ribs examined is

Ans: False = no direct sternal attachment, not floating → 8-10

Why: Ribs 1-7 attach directly to the sternum (true). Ribs 8-10 reach it only through the costal cartilage of the rib above, so they are the false ribs in this narrow sense.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Choices starting at 6 or 7 include true ribs (1-7). Choices running to 11 include a floating rib. 1-8 mixes true ribs with one false rib. The IA7 slide calls 8-12 false with 11-12 also floating; with no 8-12 choice, 8-10 is the answer.

467Rib classification

What defines "true" and "false" ribs?

Ans: True = attach directly to sternum → false = no direct sternal attachment

Why: True ribs (1-7) articulate directly with the sternum. False ribs (8-12) do not; the 2026 IA7 slide words it as "don't articulate with sternum."

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A reverses the relationship. All ribs connect to the vertebral column and none attach to the clavicle, so C is wrong. D describes location, not the definition. Strictly, ribs 8-10 reach the sternum indirectly through costal cartilage.

471Rib classification

Which of the following ribs are considered atypical?

Ans: Rib 3 is typical → drop A, B, C → 1, 11, 12

Why: Ribs 1, 11, and 12 are atypical under every convention. D is the keyed answer and the only choice that lists no typical rib and includes both floating ribs.

Heads up: The 2022 TA key (D) follows the older "atypical 1, 11, 12" convention. The 2026 review deck adds rib 2 (atypical 1, 2, 11, 12). That full list is not offered here, so D remains the best choice.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A, B, and C include rib 3, which is typical. E includes rib 2 but leaves out rib 11. Under the 2026 slides rib 2 is also atypical, so the complete list would be 1, 2, 11, 12.

476asked 2×2026Rib classification

A female with a history of asthma is receiving osteopathic manipulative treatment to improve her costal cage motion. The typical ribs are then palpated. Anatomic features consistent with a typical rib include

Ans: Typical ribs (mostly 3-7 true ribs) → costosternal attachment

Why: Typical ribs have a costosternal attachment in front, directly for the true ribs and through costal cartilage for 8-9.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The tubercle articulates only with its own transverse process, not the one above (A). The costal groove carries the intercostal vein, artery, and nerve, not the azygos (B). Typical ribs have two facets on the head (D), and the tubercle meets the transverse process, not the vertebral body (E).

477Rib classification

Which statement is TRUE regarding the classification of ribs and their vertebral articulation?

Ans: 2026 slides: rib 2 atypical, rib 10 single unifacet (sometimes atypical) → C

Why: Rib 10 has a single unifacet on T10, and the 2026 review deck lists it among the atypical ribs ("sometimes rib 10"). Rib 2 articulates with T1 and T2 but is atypical because of its serratus anterior tuberosity.

Heads up: The 2025 TA key marks B (rib 2 typical). The 2026 IA7 slide says rib 2 "is still atypical," and the 2026 review deck lists rib 10 among the atypical ribs, so C fits the 2026 slides. The 2026 sources disagree on rib 10 (IA7 calls it "the only typical rib with a unifacet"), so expect the exam to avoid this exact question.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Rib 1 is atypical and articulates only with T1 (A). Ribs 3-9 are typical with demifacets, not unifacets (D). B states the older "rib 2 is typical" convention.

478Rib articulations & landmarks

What is the name of the joint the blue arrow is pointing to? (The arrow points to where the rib head meets the vertebral body.)

Ans: Rib head + vertebral body → costovertebral joint

Why: The costovertebral joint is where the rib head meets the demifacets (or facet) of the vertebral body.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The costotransverse joint is the rib tubercle against the transverse process, which is lateral to the arrow. "Vertebral-transverse" and "vertebral-neck" are not real joint names. The costotransverse joint is absent in ribs 11 and 12.

490Rib cage function & shape

Which function is NOT typically associated with the rib cage?

Ans: Rib cage: protect, breathe, pump, platform → not digestion

Why: The lecture's four rib-cage functions are protection of vital organs, respiration, a pump for venous and lymphatic return, and a platform for the upper extremities. Digestion is not one.

A, B, and C are all on the Lect 8 list. The pump function is why rib treatment helps lymphatic and venous return.

491Rib cage function & shape

Among the following, which is NOT associated with the ribs and their function?

Ans: Lecture list: viscera, surgery, spasm, posture → not genetics

Why: The lecture lists what can affect the ribs: visceral organs, any surgery (even abdominal or pelvic), muscle spasm, and postural compensation. Genetics and family history is not on the list.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Pelvic surgery is on the list because it disturbs reciprocal tension through the body. Dowager's hump is a postural compensation. Visceral organs hang from the bones by ligaments and fascia, so problems spread in both directions.

499Pump, bucket, caliper motion

Which ribs move primarily in pump-handle motion, primarily in bucket-handle motion, and primarily in caliper motion?

AnswerPump handle: ribs 1-5. Bucket handle: ribs 6-10. Caliper: ribs 11-12. Ribs 1-10 have both pump and bucket components; one predominates.

Ans: Upper 1-5 pump · middle 6-10 bucket · floating 11-12 caliper

Why: Upper ribs (1-5) are mainly pump handle (↑ AP diameter). Middle ribs (6-10) are mainly bucket handle (↑ transverse diameter). Floating ribs (11-12) move in caliper motion.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

All ribs have both pump and bucket components; the classification names the predominant one. Caliper motion of 11-12 helps stabilize the origins of the diaphragm.

507Pump, bucket, caliper motion

Fill in the blanks: caliper motion of ribs 11 and 12 consists of the lateral ends moving ____, increasing the ____ and ____ diameters and stabilizing the origins of the diaphragm. Caliper motion moves along a ____ plane.

AnswerPosteriorly-inferiorly-laterally; AP and transverse; horizontal plane.

Ans: Floating ribs → lateral ends post/inf/lat → AP + transverse ↑ → horizontal plane

509Pump, bucket, caliper motion

Fill in the blanks: during inspiration, the anteroposterior diameter of the thorax is ____ when the ribs are ____. Because the ribs slope ____, any elevation during inspiration results in an ____ movement of the sternum at the ____ joint.

AnswerIncreased; raised (elevated); downward; upward (and forward); manubriosternal.

This is pump-handle motion of the upper ribs. Bucket-handle motion of the lower ribs instead increases the transverse diameter.

512asked 2×2026Pump, bucket, caliper motion

A female with a history of asthma is receiving osteopathic manipulative treatment to improve her costal cage motion. In examining for bucket-handle motion of her ribs, the optimal placement of the operator's hands is over the

Ans: Bucket = lateral rib rises → hands on lateral border

Why: Bucket-handle motion is elevation of the lateral part of the rib, so the hands go over the lateral borders of the rib cage, fingers along the intercostal spaces.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The anterior margin and sternum are where you feel pump handle. The rib angles and transverse processes are posterior landmarks for rib and spine SD, not respiratory bucket motion.

513Pump, bucket, caliper motion

In the image below, what is the physician evaluating? (Supine patient; the physician's hands are at the base of the neck, just above the clavicles.)

Ans: Thumbs behind trapezius, fingers by clavicle → first rib

Why: The physician is evaluating the first rib: the thumbs push the trapezius back to contact the posterior first rib while the fingers rest near the clavicle.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The scalenes and trapezius are soft tissues the hands pass over, not the target. Upper thoracics are assessed at the spinous and transverse processes, usually with the patient seated or prone.

514Pump, bucket, caliper motion

What are the contact points when palpating the first rib?

AnswerPatient supine. Thumbs push the trapezius posteriorly to contact the posterior first rib; index finger rests above the clavicle; middle finger below the clavicle beneath the sternoclavicular joint.

Ans: Rib 1 hides under trapezius and clavicle → thumbs behind, fingers around clavicle

Why: The first rib sits under the trapezius and clavicle. The thumbs push the trapezius back to reach it posteriorly, and the fingers straddle the clavicle near the sternoclavicular joint.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Compare the two sides as the patient breathes: a rib that stops first on inhalation is an exhalation SD, and one that stops first on exhalation is an inhalation SD.

Why: Inhalation uses the diaphragm (with its crura) and external intercostals, helped by accessory muscles such as the SCM and scalenes.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Rectus abdominis and transversus abdominis are expiratory (A, B). Internal intercostals are the primary expiratory muscle (C). B is the list of expiratory accessory muscles.

516asked 4×2026Muscles of respiration

Which is a primary muscle of inspiration?

Ans: Primary inspiration = diaphragm + external intercostals

Why: The primary inspiratory muscles are the diaphragm and the external intercostals.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Scalenes, pectoralis minor, and serratus anterior are accessory inspiratory muscles for forced breathing. Internal intercostals are the primary expiratory muscle. The diaphragm does 100% of quiet inspiration and about 60% of deep inspiration.

517Muscles of respiration

A patient presents with upper back pain and trouble breathing. You notice difficulty during inhalation. Which muscle might be causing this dysfunction?

Ans: Inhalation problem → inspiratory muscle → external intercostals

Why: The external intercostals are a primary muscle of inhalation, so they are the only choice tied to the inspiratory phase.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Internal intercostals are the primary expiratory muscle. Transversus abdominis, rectus abdominis, and external oblique are accessory expiratory muscles.

518Muscles of respiration

A patient comes in and you auscultate their breath sounds. As they breathe in normally, what muscles are they using? What about for breathing out normally?

AnswerIn: diaphragm and external intercostals. Out: internal intercostals (quiet exhalation is largely passive recoil).

Ans: Quiet in → diaphragm + external intercostals · quiet out → internal intercostals

Why: Quiet inspiration uses the diaphragm and external intercostals. The lecture lists the internal intercostals as the primary expiratory muscle.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Accessory inspiration (forced): SCM, scalenes, pectoralis major/minor, serratus anterior, latissimus dorsi, serratus posterior superior, iliocostalis. Accessory expiration: abdominals, iliocostalis, longissimus, serratus posterior inferior, quadratus lumborum.

519asked 2×Muscles of respiration

Which of the following are the accessory muscles of expiration?

Ans: Internal intercostals = primary → accessory = abdominals, serratus posterior inferior

Why: Rectus abdominis and serratus posterior inferior are accessory expiratory muscles that help with forced exhalation.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The internal intercostals are the primary expiratory muscle, not accessory, so A and E are wrong. Other accessory expiratory muscles: transversus and obliques, iliocostalis (lowest fibers), longissimus, quadratus lumborum.

Why: Serratus anterior is an accessory muscle of inspiration that attaches to ribs 2-9, including the restricted upper ribs.

Explanation

Internal intercostals are the primary expiratory muscle. The diaphragm is a primary (not accessory) inspiratory muscle. Rectus abdominis is an accessory expiratory muscle.

530Muscles that move ribs

Increased tone of the quadratus lumborum will cause the 12th rib to

Ans: QL pulls rib 12 toward the pelvis → depresses

Why: The QL depresses rib 12 (during forced exhalation) and fixes it during inhalation, so increased tone pulls the 12th rib down.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

QL pulls rib 12 toward the iliac crest, so it cannot elevate it. Rotation and compression are not QL actions on the rib.

532Muscles that move ribs

A patient has persistent low back pain radiating toward the iliac crest and difficulty breathing. The 11th and 12th ribs are restricted during inhalation. What muscle would you expect to have a somatic dysfunction that could explain the dyspnea?

Ans: Pain to iliac crest + ribs 11-12 → quadratus lumborum

Why: The quadratus lumborum runs from the iliac crest to rib 12. A tight QL holds the lower ribs down and causes pain toward the iliac crest.

536asked 2×2026Muscles that move ribs

An 18-year-old female has a non-productive cough of 3 days' duration and sore ribs from coughing. She is febrile with scant rhonchi bilaterally. Structural exam shows the right first rib is held in inhalation and ribs 7-10 on the left are held in exhalation. A likely cause of the right rib dysfunction is

Ans: Rib 1 held up + coughing → scalenes (attach rib 1) in spasm

Why: The anterior and middle scalenes attach to rib 1 and are strained by coughing. A scalene spasm holds rib 1 up in inhalation.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Infiltrates do not displace ribs. The first intercostal space lies between ribs 1 and 2, so intercostal spasm would not hold rib 1 up. Pectoralis minor attaches to ribs 3-5. A somatovisceral reflex goes from soma to viscera, the wrong direction here.

While examining your patient's thoracic inlet, you find that during deep breathing the right first rib stays stuck higher than the left. You diagnose an inhalation somatic dysfunction of the right first rib. What muscle is likely hypertonic and causing it?

Ans: Rib 1 held up → hypertonic scalene on rib 1 → anterior scalene

Why: The anterior scalene (with the middle scalene) attaches to rib 1 and pulls it up. When hypertonic it holds the rib in inhalation.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The posterior scalene goes to rib 2. Trapezius does not attach to the ribs. Serratus posterior superior attaches to ribs 2-5. The diaphragm attaches to the lower 6 ribs.

538asked 6×2026Thoracic outlet syndrome

A 44-year-old male presents to the ED with right upper extremity pain and paresthesias. You determine he has thoracic outlet syndrome. Which of the following structures has been implicated as a potential cause?

Ans: TOS = compression between collarbone and 1st rib → clavicle + 1st rib

Why: TOS is compression of the brachial plexus and subclavian vessels in the space between the clavicle and the first rib. Entrapment there is the costoclavicular type.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The third TOS site is pectoralis minor, not major. The posterior scalene goes to rib 2 and is not part of the scalene triangle (anterior + middle scalenes). The other two TOS sites are the scalene triangle and the pectoralis minor near the coracoid.

539Thoracic outlet syndrome

Which structure or pair of structures is involved in thoracic outlet syndrome?

Ans: Scalene triangle = anterior + middle scalenes over 1st rib

Why: The plexus and subclavian artery can be compressed in the scalene triangle between the anterior and middle scalenes over the first rib. The 2026 review deck lists these as the abnormal muscles in TOS.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The pectoral site is pectoralis minor, not major (A). The posterior scalene goes to rib 2 (B). Costoclavicular TOS involves the clavicle and first rib, not the second (D).

540asked 2×Thoracic outlet syndrome

A 66-year-old female has headaches and left otitis media. Exam: numbness of the left thumb and along the left arm; the left face is slightly more edematous; biceps reflex 2/4, strength 5/5; pupils equal and reactive. What is the most likely cause?

Ans: Arm numbness + facial venous congestion, no Horner's → thoracic inlet/outlet syndrome

Why: Compression at the thoracic inlet (thoracic outlet syndrome) can squeeze the brachial plexus (arm and thumb numbness) and the venous drainage (facial edema).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Equal reactive pupils argue against Horner's syndrome and a Pancoast tumor, which usually causes Horner's. Erb's palsy (C5-C6) would weaken the biceps and reduce its reflex. Klumpke's palsy (C8-T1) affects the ulnar hand, not the thumb.

Inhalation vs exhalation SD

541Inhalation vs exhalation SD

Fill in the blank: if a rib stops moving relative to others on inhalation, it is classified as an ____ somatic dysfunction. If a rib stops moving relative to others on exhalation, it is classified as an ____ somatic dysfunction.

AnswerStops on inhalation = exhalation SD (depressed rib). Stops on exhalation = inhalation SD (elevated rib).

Ans: Stops early in a phase → free in the other → named for the freedom

Why: Rib SDs are named for the freedom. A rib that stops first on inhalation moves freely into exhalation, so it is an exhalation SD (depressed). A rib that stops first on exhalation is an inhalation SD (elevated).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Exhalation SD = inhalation restriction; inhalation SD = exhalation restriction. Do not mix the SD name with the restriction name.

542Inhalation vs exhalation SD

When a rib is restricted in its ability to move into exhalation, it is typically held in what position?

Ans: Can't exhale → stuck up → held in inhalation

Why: A rib that cannot move into exhalation is stuck up, held in the inhalation position (an elevated rib, inhalation SD).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

"Restriction" is not a position. Depression and exhalation describe the opposite problem: a rib that cannot inhale.

Explanation

"Exhalation restriction" (A) correctly names the barrier but not the SD, which is what the question asks. B and C are the opposite pattern.

548asked 5×2026Rib SD findings

Osteopathic structural exam of your patient reveals: ribs 3-5 on the right move freely on inhalation and are restricted in exhalation; anterior narrowing of the right 2nd intercostal space; prominence of the superior edge of the angles of right ribs 3-5 posteriorly; tenderness at the angles of ribs 3-5 on the right. What is the correct diagnosis of right ribs 3-5?

Ans: Free into inhalation + narrowing above + superior edge → pump-handle inhalation SD

Why: Ribs 3-5 are pump-handle ribs held up (free into inhalation). An inhalation pump-handle SD shows anterior narrowing of the space above and a prominent superior edge of the rib angle.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Bucket-handle findings are lateral (lateral narrowing, prominent lower edge of the shaft). An exhalation SD would show narrowing below and a prominent inferior edge. A-P compression is a rare trauma pattern.

550Rib SD findings

A 45-year-old female has shortness of breath, pain when breathing in, and accessory muscle use. Supine A/P rib motion: her right upper ribs do not fall like her left upper ribs when breathing out. How would you describe this somatic dysfunction?

Ans: Upper ribs don't fall → right pump-handle inhalation SD → findings

Why: The right upper ribs are stuck up, so this is a pump-handle inhalation SD: anterior narrowing above, the rib moves cephalad on inhalation, and the superior edge of the rib angle is prominent.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Narrowing is anterior, not posterior (A). The rib moves cephalad on inhalation, not exhalation (A, C, D). A prominent inferior edge belongs to an exhalation SD (C).

551Rib SD findings

When diagnosing an elevated rib on the anterior thoracic cage, you would expect the space between the affected rib and the rib below it to be:

Ans: Elevated rib → narrows space above → widens space below

Why: An elevated (inhalation SD) rib narrows the intercostal space above it, so the space below it is increased.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Narrowing below would point to a depressed rib (exhalation SD). "Lateral" is not a description of the space.

552asked 2×Rib SD findings

Which is/are true for a depressed rib? (Select all that apply.)

Ans: Depressed = exhalation SD → holds ribs below down → space below narrows

Why: A depressed rib (exhalation SD) is the top/key rib of its group and holds the ribs below it from rising on inhalation. The intercostal space below it narrows.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

B gets the direction wrong: the group lies below the key rib. D, narrowing above, is the finding for an elevated (inhalation SD) rib.

553asked 2×2026Rib SD findings

A 35-year-old male has chest pain after a horse kicked him in the right anterior chest wall. The pain is worse with inhalation. Lungs are clear, ribs without point tenderness, and X-ray is negative. Structural exam: increased intercostal space between ribs 2 and 3 anteriorly on the right; inferior edge of the rib angle prominent from ribs 3-7; decreased excursion of ribs 3-7 on the right during inhalation. The most likely dysfunction in ribs 3-7 on the right is

Ans: Restricted inhalation + inferior edge prominent + mostly ribs 3-5 → exhalation pump-handle SD

Why: Ribs 3-7 are restricted in inhalation, so this is an exhalation SD. A prominent inferior edge of the rib angle is the exhalation pump-handle finding, and most of ribs 3-7 are pump-handle ribs.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Inhalation SD choices get the freedom backward. Bucket-handle findings are lateral, with lateral narrowing. Torsional SD is not supported by these findings.

554Rib SD findings

A 56-year-old female has chest pain and difficulty breathing, with tenderness at the angle of rib 6 and its intercostal muscles. Anterior ribs move caudad on exhalation and are restricted on inhalation, with anterior narrowing of the intercostal space below the dysfunction and a prominent posterior rib angle. How would you diagnose this somatic dysfunction?

Ans: Restricted inhalation → exhalation SD → key = top rib (6) → 6-10 bucket

Why: Restriction on inhalation with narrowing below is an exhalation SD, and the key rib is the top rib (BITE). Only C pairs an exhalation SD with the top rib (6) of the group.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A and B are inhalation SDs. D calls rib 6 the key of ribs 2-6, but the top rib (2) would be key. The findings are written for a pump-handle rib, but ribs 6-10 move mainly in bucket-handle motion.

555asked 6×2026Key rib (BITE)

On structural examination of your OMM lab partner, you find an exhalation somatic dysfunction involving bucket-handle motion of ribs 6-10 on the left. The key rib(s) to treat with osteopathic manipulation is/are:

Ans: BITE: exhalation → top rib → rib 6

Why: BITE: Bottom rib for Inhalation SD, Top rib for Exhalation SD. The top rib of 6-10 is rib 6.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Rib 10 would be the key for an inhalation SD. Ribs 5 and 11 are outside the group. The key rib is a single rib, not the middle ribs. Treating the key rib usually releases the rest of the group.

556Key rib (BITE)

What is the first rib to treat for an inhalation somatic dysfunction of ribs 3-8?

Ans: BITE: inhalation → bottom rib → rib 8

Why: For an inhalation SD, the key rib is the bottom rib of the group (BITE), so treat rib 8 first.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The top rib (3) is the key for an exhalation SD. The middle rib is never the key rib. You treat the key rib first, not all of them together.

557asked 4×2026Key rib (BITE)

A 40-year-old male reports right-sided thoracic pain after a work injury about one week ago. The pain has improved but is still present and exquisite at maximum inhalation. Structural examination reveals dysfunction of ribs 6-9. Radiographs are negative for fracture. Which statement describes the most appropriate diagnosis and treatment?

Ans: Pain/restriction at full inhalation → exhalation SD → BITE top → rib 6

Why: Pain at full inhalation means the ribs are restricted in inhalation, which is an exhalation SD. BITE: the top rib (6) is the key rib.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Rib 9 would be the key for an inhalation SD (B, D). C pairs inhalation SD with the top rib, which mixes the two rules. Nothing suggests torsion (E). Other versions of this question give ribs 6-10 "restricted in inhalation"; the answer is the same: exhalation SD, treat rib 6.

560Key rib (BITE)

A 23-year-old has difficulty breathing. Rib exam: both sides of the rib cage rise evenly, but the left side stays higher during expiration. Ribs 2-5 are restricted in A/P springing on the left. What is your diagnosis?

Why: The left ribs fail to fall on expiration, so they are a left inhalation SD. Ribs 2-5 are pump handle, and the key rib for an inhalation SD is the bottom rib, 5.

564asked 2×2026Key rib (BITE)

A 40-year-old has right-sided pain after weightlifting one week ago. The pain has improved but is still present at maximum inhalation. Exam reveals a winged scapula on the right. Fill in: an ____ somatic dysfunction at ribs ____ with treatment directed at rib ___ using this muscle ____.

Ans: Winged scapula → serratus anterior · pain on inhalation → exhalation SD → top rib 6

Why: Medial scapular winging points to serratus anterior (long thoracic nerve). Pain at full inhalation means an exhalation SD, so the key rib is the top rib (6) of ribs 6-9.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

B gives an exhalation SD but takes the bottom rib (5) as key. C, D, and E are inhalation SDs, which would hurt on exhalation. They also use muscles unrelated to scapular winging.

565Rib ME & HVLA techniques

In muscle energy, what three items are used to correct inhalation and exhalation restrictions of the ribs?

Ans: ME = direct: contract muscle + push into barrier + breathing

Why: Rib ME is direct: an isometric muscle contraction, force that moves the rib into the barrier, and respiratory assistance.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

ME uses contraction, not relaxation (A, C). Guiding the rib into its freedom (A, D) would be an indirect approach, and ME is direct.

Asked in

  • 2023 Canvas Quizzes 4-9 (identical file: OMM 1 Quizzes (Thoracic Spine, Neuromuscular, Ribs).pptx) · Canvas quiz · Quiz 9, slides 98-99
566Rib ME & HVLA techniques

Where does your hand (the "applicator") go when you treat an exhalation SD of the ribs with muscle energy?

AnswerOn the posterior rib angle of the key (top) rib, pulling it caudad on inhalation while the patient contracts the attached muscle (e.g., arm or hand on forehead for pectoralis minor).

Ans: Exhalation SD → key = top rib → contact posterior angle → patient pulls rib up

Why: For an exhalation SD the physician contacts the posterior rib angle of the top (key) rib. The patient contracts the muscle attached to that rib (scalenes, pectoralis minor, serratus anterior, or latissimus) to lift the rib into inhalation.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

For an inhalation SD the contact is on the anterior bottom (key) rib, which is pushed down on exhalation with the trunk or head flexed to it.

567asked 2×2026Rib ME & HVLA techniques

A 30-year-old male with allergic rhinitis sneezes frequently. Structural exam reveals an exhalation dysfunction of rib 2. Which of the following would be most useful in correcting this with a direct method?

Ans: Rib 2 → posterior scalene → contract to lift rib 2

Why: The posterior scalene inserts on rib 2. Contracting it pulls rib 2 up into inhalation, which is the direct ME correction.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The middle scalene treats rib 1. Pectoralis minor treats ribs 3-5. Latissimus dorsi works the lowest ribs. Pectoralis major is not one of the rib ME muscles.

568asked 2×Rib ME & HVLA techniques

Which muscle do you use if treating rib 1 with muscle energy?

Ans: Rib 1 → anterior + middle scalene

Why: Rib 1 is moved by the anterior and middle scalenes (IA7 slide 28). In rib 1 exhalation ME, the patient lifts the head into resistance to fire them.

Heads up: The 2020 TA answer slide marks A (SCM). The 2026 IA7 slide lists rib 1's muscles as the anterior and middle scalene, so B and C are correct.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The SCM attaches to the sternum and clavicle, not rib 1, so it cannot lift the rib. The posterior scalene is the muscle for rib 2.

569Rib ME & HVLA techniques

Match the muscle energy steps for the first rib to exhalation SD vs inhalation SD: A. Physician's hand contacts the first rib posteriorly; B. The patient's head and neck are flexed; C. Physician contacts the first rib between the two heads of the SCM; D. Patient places hand on forehead, palm up, with physician's hand on top; E. Physician pulls rib down during inhalation; F. Physician pushes the rib inferiorly during exhalation; G. Patient pushes head into hand during inhalation while physician resists; H. Physician resists the movement of the rib during inhalation.

AnswerExhalation SD: D, A, G, E. Inhalation SD: C, B, H, F.

Ans: Exhalation SD → scalenes lift rib (head into hand) · inhalation SD → push rib down on exhale

Why: Exhalation SD: hand on forehead, contact rib 1 posteriorly, patient lifts head against resistance on inhalation (scalenes pull rib 1 up), physician pulls the posterior rib caudad. Inhalation SD: contact rib 1 anteriorly between the SCM heads, flex the head and neck, resist inhalation, push the rib inferiorly on exhalation.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

This pattern holds for all ribs: exhalation SD uses a muscle to pull the top rib up, and inhalation SD uses breathing to push the bottom rib down.

570Rib ME & HVLA techniques

In the image, which answer best describes the physician's action during this muscle energy treatment for rib exhalation somatic dysfunction? (Patient supine with hand on forehead; physician's hand behind the first rib.)

Ans: Exhalation SD rib 1 → scalenes lift front · physician pulls posterior rib caudad

Why: The physician grasps the posterosuperior first rib and pulls it caudad while the patient lifts the head. Lowering the posterior rib helps the anterior rib rise into inhalation.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Lifting the posterior rib cephalad (B) moves it the wrong way. Anterior-lateral pushing (C) is not part of this technique. Lifting "into its freedom" (D) would be indirect, and ME is direct.

572Rib ME & HVLA techniques

In the photo, what is a possible somatic dysfunction being treated by this muscle energy technique? (Patient supine with right forearm on forehead; physician behind the upper ribs.)

Ans: Hand on forehead, upper rib contact → rib 1 exhalation SD

Why: Hand on forehead with resisted head or arm lift and a posterior contact on the upper rib is ME for a right 1st rib exhalation SD.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

B gets BITE backward: an exhalation SD's key rib is the top rib, and ribs 3-5 are pump, not bucket. C is an inhalation SD, which is treated by flexing down to the key rib and pushing it down on exhalation. D pairs pump handle with rib 10, a bucket-handle rib. Ribs 11-12 (E) are treated prone.

573Rib ME & HVLA techniques

An older man is having a really hard time inhaling. His key rib is rib 3. What is his somatic dysfunction, what position do you put him in, and what muscle are you activating?

Ans: Can't inhale → exhalation SD (top rib 3) → pec minor → hand on forehead pushing up

Why: Trouble inhaling with a top key rib is an exhalation SD. Rib 3 is moved by pectoralis minor, activated with the patient supine, hand on forehead, pushing the arm up against resistance.

Explanation

Inhalation SD choices (B, D) are wrong because rib 3 as key means the top rib. Head and neck flexion pushing into exhalation is the inhalation SD setup (B, C). Serratus anterior is for ribs 6-9.

575Rib ME & HVLA techniques

Why: Restricted inhalation is an exhalation SD (stuck down) with key rib 3. On exhalation, resist the rib dropping, and on inhalation, guide it up.

576asked 2×2026Rib ME & HVLA techniques

A 35-year-old male has chest pain after a horse kicked him in the right anterior chest wall, worse with inhalation. X-ray is negative. 579Rib ME & HVLA techniques

How would you set up and perform muscle energy for a rib 7-9 exhalation somatic dysfunction?

Ans: Exhalation SD → top rib 7 → posterior contact, pull caudad on inhale → serratus (45°)

Why: Exhalation SD: sit at the side of the supine patient, contact the back of the top rib (7), and pull caudad on inhalation while the patient pushes the hand against yours at a 45° angle (serratus anterior).

A and B are the inhalation SD setup (flex the patient and push the rib down). A also uses rib 9. D uses rib 9 and exhalation. E's "straight up from the forehead" is the pectoralis minor setup for ribs 3-5.

581Rib ME & HVLA techniques

583Rib ME & HVLA techniques

You treat a patient who has a right inhalation SD of ribs 6-9 (bucket handle, key rib 9) with muscle energy. What must be done?

Ans: Inhalation SD ME → flex head/trunk down to key rib → push rib down on exhale

Why: For an inhalation SD, the physician flexes the patient's head and trunk down to the key rib (with sidebending for bucket ribs) and pushes the rib into exhalation.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The patient is supine, not prone (A). Hand on forehead (B) and pulling the posterior rib down (C) are exhalation SD steps.

584Rib ME & HVLA techniques

Your patient's left ribs 11 and 12 fully come up as they breathe in but don't fall as they breathe out. How do you set up ME for this somatic dysfunction?

Ans: Don't fall on exhale → inhalation SD → push ribs during exhalation, no arm overhead

Why: This is an inhalation SD of ribs 11-12. With the patient prone, stand on the opposite side, curve the legs toward you, and push the ribs laterally while pulling the ASIS during exhalation.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

B raises the arm overhead (latissimus) and works on inhalation, which is the setup for an exhalation SD of ribs 11-12.

585Rib ME & HVLA techniques

Describe the muscle energy technique for ribs 11 and 12.

Ans: Ribs 11-12 ME → prone, ASIS lift + rib push

Why: Ribs 11-12 are treated prone. The physician stands opposite the dysfunction, the caudad hand lifts the ASIS, and the cephalad hand pushes the ribs laterally with breathing.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Ribs 11-12 are not treated seated or supine (A, B). D describes no standard rib technique.

586Rib ME & HVLA techniques

When treating a posterior rib head somatic dysfunction with HVLA thrust, where does the physician place the thenar eminence?

Ans: Rib HVLA → contact the rib, not the vertebra → lateral to costotransverse joint

Why: For rib HVLA the thenar eminence goes on the rib, just lateral to the costotransverse joint (at the rib angle).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Over the transverse process (C) or spinous process (D) is the contact for a thoracic vertebral thrust. The cervicothoracic junction (B) is not a rib contact.

587Rib ME & HVLA techniques

What technique is being used in the figure? (Patient seated; her arm is draped over the physician's knee while he sidebends her head and contacts the first rib.)

Why: This is the seated HVLA for the first rib: the head is locked by sidebending and rotation, then a thrust is delivered through the rib contact.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

Rib 1 ME is done supine with the hand on the forehead. Counterstrain and FPR are passive positioning techniques without a thrust setup.

How do you correctly perform HVLA of the first rib?

Ans: Seated, arm over physician's knee → lock head → thrust rib down and medial

A and B are supine setups, not the taught HVLA. C rotates toward the dysfunction, which does not lock the rib.

8.1 · 3 questions · Questions 589–591

ANS anatomy

589asked 2×ANS anatomy

What nerves in the body are parasympathetic?

AnswerCranial nerves III, VII, IX, and X, plus the pelvic splanchnic nerves from S2-S4 (craniosacral outflow).

Ans: Parasympathetic = craniosacral → CN III, VII, IX, X + S2-S4

Why: The parasympathetic system is craniosacral: cranial nerves III, VII, IX, and X and the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

No thoracic or lumbar level is parasympathetic; sympathetic cell bodies sit in the intermediolateral column from T1 to L2. The vagus connects to the spinal cord at C1-C2, which is why OA-C2 findings are linked to vagal viscera, and S2-S4 findings to the pelvic organs and distal colon.

Asked in

  • 2025 TA Review Exam 1 (Harlem) · TA review · slides 133-134
  • 2024 TA Review (Harlem) Exam 1 · TA review · slides 114-115
590ANS anatomy

Which nerve provides the most parasympathetic innervation to the body?

Ans: Largest parasympathetic territory → heart, lungs, most of gut → vagus (CN X)

Why: The vagus nerve carries parasympathetic supply to the heart, lungs, and the gut down to about the splenic flexure, far more territory than any other parasympathetic nerve.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

CN III (pupil, ciliary muscle), CN VII (lacrimal and salivary glands), and CN IX (parotid) serve only head structures. The pelvic splanchnics (S2-S4) cover only the descending and sigmoid colon, rectum, bladder, and genitals. The vagus is up to 90% afferent and connects to the spinal cord at C1 and C2.

Asked in

  • 2025 TA Review Exam 1 (Middletown) · TA review · slides 194-195
591asked 2×ANS anatomy

Match each cervical sympathetic ganglion (superior, middle, inferior) to its usual location. A. Typically lies anterior to the C6 transverse process. B. Typically lies anterior to the transverse process of C2/C3. C. Typically lies in relation to C7-T1, often fusing with T1 to become the stellate ganglion.

AnswerSuperior cervical = B (anterior to C2/C3 TP); middle cervical = A (anterior to C6 TP); inferior cervical = C (C7-T1, fuses with T1 to form the stellate ganglion).

Ans: Superior high at C2-3 → middle at C6 → inferior at C7-T1 = stellate

Why: The superior cervical ganglion lies in front of the C2/C3 transverse process, the middle in front of C6, and the inferior at C7-T1, where it often fuses with T1 as the stellate ganglion.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

All cervical sympathetic ganglia receive their preganglionic fibers from T1-T4, and all send fibers to the cardiac plexus. The superior cervical ganglion has many connections with CN IX and X.

592PANs & reflexes

What is the definition of a viscerosomatic reflex?

Ans: Viscero → somatic: organ stimulus → SNS → palpable changes in segmental soma

Why: In a viscerosomatic reflex the visceral stimulus comes first and produces palpable reflex changes in segmentally related somatic tissue through the SNS.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A reverses the direction; that is a somatovisceral reflex. B describes a Chapman point (pea-sized, beneath the subcutaneous tissue). D describes a Jones tender point (dime-sized, in muscle, tendon, ligament, or fascia).

593asked 3×2026PANs & reflexes

A male patient presents with indigestion and is found to have tissue texture changes along the posterior spinal column. It is determined that his symptoms resulted from somatic sensory stimulation with segmental spinal facilitation that is mediated through autonomic efferent nerves. This is a description of which of the following?

Ans: Somatic input → autonomic efferents → visceral symptom → somatovisceral

Why: The trigger is somatic and the result is a visceral symptom (indigestion), so this is a somatovisceral reflex. Name the reflex by origin first, then target.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

D is the reverse direction (organ drives the somatic findings). B and E stay within one system. Central facilitation is a spinal cord process, not a named reflex arc. Review deck example of a somatovisceral reflex: tissue injury in the T1-T5 muscles worsening COPD.

594asked 2×PANs & reflexes

Nociception is mostly carried by:

Ans: Pain is sensory → afferent → PANs run with sympathetic fibers

Why: Pain is sensory, so it travels in afferents. Visceral nociceptive afferents (PANs) run along the sympathetic fibers back to the dorsal horn.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

B and D are efferents, which carry motor output, not sensation. A is tempting because the vagus is largely afferent, but most visceral pain travels with the sympathetics. This is why visceral pain and viscerosomatic findings map onto the sympathetic levels T1-L2.

595asked 3×PANs & reflexes

Visceral afferents contain naked nerve endings known as PANs (peripheral afferent nociceptors). How do they respond to thermal, mechanical and chemical stimuli?

Ans: PANs sense thermal, mechanical, chemical damage → via inflammatory mediators

Why: PANs respond to three forms of potentially damaging stimuli (thermal, mechanical, chemical) through inflammatory mediators.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A is too vague. B is unrelated. D is a downstream result of PAN activity, not how PANs sense the stimulus. When activated, PANs release substance P, somatostatin, and CGRP, which is called neurogenic inflammation.

596asked 5×2026PANs & reflexes

Which of the following is NOT a feature of PANs?

Explanation & sources

Explanation

B is true: PANs respond to thermal, mechanical, and chemical stimuli. C is true: activated PANs release substance P, somatostatin, and CGRP (neurogenic inflammation). D is true: PAN hyperactivity triggers spinal facilitation in the dorsal horn.

597asked 9×2026PANs & reflexes

Where do visceral afferents (PANs) synapse?

Ans: Afferent → passes through DRG (cell body) → synapses in dorsal horn

Why: PANs travel with the sympathetic fibers, pass through the dorsal root ganglion, and synapse in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, connecting with the interneuron pool.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

B holds the PAN cell body; nothing synapses there. C and D are where sympathetic efferents synapse, not afferents. E holds the sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies (efferent side). PANs end mainly in laminae I and II of the dorsal horn.

598PANs & reflexes

What are viscerosomatic reflexes?

AnswerVisceral irritation (inflammation) is carried by PANs along sympathetic fibers to the dorsal horn. The segment becomes facilitated, and increased sympathetic and motor outflow produce palpable TART changes in segmentally related somatic tissue.

Ans: Organ irritation → PANs → dorsal horn → facilitation → paraspinal TART

Why: A viscerosomatic reflex is a local afferent reflex from a viscus to the spinal cord that creates a segmental pattern of somatic findings. Activated PANs release substance P, somatostatin, and CGRP and become sensitized with repeated firing.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

The visceral problem is the initiating drive; the paraspinal findings are its reflection. OMT is adjunctive: it removes the somatic part of the nociceptive load and reduces sympathetic and motor outflow, but the organ still needs medical or surgical treatment.

Spinal facilitation

599Spinal facilitation

What is the basis of spinal facilitation?

Ans: Facilitated = hyperexcitable → lower threshold → less input fires it

Why: A facilitated segment has a lowered threshold, so less afferent input is needed to make it discharge.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A is the opposite. B reverses the time course: inflammatory mediators come first (acute), fibrosis comes later (chronic). D is wrong because facilitation comes from abnormal, increased afferent input (for example a strained or overstretched muscle or a sick organ), not normal input.

600Spinal facilitation

What is spinal facilitation?

Ans: Facilitation: sensitivity UP → threshold DOWN → pain UP

Why: Facilitation means increased sensitivity, a lower threshold for firing, and more pain (hyperalgesia and allodynia). All three must point the same way.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A, B, and C each pair the directions inconsistently. Strictly, sensitization of the PANs themselves is called peripheral sensitization, and spinal facilitation is the resulting sensitization of the dorsal horn neurons; D is still the only option with all directions correct.

601Spinal facilitation

What is the physiology behind spinal facilitation?

Ans: Substance P → glutamate channels OPEN → Ca2+ in → ↑ dynorphin → sensitized

Why: PANs release substance P in laminae I and II, which opens glutamate voltage-gated channels. Calcium flows in and dynorphin synthesis rises, sensitizing the dorsal horn cells.

Heads up: The TA key marks E. D (substance P release in the dorsal horn) is also a true step in the same cascade per the 2026 ANS lecture, so know the full sequence: substance P → glutamate channels open → Ca2+ influx → more dynorphin → facilitation.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A names the wrong ion (calcium, not sodium). B says closure instead of opening. C is backwards; dynorphin synthesis increases.

602Spinal facilitation

Which is true of spinal facilitation?

Ans: Lowered threshold → non-painful input felt as pain → allodynia

Why: Facilitated circuits fire so easily that non-noxious stimuli are felt as painful (allodynia) and noxious stimuli hurt more (hyperalgesia).

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A is the opposite; it causes hyperalgesia. C is backwards; less input is needed. D is wrong because the altered ventral horn and sympathetic outflow produce muscle tone, motion, vasomotor, and sudomotor changes, which are the TART findings.

603asked 2×Spinal facilitation

All of the following are true concerning a facilitated segment EXCEPT:

Ans: Facilitated = LOW threshold → 'high threshold' is the false one

Why: A facilitated segment has a low threshold of excitation, so E is false.

Explanation & sources

Explanation

A and C are the core features: less input needed and increased output. D is true: sustained afferent input (from a sick organ or somatic dysfunction) starts it. B is true: once established, even normal activity can keep the segment facilitated, which is why the findings persist.

604asked 6×2026Spinal facilitation

A facilitated segment will result in:

Ans: Facilitated thoracolumbar segment → ↑ lateral horn outflow → ↑ sympathetic tone

Why: Facilitation in the thoracic and upper lumbar cord increases outflow from the lateral horn, producing sympathicotonia (increased sympathetic tone).

A is not a stated effect; the thoracolumbar cord has no parasympathetic outflow. Since A, C, and D are false, E is out.

Facilitation in the thoracic and upper lumbar segments of the spinal cord results in:
